boundary_note: Bounded first pass for Bodart's Breslau entry (siege and capture, 6 December 1806 to 6 January 1807) in cohort v1's fourth-coalition 1806 group: the Prussian garrison of the fortress under its governor, Lieutenant General Thile, and the Silesian corps of Bavarian and Württemberg troops with French generals before it under Prince Jérôme, from the second investment, begun on 6 December, through the siege works, the bombardments and summonses, the failed storm of 23 December and the armistice of 26 December, to the capitulation (signed on 3 January by Foucart, on 5 January by Höpfner) and the garrison's march-out on 7 January (Höpfner). The first investment by side A's cavalry in mid-November, the King's order of 22 November, the corps' formation at the start of operations and the French covering detachments are context. The Prussian relief attempts under the Prince of Anhalt-Pless, among them the combat of Strehlen and the advance of 30 December, and the French operations against them are outside this entry. Draft claims do not alter model inputs.

claims.value: Bodart gives side A as the French, Bavarians and Württembergers, together 27,000 men with 52 field and siege guns, under Prince Jérôme Bonaparte, and side B (Prussian) as the garrison of 6,000 men with 272 guns under Lieutenant General v. Thiele, which side A compelled to surrender the place; the garrison was allowed to march out with all military honours but had to lay down its arms and fell into captivity as prisoners of war, and the officers, 135, were set free on their word of honour not to serve again in this war against France or its allies. By his stated rule his figures are the forces available for the engagement, rounded up.
claims.rationale: Bodart's printed entry, read from the page image in the frame transcription; one claim among several. Höpfner gives the garrison's returns (claim side-b-strength), the Emperor's letter of 3 December another view of it (claim side-b-strength-other), and Höpfner, Jérôme's letter and the Emperor's letters side A's troops (claim side-a-strength). Bodart's 6,000 men are Höpfner's reckoning of 6000 at the beginning of the second investment, and his 135 officers are the officers of Höpfner's return of 1 January, while Höpfner has 116 officers and 5270 non-commissioned officers and men march out (claim side-b-losses) (our comparison). His 272 guns are not a figure in the passages read: Höpfner has 208 pieces on the walls and 46 in reserve or unusable, which make 254, and 240 guns handed over (our arithmetic and comparison). No passage read gives side A 27,000 men or 52 guns: by the assurance of Jérôme's adjutant on 18 December the siege corps was to reach 22,000 with Deroy's division, and the Emperor reckoned Jérôme's corps on 7 January at more than 30,000 with two units arriving (our comparison). His dates, 6 December 1806 to 6 January 1807, are the day Höpfner has side A's cavalry appear before Breslau for the second time and the evening he has the Nikolai and Oder gates handed over to side A; Foucart has the capitulation signed on 3 January and Höpfner on 5 January (claims posture and capitulation; our comparison). Which source Bodart used was not checked. English rendering (ours) of Bodart's rules: p. 46, 'the strengths given are always those forces that were disposable for the battle'; p. 47, 'the strength and loss figures were rounded up by the author'. English rendering (ours) of the heading and entry: '1806 6/12 to 1807 6/1. Siege and capture of Breslau'; 'the French, Bavarians and Württembergers (together 27,000 men with 52 field and siege guns) under Prince Jerôme Bonaparte compel the Prussian garrison (6,000 men with 272 guns) under Lieutenant General v. Thiele to surrender the place'; 'the garrison was allowed to march out with all military honours, but had to lay down its arms and fell into captivity as prisoners of war'; 'the officers (135) were set free against an undertaking on their word of honour not to serve again in this war against France or its allies'.

citations.quote: 1806 6./12. bis 1807 6./1. BELAGERUNG und EINNAHME von Breslau

Die Franzosen, Bayern und Württemberger (zus. 27.000 M. mit 52 Feld- und Belagerungsgeschützen) unter Pz. Jerôme Bonaparte nötigen die preußische Besatzung (6.000 M. mit 272 Geschützen) unter Gen.-Lt. v. Thiele zur Übergabe des Platzes.
Die Garnison durfte mit allen militärischen Ehren ausmarschieren, mußte jedoch die Waffen niederlegen und geriet in Kriegsgefangenschaft.
Die Offiziere (135) wurden gegen ehrenwörtliche Verpflichtung, in diesem Kriege nicht mehr gegen Frankreich oder dessen Bundesgenossen zu dienen, auf freien Fuß gesetzt.

claims.value: Side B (Prussian) in Höpfner: at the beginning of the arming works the garrison consisted of the infantry regiment Thile, the 3rd musketeer battalions von Hohenlohe and Treuenfels and the fusilier depot Greifenberg, 68 officers and 3046 men; men of several cavalry depots, 4 officers and 118 men; and artillery, 24 officers and 690 men; together 96 officers and 3854 men. Reinforced by men returning from leave, Ranzionirte, Jäger called in and several invalid companies, on 1 January it still counted infantry, 89 officers and 3909 men; Jäger, 1 and 74; invalids, 10 and 363; artillery, 26 and 854; cavalry, 9 and 641, with 240 horses; together 135 officers, 5841 men and 240 horses; so that, counting the loss in dead, wounded and deserters, the garrison at the beginning of the second investment may be reckoned at 6000 men. Assuming that only part of the invalids was fit for duty on the walls, that about 400 men served as helpers to the artillery and in the laboratories and that about 450 lay in hospital, Höpfner regards only 5000 men as real defenders of the walls, while the arming plan of 1805 required 10,320 men to garrison all the works; and the men of the regiment Thile, mostly Poles, could not be particularly counted on. The government had about 2000 recruits who had come back from the march to Graudenz removed from the town instead of enrolling them, by its statement because it saw no means of arming them. On the walls stood 208 pieces of various calibres, with 46 guns partly in reserve and partly unusable in the arsenal.
claims.rationale: Side B's history, read from the page images of pp. 48-50; the tables' figures were checked on full-resolution crops. The garrison and its guns were in Breslau before the second investment, so the claim is tagged inherited; the return of 1 January, from which Höpfner reckons the strength at the investment, is kept with it. The rows of both tables make their printed totals (our arithmetic). Höpfner names no source for the tables; his 6000 is a reckoning and his 5000 an estimate. 'Ranzionirte' is read as soldiers who had got away from the enemy and rejoined (our reading). The garrison's losses, desertion and the numbers that marched out are in claim side-b-losses. English renderings (ours): 'at the beginning of the arming works the garrison consisted of: the infantry regiment Thile, the 3rd musketeer battalion von Hohenlohe, the 3rd musketeer battalion Treuenfels and the fusilier depot Greifenberg, 68 officers, 3046 men; men of several cavalry depots, 4 officers, 118 men; artillery, 24 officers, 690 men; together 96 officers, 3854 men'; 'it was so reinforced by men of the regiment Thile and of the artillery returning from leave, by Ranzionirte, Jäger called in and several invalid companies, that on 1 January it still consisted of: infantry, 89 officers, 3909 men; Jäger, 1 officer, 74 men; invalids, 10 officers, 363 men; artillery, 26 officers, 854 men; cavalry, 9 officers, 641 men, 240 horses; together 135 officers, 5841 men, 240 horses'; 'so that, counting in the loss in dead, wounded and deserters, the garrison at the beginning of the second investment may be reckoned at 6000 men'; 'but if one assumes that of the invalids only a part was fit for duty on the walls, that about 400 men were taken away as helpers to the artillery, for service in the laboratories, etc., and that about 450 men lay in the hospitals, one can regard only 5000 men as real defenders of the walls, whereas by the arming plan of 1805, 10,320 men were needed to provide all the works with a suitable garrison. On' (the sentence continues on p. 50); 'the men of the regiment Thile, who for the mass were Poles, there was no particular counting' (the end of the sentence begun on p. 49: on the men of the regiment Thile, mostly Poles, one could not particularly count); 'if the government had about 2000 of the recruits who had been sent off to Graudenz but had come back because of the Polish insurrection removed from the town, instead of enrolling them at once to reinforce the garrison, this was done, by its statement, because it saw no possibility of arming them'; 'of ordnance, 208 pieces of various calibres were distributed on the walls, and 46 guns were partly in reserve, partly unusable in the arsenal'.

claims.value: Side B (Prussian), other evidence: the Emperor wrote to Prince Jérôme from Posen on 3 December that it appeared from intercepted letters that Breslau had only a fifth of the garrison necessary for the defence of the place, and that the general commanding there declared that he would be obliged to surrender if he were blockaded for several days in succession by infantry; a hundred or so bombs thrown into the town would force it to surrender.
claims.rationale: The Emperor's letter, read from the page image. The intercepted letters were not seen, and the letter gives neither the garrison's number nor the garrison it took as necessary; it stands beside Höpfner's 5000 real defenders against the 10,320 men required by the arming plan of 1805 (claim side-b-strength) and is not reconciled with it (our comparison). The garrison was in Breslau before the investment, so the claim is tagged inherited. The letter as side A's information is in claim side-a-information. English renderings (ours): 'the Emperor to Prince Jérôme. Posen, 3 December 1806'; 'it appears from intercepted letters that Breslau has only a fifth of the garrison necessary for the defence of the place, and that the general commanding there declares that he will be obliged to surrender if he is blockaded for several days in succession by infantry. A hundred or so bombs thrown into this large and beautiful town will force it to surrender'.

claims.value: Side A (the Silesian corps of Bavarian and Württemberg troops under Prince Jérôme, with French generals, sappers and artillerymen). Höpfner's formation of the corps at the beginning of operations: the first Bavarian division, Lieutenant General Deroy, 8185 men; the second, Lieutenant General Wrede, 5830 men, together 14,015 Bavarians; the Württemberg division, Lieutenant General Seckendorf, 8642 men; the corps 29½ battalions, 26 squadrons and 48 guns, or 17,650 men of infantry, 3241 of cavalry and 1055 of artillery, or 22,946 men; the 6th and 14th Line Infantry Regiments, the 5th light battalion La Motte and apparently several batteries arrived only later. For Breslau the Emperor wrote on 3 December that Jérôme was to go there with Wrede's division and Vandamme with the Württembergers, Deroy's division staying where it was with half the cavalry, and the major general that Vandamme was to leave 1,000 men at Glogau. Höpfner: Montbrun set out with the Württemberg cavalry on 4 December and Vandamme followed with the Württemberg infantry, and Jérôme left Kalisch on the 5th with Wrede's division and Lefebvre's cavalry, Deroy's division and Mezzanelli's cavalry brigade staying at Kalisch; Vandamme reached Lissa on the 6th with the advance guard of the Württemberg infantry; on 9 December the Bavarian infantry crossed to the left bank at Kosel, the two light battalions and Lefebvre's cavalry brigade with 4 12-pounders and 6 field howitzers staying on the right bank. Foucart: Montbrun formed the investment on the left bank on the 7th with the 1st and 2nd regiments of chevau-légers and the chasseurs à pied, and Vandamme arrived before Breslau on the 8th; Jérôme wrote on 8 December that the 2nd division, 4,700 men strong, would be before Breslau on the right bank that evening. Höpfner: on 13 December 2 companies of French sappers and miners of 66 men each arrived, and on the 17th the artillery was reinforced by 1½ companies of French. In the middle of December the Württembergers, supported by Wrede's division, most of the sappers, miners and artillery and part of Montbrun's cavalry brigade were employed in the siege on the left bank, with 2 squadrons and half a light battalion at Gnichwitz and 1 squadron at Neumarkt; the two battalions of Württemberg Jäger and Lefebvre's brigade were on the right bank; and Deroy's division and Mezzanelli's brigade were at Polnisch Wartenberg, 2 days' marches away, until Jérôme called them up on the 16th, the besieging troops already suffering exceedingly from the bad season and their comparatively small strength. By the assurance of Jérôme's adjutant on 18 December, Deroy's division, 10,000 men strong, was to arrive that day and bring the siege corps to 22,000 men; the division arrived and took post partly on the left bank and partly on the right. Foucart has Deroy's division only then arriving on the right bank, and 2 infantry regiments and 2 light infantry battalions of Minucci's division crossing to the left bank, when Jérôme left on the 20th. By the disposition for the storm (claim side-a-command), it was to be made by a column of 2 Württemberg battalions, General Minucci at the head of 3 Bavarian infantry regiments followed by the Württemberg infantry, 2 Bavarian companies, a detachment of 150 Bavarian volunteers and another detachment. After the capitulation General Minucci remained in Breslau with 9 battalions, 1 squadron and some batteries. The Emperor wrote on 7 January that Jérôme's corps must now be more than 30,000 men strong, with the arrival of the 5th light infantry battalion and the 14th Bavarian infantry regiment. No passage read gives a return of side A at the capitulation.
claims.rationale: Höpfner, the French letters and Foucart's narrative, read from the page images; the figures were checked on full-resolution crops. The troops before Breslau changed with the Emperor's and Jérôme's orders, so the phase is left unresolved. Höpfner's formation table, of the beginning of operations, was read for the Glogau entry; as recorded there, his corps figures make 21,946, not the printed 22,946, his three division totals make 22,657, and the rows of the second Bavarian division and of the Württemberg division make 7018 and 8652, not the printed 5830 and 8642 (our arithmetic). Jérôme's 2nd division is read as Wrede's, which Höpfner has marching with him from Kalisch (our reading); its 4,700 compare with Wrede's printed 5830 at the beginning of operations, and the adjutant's 10,000 for Deroy's division with its 8185 (our comparison). The adjutant's 22,000 is an assurance given to the enemy, and the Emperor's 'more than 30,000', which counts two units still arriving, a reckoning from Warsaw; neither is a return (our reading). Höpfner has Vandamme reach Lissa with the advance guard on the 6th and Deroy's division arrive about the 18th, Foucart has Vandamme arrive before Breslau on the 8th and Deroy's division only on the 20th (our comparison). The 1,000 men to be left at Glogau and the troops named for the storm are an order and a disposition, not counts. Bodart's 27,000 with 52 guns are in claim bodart-strength; no passage read totals side A's guns before Breslau, and the guns Höpfner names in the batteries are in claim means-and-supply. English renderings (ours): 'First Bavarian Division. Lieutenant General Deroy'; '[total] 8185 men' (the division's total, at the foot of its table); 'Second Bavarian Division. Lieutenant General Wrede'; '[total] 5830 men. Together 14,015 men Bavarians.1)' (the second division's total and the two divisions' sum, at the foot of the table continued from p. 15); 'Württemberg Division. Lieutenant General Seckendorf'; 'together 8642 men Württembergers'; 'the Silesian corps thus consisted at the time of 29½ battalions, 26 squadrons and 48 guns, or 17,650 men' (the sentence continues on p. 17); 'infantry, 3241 men cavalry and 1055 men artillery, or 22,946 men' (the end of the sentence begun on p. 16); '1) there arrived only later the 6th and 14th Line Infantry Regiments and the 5th light battalion La Motte and, as it seems, also several batteries'; 'the Emperor to Prince Jérôme. Posen, 3 December 1806'; 'I wish you to have the honour of taking it in person. You will receive through the staff the order to go there with Wrede's division. General Vandamme, with the Württembergers, is going there for his part. The mortars will follow. The major general is sending you instructions on the conduct of the siege. I do not doubt that in four days it will fall into your hands. Deroy's division stays where it is, with half the cavalry'; 'the major general to Prince Jérôme. Posen, 3 December 1806'; '(the major general informs the prince of the Emperor's instructions)' (Foucart's summary); '.... General Vandamme is to leave 1,000 men at Glogau'; 'as early as 4 December, after the garrison of Glogau had laid down its arms, General Montbrun set out with the Württemberg cavalry; General Vandamme followed with the Württemberg infantry on the left bank of the Oder against Breslau, and on 5 December Jerome set out from Kalisch with the division Wrede and General Lefebvre's cavalry, likewise to move before Breslau. At Kalisch there remained only the division Deroy and the cavalry brigade Mezzanelli, from which the 1st Chevauxlegers Regiment Kronprinz marched off to the great French army.1)'; 'General Vandamme still reached Lissa on the 6th with the advance guard of the Württemberg infantry'; 'on 9 December the Bavarian infantry that had arrived crossed to the left bank of the Oder at Kosel; only the two light battalions and the cavalry brigade Lefebvre, with 4 12-pounders and 6 field howitzers, remained behind on the right bank. Jerome moved his headquarters to Lissa'; 'the next day, the 7th, the general formed the investment of Breslau on the left bank; he placed the 2nd regiment of chevau-légers at Gross-Möchbern, the chasseurs à pied at Neukirch and Höflchen (headquarters), the 1st of chevau-légers, 2 squadrons at Klein-Möchbern and the two others at Kleinburg, with a reconnaissance of 25 horse toward Schweibnitz and a post of the same strength at Roth-Kretschen'; 'General Vandamme, having left Glogau on the 5th, arrived before Breslau on the 8th. The detachment at Gnichwitz having been attacked in the night of the 7th to the 8th and forced to fall back, General Montbrun sent 2 squadrons and half a battalion of light infantry to that point, and himself moved his quarters to Kriethern to watch the Schweibnitz road better'; 'Prince Jérôme to General Vandamme. Oëls, 8 December 1806'; '(he arrived at Oëls on the 7th and will be at Hundsfeld on the 8th at midday)' (Foucart's summary); 'this evening the 2nd division, 4,700 men strong, will be before Breslau on the right bank. I mean to attack only tomorrow'; 'on 13 December 2 companies of French sappers and miners, of 66 men each, arrived, and were used at once to dig cuts into the Nikolai suburb and to the right of the churchyard there, and to build batteries in the second parallels'; 'accordingly the corps employed in Silesia had in the middle of December the following positions: headquarters at Lissa; the Württembergers, supported by the division Wrede, the greater part of the sappers, miners and artillery, the last reinforced on the 17th by 1½ companies of French, and a part of the cavalry brigade Montbrun on the left bank of the Oder, employed directly in the siege. At Gnichwitz on the Schwarzwasser, halfway to Schweidnitz, 2 squadrons and ½ a light battalion, to watch the roads from Schweidnitz to Breslau and to Glogau. At Neumarkt 1 squadron. A part of the cavalry brigade Montbrun roaming in the neighbourhood of Breslau. On the right bank of the Oder the two battalions of Württemberg Jäger, behind them the cavalry brigade Lefebvre; at Polnisch Wartenberg, 7 Meilen (German miles) from Breslau, the division Deroy and the cavalry brigade Mezzanelli, thus 2 days' marches away'; 'when Jerome now received from all sides the news that the Prince of Anhalt-Pless was assembling in Upper Silesia a force of 15-16,000 men to relieve Breslau as soon as possible, that line troops were being drawn for it from all the fortified places to form the core of a force that was to be reinforced by recruits and volunteers called to the colours by a proclamation of the aide-de-camp Count Götzen, and when he further learned that the garrison of Schweidnitz was said to have been reinforced by 3000 recruits, so that it now counted 6000 men of infantry and 400 horse, he had, in view of the obstinacy of the governor of Breslau, the troops available at Polnisch Wartenberg ordered up on the 16th, so as to be equal to every possible event. The besieging troops were already suffering exceedingly from the bad season and their comparatively small strength'; 'on 18 December Captain Ducaudras, Jerome's adjutant, presented himself and demanded the release of all the Prussian officers who were prisoners of war released on their word of honour and were staying in Breslau without' (the sentence continues on p. 60); 'taking part in the defence. By the adjutant's assurance the Bavarian division Deroy, 10,000 men strong, was to arrive on that day and reinforce the siege corps to 22,000 men. Indeed considerable movements in the enemy's positions were observed soon afterwards' (the first words end the sentence begun on p. 59); 'the division had arrived, and the siege corps now took the following positions: General Vandamme on the left bank of the Oder, with the Württembergers on the right wing, the division Wrede in the centre and part of the division Deroy on the left wing at Pöpelwitz on the Oder, from where these last troops occupied the parallels on the Oder; further General Deroy on the right bank with the rest of his infantry, of which 3 companies of the light battalion Taxis were detached to Steinersdorf - south-east of Breslau - toward Brieg, and the cavalry brigade Mezzanelli, which was to reconnoitre the neighbourhood and especially watch Brieg, where the Prince of Anhalt-Pless was believed to be assembling the relief corps; further the cavalry brigade Lefebvre, reinforced by the light battalion Zoller, in front of Lissa toward Neumarkt, to cover headquarters and secure the transports from the lower part of Silesia; finally the cavalry brigade Montbrun in front of Krietern, which in connection with the brigade Lefebvre was to watch all the roads to Breslau on the left bank of the Oder by pickets and patrols pushed forward, so as to be able to report the approach of the relief troops early. The dragoon regiment Taxis had been detached to Liegnitz'; 'the prince left Lissa on the 20th with General Lefebvre and the 2nd regiment of Bavarian chevau-légers. Deroy's division was only then arriving on the right bank before Breslau, and 2 infantry regiments and 2 battalions of light infantry of Minucci's division were crossing to the left bank'; 'the disposition for the attack laid down the following: a column of 2 Württemberg battalions was to climb the unrevetted walls on the bridges to be thrown, advance against the Ohlau gate, seize it, and make the entry into the town easier for General Minucci at the head of 3 Bavarian infantry regiments, followed by the Württemberg infantry. 2 Bavarian companies were at the same time to attack the tambour before the bridge of the outer ditch at the Ohlau gate; finally a detachment of 150 Bavarian volunteers was to advance along the Ohlau and another against the Schweidnitz gate, and all the batteries were to keep up their fire briskly, to divide the attention of the besieged during the storm'; 'the besiegers, at their head Jerome, who had arrived again, filed through Breslau and marched out again by the Schweidnitz gate. General Minucci remained behind in Breslau with 9 battalions, 1 squadron and some batteries'; 'the Emperor to the major general. Warsaw, 7 January 1807'; 'Prince Jérôme's corps must now be more than 30,000 men strong, with the arrival of the 5th light infantry battalion and of the 14th Bavarian infantry regiment'.

citations.quote: Demgemäß hatte das in Schlesien verwandte Korps Mitte Dezembers folgende Aufstellung: Hauptquartier in Lissa; die Württemberger, unterstützt durch die Division Wrede, der größere Theil der Sapeurs, Mineurs und Artillerie, welche letztere am 17. noch durch 1½ Kompagnien Franzosen verstärkt wurde, und ein Theil der Kavallerie-Brigade Montbrun auf dem linken Oder-Ufer, unmittelbar zur Belagerung verwandt. In Gnichwitz am Schwarzwasser, auf dem halben Wege nach Schweidnitz, 2 Schwadronen und ½ leichtes Bataillon, zur Beobachtung der Straßen von Schweidnitz nach Breslau und nach Glogau. In Neumarkt 1 Schwadron. Ein Theil der Kavallerie-Brigade Montbrun in der Umgegend von Breslau streifend. Auf dem rechten Oder-Ufer die beiden Bataillone württembergischer Jäger, dahinter die Kavallerie-Brigade Lefebvre; bei Poln. Wartenberg, 7 Meilen von Breslau, die Division Deroy und die Kavallerie-Brigade Mezzanelli, also 2 Tagemärsche entfernt.

citations.locator: Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 4 (1851), p. 59 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: Als nun Jerome von allen Seiten die Nachricht erhielt, daß der Fürst von Anhalt Pleß in Oberschlesien eine Macht von 15—16,000 Mann versammele, um so bald als möglich Breslau zu entsetzen, daß hierzu aus allen festen Plätzen Linientruppen herangezogen würden, um den Kern einer Macht zu bilden, die mittelst Rekruten und Freiwilliger, durch eine Proklamation des Flügel-Adjutanten Grafen Götzen zu den Fahnen gerufen, verstärkt werden sollte, als er ferner erfuhr, daß die Garnison von Schweidnitz durch 3000 Rekruten verstärkt sein solle, so daß sie nunmehr 6000 Mann Infanterie und 400 Reiter zähle, ließ er, in Betracht der Hartnäckigkeit des Gouverneurs von Breslau, am 16. die bei Poln. Wartenberg zur Disposition stehenden Truppen herbeibeordern, um allen möglichen Ereignissen gewachsen zu sein. Die Belagerungstruppen litten bei der üblen Jahreszeit und der verhältnißmäßig geringen Stärke bereits ungemein.

citations.locator: Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 4 (1851), p. 60 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: Die Division war eingetroffen, und das Belagerungskorps erhielt nunmehr folgende Aufstellung: der General Vandamme auf dem linken Oder-Ufer, mit den Württembergern auf dem rechten Flügel, der Division Wrede in der Mitte und einem Theil der Division Deroy auf dem linken Flügel bei Pöpelwitz an der Oder, von wo letztere Truppen die Parallelen an der Oder besetzten; ferner der General Deroy auf dem rechten Ufer mit dem Rest seiner Infänterie, von der 3 Kompagnien des leichten Bataillons Taxis nach Steinersdorf — s. ö. von Breslau — gegen Brieg detaschirt wurden, und der Kavallerie-Brigade Mezzanelli, welche die Umgegend aufklären und besonders Brieg beobachten sollte, wo man den Fürsten von Anhalt Pleß in der Versammlung des Entsatzkorps begriffen glaubte; weiter die Kavallerie-Brigade Lefebvre, verstärkt durch das leichte Bataillon Zoller, vorwärts von Lissa gegen Neumarkt zur Deckung des Hauptquartiers und zur Sicherung der Transporte aus dem unteren Theile von Schlesien; endlich die Kavallerie-Brigade Montbrun vorwärts von Krietern, welche, in Verbindung mit der Brigade Lefebvre, alle Straßen nach Breslau auf dem linken Oder-Ufer durch vorgeschobene Pikets und Patrouillen beobachten sollte, um frühzeitig von der Annäherung der Entsatztruppen unterrichten zu können. Das Dragoner-Regiment Taxis war nach Liegnitz detaschirt worden.

citations.quote: Die Disposition zum Angriff bestimmte Folgendes: Eine Kolonne von 2 württembergischen Bataillonen sollte auf den zu schlagenden Brücken die nicht bekleideten Wälle ersteigen, gegen das Ohlauer-Thor vordringen, sich desselben bemächtigen, und dem General Minucci, an der Spitze von 3 bayerschen Infanterie-Regimentern, gefolgt von der württembergischen Infanterie, das Eindringen in die Stadt erleichtern. 2 bayersche Kompagnien sollten gleichzeitig den Tambour vor der Brücke des Vorgrabens am Ohlauer-Thor angreifen; ein Detaschement von 150 bayerschen Freiwilligen endlich längs der Ohlau, ein anderes gegen das Schweidnitzer-Thor vordringen, und alle Batterien ihr Feuer lebhaft unterhalten, um die Aufmerksamkeit der Belagerten während des Sturmes zu theilen.

claims.value: Bodart names Prince Jérôme Bonaparte as side A's commander and Lieutenant General v. Thiele as side B's. Höpfner: the governor of Breslau was Lieutenant General Thile, the commandant Major General Kraft and the engineer officer of the place Lieutenant Poblotzky, while General Lindener, engineer general and brigadier of the Silesian fortresses, who had let himself be enclosed on 6 December despite Count Götzen's instruction to leave Breslau, gained a weighty voice in the arrangements for the defence. The Emperor wrote on 3 December that he wished Jérôme to have the honour of taking Breslau in person, and the major general that Jérôme would take command of the siege. On 17 December the Emperor told the major general to send Jérôme the order to leave the command of the siege to General Vandamme and to reach Warsaw with all speed; Jérôme left on the 20th. Höpfner says that, so as not to leave Vandamme the supreme command in Silesia, Jérôme continued to regard himself as commander of the Silesian corps and gave the conduct of business to the chief of the general staff, General of Division Hédouville, a measure he holds the more justified as the troops of the Confederation of the Rhine, especially the Bavarians, had given continual cause for complaints of indiscipline, levying contributions and ill-treating the inhabitants, in the higher ranks too; and that Vandamme's new batteries and his bombardment and summons of 25 December were undertaken without Hédouville's knowledge. Vandamme's general staff officer, Colonel Duveyrier, carried the summons of 25 December and the negotiations that ended in the capitulation, signed on 5 January by Höpfner. Jérôme came back for the end: Höpfner has the besiegers, Jérôme at their head, file through Breslau after the garrison marched out, and Foucart has him arrive at Lissa on the 6th to see the garrison file past him on the 8th.
claims.rationale: Bodart's printed commanders, read from the frame transcription, with Höpfner, the Emperor's and the major general's letters and Foucart's narrative, read from the page images. Side A's command passed during the siege, on the Emperor's order, from Jérôme in person to others, while side B's commanders were in post before the investment; one claim carries one phase, so it is unresolved. Bodart's Thiele is Höpfner's governor Thile (our comparison); Höpfner prints the commandant's name 'Kraft' on p. 51 and 'Krafft' on pp. 87 and 110 (claim side-b-command). Bodart's Jérôme commanded before Breslau until 20 December; by the Emperor's letter of 17 December the command of the siege was then to pass to Vandamme, while by Höpfner the conduct of business passed to Hédouville and Vandamme acted on his own; the order and Höpfner's account may concern different commands, of the siege and of the corps, and who commanded from the 20th is left open (our comparison and reading). The capitulation's text, which would show who signed it, was not seen. The credit is not assigned here to any one commander. English renderings (ours): Bodart, as in claim bodart-strength; 'governor of Breslau was Lieutenant General Thile, a generally respected, strict and brave officer,' (the sentence continues on p. 51); 'commandant Major General Kraft, engineer officer of the place Lieutenant Poblotzky. From a government so composed a capable defence could be expected despite the unfavourable circumstances, but unfortunately General Lindener, who despite Count Götzen's instruction to leave Breslau had nevertheless let himself be enclosed on 6 December, gained as engineer general and brigadier of the Silesian fortresses a weighty voice in the arrangements for the defence and a sure influence on the government's views of the tenability of the place' (the end of the sentence begun on p. 50); 'the Emperor to Prince Jérôme. Posen, 3 December 1806'; 'I wish you to have the honour of taking it in person. You will receive through the staff the order to go there with Wrede's division. General Vandamme, with the Württembergers, is going there for his part. The mortars will follow. The major general is sending you instructions on the conduct of the siege. I do not doubt that in four days it will fall into your hands. Deroy's division stays where it is, with half the cavalry'; 'the major general to Prince Jérôme. Posen, 3 December 1806'; '(the major general informs the prince of the Emperor's instructions)' (Foucart's summary); '.... you will have a bridge thrown over the Oder to establish your communications with General Vandamme; you will take command of the siege...'; 'the Emperor to the major general. Kutno, 17 December 1806'; 'send a Pole to the camp before Breslau with the order to Prince Jérôme to leave the command of the siege to General Vandamme and to set out in person with all speed, so as to reach Warsaw on the 21st or 22nd. He will order General Deroy to march with his division from Wartenberg, where it must be, on Lowicz'; 'on the 20th Jerome left the troops before Breslau to go to the great army in Poland, whither Napoleon had called him on his repeated request. So as not to leave General Vandamme, with all recognition of his brilliant military qualities, the supreme command in Silesia, a province in which Napoleon had most strictly ordered the maintenance of order, Jerome continued to regard himself as commander of the Silesian corps and gave the conduct of business to the chief of the general staff, General of Division Hédouville'; 'this measure was all the more justified as the troops of the Confederation of the Rhine, but especially the Bavarians, had since entering Prussian soil continually given cause for complaints of a lack of discipline, of a taste for levying contributions under threat of fire, of ill-treatment of the inhabitants, etc., complaints that did not concern the common man only but were well founded in the higher ranks too.1)'; 'on General Minucci's return, General Vandamme, who had ordered the building of 4 new batteries in order to bring into them a further 8 24-pounders, 6 12-pounders and 2 mortars that were arriving from Glogau, believed he must set the town seriously on fire and inform the governor of the defeat of the relief troops and of the means he possessed to destroy the town. He expected that a population of 60,000 inhabitants would not be sacrificed to the holding of works that owed their preservation only to the mild weather. All this was done without the knowledge of General Hédouville, although this general, as mentioned, was to continue the command in Jerome's name'; 'the bombardment was therefore, on the 25th after 1 o'clock, o-' (the sentence continues on p. 80: 'opened again'); 'pened again and lasted until 3 o'clock. At that time Colonel Duveyrier, general staff officer of General Vandamme, appeared with the summons to surrender, with the most boastful statements about the advantages won against the Prince of Pless as well as in Poland and Prussia. The governor gave a refusal' (the first words end the sentence begun on p. 79); 'at 4 in the afternoon Colonel Duveyrier came, empowered to negotiate the surrender. The bombardment still went on even now. The governor could no more obtain the armistice of 8 days he asked for, to give the Prince of Pless time for a new attempt at relief, than the dispatch of an officer to Kalisch, by whom he wished to make sure whether Russians were approaching or not. Only for arranging the affairs of the town and the garrison were 3 days granted'; 'on 5 January Colonel Duveyrier appeared again, and the points of capitulation were signed by both sides, not without disputes, representations and counter-representations, after 6 o'clock'; 'the besiegers, at their head Jerome, who had arrived again, filed through Breslau and marched out again by the Schweidnitz gate. General Minucci remained behind in Breslau with 9 battalions, 1 squadron and some batteries'; 'Prince Jérôme, having left Pultusk on 30 December, arrived at Lissa on the 6th to see the garrison of Breslau, 5,500 men strong, file past him on the 8th'.

citations.quote: Am 20. verließ Jerome die Truppen vor Breslau, um sich zur großen Armee nach Polen zu begeben, wohin ihn Napoleon auf mehrfaches Ansuchen berufen hatte. Um nicht dem General Vandamme, bei aller Anerkennung für dessen glänzende militärischen Eigenschaften, den Oberbefehl in Schlesien zu belassen, in welcher Provinz Napoleon die Aufrechthaltung der Ordnung auf das Strengste befohlen hatte, betrachtete sich Jerome auch weiterhin noch als den Kommandirenden des schlesischen Korps, und übertrug dem Chef des Generalstabes, Divisions-General Hédouville, die Leitung der Geschäfte.

citations.locator: Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 4 (1851), p. 61 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: Es war diese Maßregel um so mehr gerechtfertigt, als die Rheinbundstruppen, besonders aber die Bayern, seit dem Betreten des preußischen Bodens fortgesetzt zu Klagen über Mangel an Disziplin, über Lust zum Brandschatzen, Mißhandeln der Einwohner ꝛc. Veranlassung gegeben hatten, Klagen, die nicht nur den gemeinen Mann trafen, sondern auch in den höheren Stellen ihre Begründung fanden.¹)

citations.locator: Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 4 (1851), p. 79 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: Bei der Rückkehr des Generals Minucci glaubte der General Vandamme, der den Bau von 4 neuen Batterien befohlen hatte, um darin noch 8—24pfünder, 6—12pfünder und 2 Mörser, welche von Glogau anlangten, einzuführen, die Stadt ernsthaft in Brand setzen, und dem Gouverneur von der Niederlage der Entsatztruppen, so wie von den Mitteln Nachricht geben zu müssen, die er besaß, um die Stadt zu vernichten. Er erwartete, daß eine Bevölkerung von 60,000 Einwohnern nicht der Behauptung von Werken würde aufgeopfert werden, die ihre Erhaltung nur der gelinden Witterung verdankten. Das Alles geschah ohne Vorwissen des Generals Hédouville, obgleich dieser General, wie erwähnt, im Namen Jerome's den Befehl fortführen sollte.

Um diese Zeit erschien der Oberst Duveyrier, Generalstabs-Offizier des Generals Vandamme, mit der Aufforderung zur Uebergabe unter den prahlerischsten Angaben über die errungenen Vortheile gegen den Fürsten von Pleß, so wie in Polen und Preußen. claims.value: Höpfner: on 7 December Vandamme, with the artillery General Pernety and the engineer Colonel Blein, reconnoitred the place to determine the point of attack; the troops disposable for the siege being too weak to deploy on the upper Oder, they kept to the lower Oder and decided on two parallels and two mortar batteries right and left of the Nikolai suburb, chosen as the point of attack because Blein hoped to find an earthen batardeau there. The siege works began in the night to the 8th with few workers; batteries were built from the night to the 9th, guns were brought into them in the night to the 10th, and the bombardment of the front at the Nikolai gate and the Dom began on the 10th at 6 in the morning, the fire being directed more at the town than at the walls. After 1 o'clock Jérôme's adjutant, Captain Desterno, summoned the place, announcing the fall of Magdeburg, Stettin, Küstrin and Glogau and the French entry into Warsaw. The parallels were extended and second parallels begun from the night to the 12th; the fire was slow on the 12th while side A awaited munition and replacement guns from Glogau; French sappers and miners arriving on the 13th dug cuts and built batteries; an approach trench from the left second parallel struck an arm of the Oder in the night to the 14th; and the batteries were armed in the night to the 15th. On the 15th the bombardment lasted from 6 in the morning to 1 in the afternoon, and at 2 Jérôme had Lefebvre summon the fortress again, threatening to turn the town into a heap of ashes and saying that Napoleon had ordered the works razed after the capture; after the refusal the bombardment was renewed at 3. In the night to the 16th side A set fire to the woodpiles before the Ohlau gate, burning 24,000 Klafter of wood. It bombarded again from 5 in the evening of the 16th and on the 17th, when an adjutant of Jérôme's brought back the body of Lieutenant Lehsten; on the 20th from 4 to 9 in the morning, after 24-pounders and 2 heavy mortars had been brought in, the besiegers firing exclusively at the town; and on the 21st and 22nd. On the plan of Blein, who had reconnoitred the works on the left bank on 17, 18 and 19 December for want of a good plan of Breslau, and with Jérôme's approval, side A attempted a storm at the unrevetted wall near the Ohlau gate, where two very wide and deep water ditches had to be crossed: Blein had rafts built of ladders joined in pairs, to be held above the water by empty casks and covered with planks; on the 22nd the means of crossing were gathered by day behind Neudorf, opposite the Schweidnitz gate, to make the garrison expect an attack there; Hédouville, Vandamme, Pernety and Blein went to the Ohlau suburb at 11 at night, and the troops were posted at 4 in the morning of the 23rd, but the carriers asked for to carry the rafts had not come, the inexperienced sappers bound the rafts slowly, a drunken officer hindered them, and a shout and a sapper's leap into the water alerted an artilleryman on the Ohlau ravelin; under canister and musket fire the attackers retreated with considerable loss. Vandamme, who had ordered 4 new batteries to take a further 8 24-pounders, 6 12-pounders and 2 mortars arriving from Glogau, resolved on General Minucci's return to set the town seriously on fire and to tell the governor of the relief's defeat and of his means to destroy the town, expecting that a population of 60,000 would not be sacrificed to works that owed their preservation only to the mild weather, all without Hédouville's knowledge; the bombardment was resumed on the 25th and Duveyrier summoned the town. Vandamme refused an armistice but empowered Duveyrier to conclude a capitulation, and then granted an armistice until 8 in the morning of the 27th, during which side A continued its works and alarmed the Springstern. On 2 January Duveyrier and Captain Hammerer repeated all the reasons for surrender; on the 3rd side A answered the walls' fire with the most violent bombardment of the siege, and at 4 in the afternoon Duveyrier came empowered to negotiate the surrender while the bombardment went on; the governor obtained neither an armistice of 8 days nor leave to send an officer to Kalisch, and 3 days were granted only for arranging the affairs of the town and the garrison; on 5 January the points of capitulation were signed after 6. Höpfner judges the French siege works very irregular: the whole attack was directed at the town, a siege against the works being thought useless against the defender's superior artillery, and side A counted on frost robbing the fortress of its wet ditches.
claims.rationale: Höpfner, read from the page images. These were the steps of side A's commanders before Breslau, so the claim is tagged commander-created. Höpfner cites no document for the reconnaissances, the summonses or the negotiations; his account of the storm's planning gives details from the besieger's side without naming its source on these pages; he cites Blein's report to Napoleon on p. 112 (claim side-b-command) and Blein's confirmation on p. 118 (our reading). In his garrison-side account it became apparent at 6 in the morning that side A was trying to cross the outer ditch by two cask bridges at the ravelin R., which he places before the Ziegel gate, while his account of the attack has the first raft brought into the outer ditch at 5 near the Ohlau gate and an artilleryman on the Ohlau ravelin give the alarm; the two are not reconciled here, and Höpfner's Plan XVIII of Breslau, which would show where the works lay, was not inspected (our comparison). Foucart's narrative leaves the operations against the place aside by its own footnote (claim side-a-objectives). English renderings (ours): 'likewise on the 7th General Vandamme, accompanied by the artillery General Pernety and the engineer Colonel Blein, reconnoitred the place to determine the point of attack'; 'the troops disposable for the siege were too weak to deploy on the upper Oder, where they seemed too exposed to harassment by the Prussian parties from the other fortresses; they therefore restricted themselves for the time being to the ground on the lower Oder and meant to extend on the right up to the Ohlau suburb. The building of two parallels and two mortar batteries, right and left of the Nikolai suburb, was decided, and this suburb was chosen as the point of attack all the more because Colonel Blein hoped to find there an earthen batardeau that could ease the crossing of the ditch'; 'the siege works began as early as the night to the 8th, with so small a number of workers that they had to be limited to building two short parallels toward the projected batteries; one parallel was to rest on the left on the Oder, the other on the left on the Nikolai suburb'; 'in the night to the 9th the besieger began building the projected batteries, and a third battery was worked at in the prolongation of the street of the Nikolai suburb; on the right bank of the Oder too, at the Elbing and behind the Mönchswiese, gun positions were completed'; 'in the night to the 10th the enemy brought, on the left bank, 2 mortars and 3 howitzers into the battery right of the Nikolai suburb, 3 howitzers into the battery in the prolongation of the Nikolai suburb, 3 mortars, 1 siege howitzer and 3 field howitzers into the battery at the left parallel, and finally the 10 pieces named into the batteries on the right bank of the Oder'; 'on the 10th at 6 in the morning the enemy was able to begin the bombardment against the front at the Nikolai gate and the Dom; the enemy's shells did the burghers' hou-' (the word and sentence continue on p. 55); 'ses considerable damage without setting them on fire. Since in general the enemy's fire was directed more at the town than at the walls, the garrison was far safer on the walls than in its quarters' (the first word ends the one begun on p. 54); 'toward midday the fire fell silent, and after 1 o'clock Captain Desterno, a former Prussian dragoon lieutenant and at the time Jerome's adjutant, appeared as parlementaire and handed over a letter of summons in which the capture of Magdeburg, Stettin, Küstrin and Glogau and the entry of the French into Warsaw were communicated and the hopelessness of a relief was declared. The parlementaire added that the French had also crossed the Vistula at Thorn and had nowhere seen Russians, that the King had already gone back behind Memel, and that Napoleon had declared he would not make peace before he had humbled Russia and broken the alliance with Prussia'; 'in the night to the 12th the enemy extended the left parallel nearer to the Oder and the right parallel to the capital of the Hunde bastion, and began a second parallel on the left at the Oder and on the right of the suburb. A parallel with a battery was also laid out on the right side of the Oder, 400 paces from the Oder crownwork'; 'on the 12th and in the night to the 13th the town was indeed fired on, but only slowly, since the enemy was still awaiting munition and, in place of the dismounted guns, replacements from Glogau'; 'on 13 December 2 companies of French sappers and miners, of 66 men each, arrived, and were used at once to dig cuts into the Nikolai suburb and to the right of the churchyard there, and to build batteries in the second parallels'; 'from the left second parallel an approach trench with a small place of arms was to be pushed forward, so that from it the Württemberg Jäger could harass the Prussian gunners on the Bürgerwerder; but in the night to the 14th they struck quite unexpectedly on the arm of the Oder that separated the enemy from the works of the Bürgerwerder'; 'in the nights to the 14th and the 15th the besieger worked at the zigzags connecting the two parallels right of the suburb of St. Nikolai, and in the latter night the batteries built one after another were armed: the 2 batteries of the first parallel right of that suburb, counted from the left wing, with 2 heavy mortars and 3 light howitzers, and with 2 light mortars and 3 heavy howitzers; the batteries of the second parallel with 2 light howitzers and 4 6-pounders and with 4 light howitzers and 4 6-pounders respectively, these last batteries for firing on the batteries of the place. On the right bank of the Oder 8 field howitzers could be brought into action. Two 24-pounders and a heavy mortar had not yet arrived from Glogau'; 'on 15 December at 6 in the morning the bombardment thus began anew and lasted until 1 in the afternoon. The town suffered considerably, especially the convent of the Elisabethines, but the fire was put out everywhere'; 'at 2 in the afternoon Jerome had the fortress summoned again by General Lefebvre. He was led with unbandaged eyes to the governor, to whom he had to say much that was flattering about the' (the sentence continues on p. 57); 'defence so far and declare that, if the garrison did not accept the honourable capitulation offered, the town would be turned into a heap of ashes, for which all the means were at hand. The general also added that Breslau was being besieged for the last time, since Napoleon had ordered the fortifications to be razed immediately after the capture. The proposal was rejected, whereupon at 3 o'clock the bombardment was renewed, though not with the violence of the morning, and toward evening it gradually fell silent' (the first words end the sentence begun on p. 56); 'since the evening and the night to the 16th passed quietly against expectation, the garrison believed all the more that it could read this quiet as a sign of the besieger's departure, as he had, without any explicable reason, set fire in the night to the 16th to the woodpiles before the Ohlau gate, whereby 24,000 Klafter of wood burnt'; 'toward 5 in the evening the enemy began the bombardment anew, whereby the first considerable fire broke out in the town; a large house at the Siebenrader mill burnt down, and the one beside it had to be pulled down. The bombardment lasted until 7½ o'clock and was' (the sentence continues in the next paragraph); 'continued on 17 December at daybreak, until at 8½ o'clock an adjutant of Jerome's with a detachment brought the body of Lieutenant Lehsten and asked for the exchange of the captured Captain Debruir, which the governor, however, did not grant. With pauses the bombardment lasted into the night. The fire it caused was put out' (the first words end the sentence begun in the preceding paragraph); 'in the night to the 20th the 24-pounders held back until then and 2 heavy mortars that had arrived by water were also brought into the batteries, and from 4 until 9 in the morning of 20 December the town was most violently shelled. The main loss fell on the burghers, since the besiegers directed their fire exclusively at the town'; 'on 21 December the bombardment was renewed from 2½ until' (the sentence continues on p. 62); '5 in the morning. A deputation of burghers again turned to the governor with the request to grant them, amid so many afflictions, the comfort and hope of an early relief. The governor had to dismiss them without such a hope' (the first words end the sentence begun on p. 61); 'in the evening at 10 o'clock the fire was repeated, and at midnight to the 22nd it was reported to the governor that the enemy was attacking the Dom. Fire from heavy guns and small arms was opened from all the works, but the enemy kept quiet. On the other hand he bombarded' (the sentence continues in the next paragraph); 'on 22 December from 3 in the morning with pauses until the evening, and the fire raged most violently in the night to the 23rd, when fires broke out in several places' (the end of the sentence begun in the preceding paragraph); 'on 23 December at 6 in the morning it became apparent that the enemy, under the protection of the fire and of those demonstrations, was trying to cross the wet outer ditch at the ravelin R. by two cask bridges, so as to storm the fortress from there'; 'for want of a good plan of Breslau, already on 17, 18 and 19 December the engineer Colonel' (the sentence continues on p. 63); 'Blein had reconnoitred the works on the left bank of the Oder as thoroughly as possible and in doing so established that the main wall was not revetted at two extended places, namely at the Schweidnitz and Ohlau gates; that before the wet main ditch, over 120 feet wide, there was an enveloppe of earth, covered at its salient angles by lunettes with retired flanks; that these works were indeed provided with storm-poles and palisades, but were occupied only before the revetted front of the Nikolai gate, against which the siege works had so far been directed; and finally that the outer ditch surrounding the enveloppe had a width of 60-70 feet and a depth of 6-7 feet' (the end of the sentence begun on p. 62); 'in consequence of this result Colonel Blein had at once laid before Jerome a plan for the attack on the fortress, whose success was to force the governor to immediate surrender. The plan required several false attacks to divert the garrison's attention from the true point of attack, the unrevetted place near the Ohlau gate, where both ditches were to be crossed before daybreak. Jerome had approved the plan, and all materials for its execution had at once been collected. On the 22nd, after Jerome's departure, Colonel Blein had reported to General Hédouville that all was ready for execution'; 'the task was to cross two very wide and deep water ditches and to make oneself master of a double rampart. To that end Colonel Blein had had rafts built of ladders joined 2 and 2, which were to be held above the water by empty casks and covered with planks'; 'since it was not thought possible to hide the preparations for these works from the garrison, all the means of crossing had been brought together by day on the 22nd behind Neudorf, opposite the Schweidnitz gate, to make the garrison believe that an attack on this point was intended, and to mislead it still more all the vessels on the Ohlau had also been moved to the same area'; 'at 11 o'clock in the night General Hédouville, with Generals Vandamme and Pernety and Colonel Blein, had also gone to the Ohlau suburb to make the arrangements still needed on the spot'; 'at 4 in the morning of the 23rd the troops ordered had been posted in the Ohlau suburb. Earlier the attack could not have begun because of the moonlight. Special workers had been asked for to carry the rafts; but they had not arrived, and the attacking troops had now had to be used to carry the rafts as well'; 'only at 5 o'clock could the first raft be brought into the outer ditch; it was 30 feet long, and 3 others of 12-15 feet had to be brought in to reach the far bank. The sappers, inexperienced in such work, had been able to bind the rafts together only slowly; a drunken officer had come onto the rafts and also greatly hindered the workers; and finally a thoughtless shout, and the leap of a French sapper non-commissioned officer into the water to fasten the rafts to the palisades of the enveloppe under attack, had drawn the attention of an' (the sentence continues on p. 65); 'artilleryman on the Ohlau ravelin; he had fired a round of canister at the place of the noise, and at once the guns of the Bernhard and Taschen bastions, which commanded the enveloppe, and the infantry garrison of the adjacent walls had joined in this fire. Two enemy soldiers carrying a raft were shot at the very beginning of the fire, the other carriers ran away, and the enemy saw himself forced to retreat with considerable loss. A French officer who was on the rafts had to surrender with some privates' (the first words end the sentence begun on p. 64); 'on General Minucci's return, General Vandamme, who had ordered the building of 4 new batteries in order to bring into them a further 8 24-pounders, 6 12-pounders and 2 mortars that were arriving from Glogau, believed he must set the town seriously on fire and inform the governor of the defeat of the relief troops and of the means he possessed to destroy the town. He expected that a population of 60,000 inhabitants would not be sacrificed to the holding of works that owed their preservation only to the mild weather. All this was done without the knowledge of General Hédouville, although this general, as mentioned, was to continue the command in Jerome's name'; 'the bombardment was therefore, on the 25th after 1 o'clock, o-' (the sentence continues on p. 80: 'opened again'); 'pened again and lasted until 3 o'clock. At that time Colonel Duveyrier, general staff officer of General Vandamme, appeared with the summons to surrender, with the most boastful statements about the advantages won against the Prince of Pless as well as in Poland and Prussia. The governor gave a refusal' (the first words end the sentence begun on p. 79); 'soon afterwards, at 10½, Colonel Duveyrier appeared again; General Vandamme had not granted the armistice, but had given the parlementaire full power to conclude a capitulation. The governor kept to his demand and regarded the negotiation as broken off'; 'on 26 December at 3 in the morning Colonel Duveyrier came back again and brought the enemy general's consent to the armistice, which was to last until 8 in the morning of the 27th'; 'in view of this favourable mood of the burghers, and because the enemy continued the works against the fortress during the armistice and also alarmed the Springstern, the governor ended the armistice as early as 10 o'clock on the 26th, so that in the afternoon the fire from the walls began anew'; 'on 2 January at 11 o'clock Colonel Duveyrier and Captain Hammerer were let in. Their business consisted in the request for the release of several persons, mostly of the female sex, and besides in the enumeration, repeated to weariness, of all the reasons that were to make the sur-' (the word and sentence continue on p. 110); 'render of the fortress necessary. Both officers were dismissed with expressions of courtesy, and at 3 o'clock the garrison's fire began again, at 5 o'clock a 2-hour bombardment by the enemy' (the first word ends the one begun on p. 109); 'toward 11 o'clock Captain Hammerer appeared again as parlementaire and took with him a letter of the governor with the request to send Colonel Duveyrier into the town to open negotiations. Nevertheless the fire from the walls was kept up, and was answered by a bombardment beginning at 1¼ in the afternoon, the most violent of the whole siege'; 'at 4 in the afternoon Colonel Duveyrier came, empowered to negotiate the surrender. The bombardment still went on even now. The governor could no more obtain the armistice of 8 days he asked for, to give the Prince of Pless time for a new attempt at relief, than the dispatch of an officer to Kalisch, by whom he wished to make sure whether Russians were approaching or not. Only for arranging the affairs of the town and the garrison were 3 days granted'; 'on 5 January Colonel Duveyrier appeared again, and the points of capitulation were signed by both sides, not without disputes, representations and counter-representations, after 6 o'clock'; 'as for the siege works of the French, they were conducted very irregularly and could probably lead to the goal only under such peculiar circumstances'; 'as already mentioned, and as the engineer Colonel Blein also confirms, the whole attack was directed exclusively at the town. A siege advancing against the works was held to be useless, because all the advantages were on the defender's side owing to his superior artillery, and it was counted on that when frost set in, robbing the fortress of its only means of protection, the wet ditches, the capitulation must follow'.

citations.locator: Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 4 (1851), p. 52 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: Ebenfalls am 7. rekognoszirte der General Vandamme, begleitet vom Artillerie-General Pernety und vom Ingenieur-Obersten Blein, den Platz, um den Angriffspunkt zu ermitteln.

citations.locator: Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 4 (1851), p. 52 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: Die zur Belagerung disponiblen Truppen waren zu schwach, um sich an der obern Oder aufzustellen, wo man den Beunruhigungen der preußischen Parteien aus den übrigen Festungen zu sehr ausgesetzt schien; man beschränkte sich daher vorläufig auf das Terrain an der untern Oder und wollte sich rechts bis gegen die Ohlauer Vorstadt ausdehnen. Der Bau zweier Parallelen und zweier Wurfbatterien, rechts und links der Nikolai-Vorstadt, wurde beschlossen, und zwar um so mehr diese Vorstadt zum Angriffspunkt bestimmt, als der Oberst Blein die Hoffnung hegte, daß er daselbst auf ein Batardeau in Erde treffen würde, das den Uebergang über den Graben erleichtern könne.

citations.locator: Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 4 (1851), p. 53 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: Die Angriffs-Arbeiten begannen bereits in der Nacht zum 8. mit einer so geringen Zahl von Arbeitern, daß man sich darauf beschränken mußte, zwei kurze Parallelen nach den projektirten Batterien zu erbauen; die eine Parallele sollte sich links an die Oder, die andere links an die Nikolai-Vorstadt lehnen.

citations.locator: Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 4 (1851), p. 54 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: In der Nacht zum 9. wurde von Seiten des Belagerers der Bau der projektirten Batterien begonnen, und eine dritte Batterie in der Verlängerung der Straße der Nikolai-Vorstadt gearbeitet; auch auf dem rechten Oder-Ufer beim Elbing und hinter der Mönchswiese wurden Geschütz-Aufstellungen zu Stande gebracht.

citations.locator: Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 4 (1851), p. 54 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: In der Nacht zum 10. führte der Feind auf dem linken Ufer in die Batterie rechts der Nikolai-Vorstadt 2 Mörser und 3 Haubitzen, in die Batterie in der Verlängerung der Nikolai-Vorstadt 3 Haubitzen, in die Batterie bei der Parallele links 3 Mörser, 1 Belagerungs- und 3 Feldhaubitzen, und endlich in die Batterien auf dem rechten Oder-Ufer die bezeichneten 10 Geschütze.

citations.locator: Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 4 (1851), p. 54 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: Am 10. Morgens 6 Uhr war der Feind im Stande, das Bombardement gegen die Front am Nikolai-Thor und den Dom zu beginnen; die feindlichen Wurfgeschosse fügten den Bürgerhäu-

citations.locator: Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 4 (1851), p. 55 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: sern erheblichen Schaden zu, ohne zu zünden. Da im Allgemeinen das feindliche Feuer sich mehr auf die Stadt als auf die Wälle richtete, so befand sich die Besatzung auf diesen weit sicherer als in ihren Quartieren.

citations.locator: Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 4 (1851), p. 55 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: Gegen Mittag schwieg das Feuer, und nach 1 Uhr erschien der Kapitain Desterno, ehemaliger preußischer Dragoner-Lieutenant und zur Zeit Adjutant Jerome's, als Parlamentair und überreichte ein Aufforderungsschreiben, in welchem die Einnahme von Magdeburg, Stettin, Küstrin und Glogau, der Einzug der Franzosen in Warschau mitgetheilt und die Hoffnungslosigkeit für einen Entsatz ausgesprochen wurde. Der Parlamentair fügte hinzu, daß die Franzosen auch bei Thorn die Weichsel überschritten und nirgends Russen gesehen hätten, daß der König bereits bis hinter Memel zurückgegangen sei und Napoleon erklärt habe, nicht früher Frieden zu machen, als bis er Rußland gedemüthigt und das Bündniß mit Preußen gesprengt habe.

citations.locator: Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 4 (1851), p. 55 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: In der Nacht zum 12. verlängerte der Feind die Parallele links näher gegen die Oder, und die Parallele rechts bis zur Kapitale des Hundebastions, und begann eine zweite Parallele links an der Oder und rechts von der Vorstadt. Auch wurde eine Parallele mit einer Batterie auf der rechten Oder-Seite, 400 Schritt vom Oder-Kronwerk, angelegt.

citations.locator: Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 4 (1851), p. 55 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: Am 12. und in der Nacht zum 13. wurde die Stadt zwar beschossen, aber nur langsam, da der Feind erst Munition und an Stelle der demontirten Geschütze Ersatz aus Glogau erwartete.

citations.locator: Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 4 (1851), p. 56 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: Am 13. Dezember langten 2 Kompagnien französischer Sapeurs und Mineurs, je zu 66 Mann, an, und bediente man sich ihrer sogleich, um Einschnitte in die Nikolai-Vorstadt und rechts vom Kirchhof daselbst zu arbeiten, auch Batterien in den zweiten Parallelen zu bauen.

citations.locator: Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 4 (1851), p. 56 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: Aus der zweiten Parallele links sollte ein Laufgraben mit einem kleinen Waffenplatz vorgeschoben werden, um aus demselben durch die württembergischen Jäger die preußischen Kanoniere auf dem Bürgerwerder zu beunruhigen; man stieß indessen in der Nacht zum 14. sehr unerwartet auf den Oderarm, der den Feind von den Werken des Bürgerwerders trennte.

citations.locator: Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 4 (1851), p. 56 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: In den Nächten zum 14. und zum 15. arbeitete der Belagerer an den Zickzacks zur Verbindung der beiden Parallelen rechts der Vorstadt St. Nikolai, und in der letzteren Nacht wurden die nach und nach gebauten Batterien armirt, und zwar die 2 Batterien der ersten Parallele rechts der genannten Vorstadt, vom linken Flügel an gerechnet, durch 2 schwere Mörser und 3 leichte Haubitzen, und 2 leichte Mörser und 3 schwere Haubitzen, die Batterien der zweiten Parallele durch resp. 2 leichte Haubitzen und 4—6pfünder, 4 leichte Haubitzen und 4—6pfünder; diese letzteren Batterien zur Beschießung der Batterien des Platzes. Auf dem rechten Oder-Ufer konnten 8 Feldhaubitzen in Thätigkeit gesetzt werden. Zwei 24pfünder und ein schwerer Mörser waren noch nicht von Glogau eingetroffen.

citations.locator: Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 4 (1851), p. 56 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: Am 15. Dezember Morgens 6 Uhr begann das Bombardement somit aufs Neue und dauerte bis 1 Uhr Nachmittags. Die Stadt litt bedeutend, besonders das Kloster der Elisabethinerin, doch wurde das Feuer überall gelöscht.

citations.locator: Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 4 (1851), p. 56 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: Um 2 Uhr Nachmittags ließ Jerome die Festung abermals durch den General Lefebvre auffordern. Derselbe wurde mit unverbundenen Augen zum Gouverneur geführt, dem er viel Schmeichelhaftes über die

citations.locator: Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 4 (1851), p. 57 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: bisherige Vertheidigung sagen und erklären mußte, daß, wenn die Besatzung die angebotene ehrenvolle Kapitulation nicht annähme, die Stadt in einen Aschenhaufen verwandelt werden würde, wozu alle Mittel vorhanden wären. Auch fügte der General hinzu, daß Breslau zum Letztenmale belagert würde, indem Napoleon befohlen habe, gleich nach der Einnahme die Festungswerke zu schleifen. Der Antrag wurde zurückgewiesen, worauf um 3 Uhr das Bombardement erneuert wurde, jedoch nicht mit der Heftigkeit als am Morgen, und gegen Abend verstummte es allmälig.

citations.locator: Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 4 (1851), p. 57 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: Da der Abend und die Nacht zum 16. wider Erwarten ruhig verliefen, so glaubte die Besatzung um so mehr, diese Ruhe auf einen Abmarsch des Belagerers deuten zu können, als derselbe ohne allen erklärbaren Grund in der Nacht zum 16. die Holzstöße vor dem Ohlauer-Thor anzündete, wodurch 24,000 Klafter Holz verbrannten.

citations.locator: Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 4 (1851), p. 58 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: Gegen 5 Uhr Abends begann der Feind das Bombardement aufs Neue, wodurch das erste bedeutende Feuer in der Stadt aufging; ein ansehnliches Haus an der Siebenrader-Mühle brannte nieder, und das nebenstehende mußte niedergerissen werden. Das Bombardement dauerte bis 7½ Uhr und wurde

citations.locator: Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 4 (1851), p. 58 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: am 17. Dezember mit Tagesanbruch fortgesetzt, bis um 8½ Uhr ein Adjutant Jerome's mit einem Kommando den Leichnam des Lieutenants Lehsten überbrachte und die Auswechselung des gefangenen Hauptmanns Debruir erbat, die indessen der Gouverneur nicht genehmigte. In Pausen dauerte das Bombardement bis in die Nacht. Das dadurch verursachte Feuer wurde gelöscht.

citations.locator: Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 4 (1851), p. 61 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: In der Nacht zum 20. wurden auch die bisher noch zurückgehaltenen 24pfünder und 2 zu Wasser angelangte schwere Mörser in die Batterien eingeführt, und um 4 Uhr bis 9 Uhr Morgens des 20. Dezembers wurde die Stadt aufs Heftigste beworfen. Der Hauptverlust traf die Bürgerschaft, da die Belagerer ihr Feuer ausschließlich auf die Stadt richteten.

citations.locator: Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 4 (1851), p. 61 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: Am 21. Dezember wurde das Bombardement von 2½ bis

citations.locator: Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 4 (1851), p. 62 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: 5 Uhr Morgens erneuert. Eine Deputation von Bürgern wandte sich abermals an den Gouverneur mit der Bitte, ihr bei so vielen Drangsalen den Trost- und die Hoffnung eines baldigen Entsatzes zu gewähren. Der Gouverneur mußte sie ohne eine solche Hoffnung entlassen.

citations.locator: Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 4 (1851), p. 62 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: Am Abend um 10 Uhr wiederholte sich das Feuer, und um Mitternacht zum 22. wurde dem Gouverneur gemeldet, daß der Feind den Dom angreife. Von allen Werken wurde das Feuer aus grobem Geschütz und kleinem Gewehr eröffnet, doch hielt sich der Feind ruhig. Dagegen bombardirte er

citations.locator: Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 4 (1851), p. 62 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: am 22. Dezember von 3 Uhr Morgens in Pausen bis zum Abend, und am heftigsten wüthete das Feuer in der Nacht zum 23., wobei es an mehreren Orten brannte.

citations.locator: Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 4 (1851), p. 62 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: am 23. Dezember um 6 Uhr Morgens zeigte es sich, daß der Feind unter dem Schutz des Feuers und jener Demonstrationen den nassen Vorgraben bei dem Ravelin R. durch zwei Tonnenbrücken zu überschreiten suchte, um von dort die Festung zu stürmen.

citations.locator: Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 4 (1851), p. 62 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: In Ermangelung eines guten Planes von Breslau hatte bereits am 17., 18. und 19. Dezember der Ingenieur-Oberst

citations.locator: Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 4 (1851), p. 63 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: Blein die Werke auf dem linken Oder-Ufer so gründlich als möglich rekognoszirt und hierbei ermittelt, daß der Hauptwall an zwei ausgedehnten Stellen, nämlich am Schweidnitzer- und Ohlauer-Thor, nicht bekleidet sei; daß sich vor dem nassen, über 120′ breiten Hauptgraben aber eine Enveloppe von Erde befände, die auf ihren vorspringenden Winkeln durch Lünetten mit zurückgezogenen Flanken gedeckt würde; daß diese Werke zwar mit Sturmpfählen und Pallisaden versehen, aber nur vor der revetirten Front des Nikolai-Thores, gegen welche bisher die Angriffs-Arbeiten geführt worden waren, besetzt seien; daß endlich der Vorgraben, der die Enveloppe umgab, eine Breite von 60—70′ und eine Tiefe von 6—7′ habe.

citations.locator: Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 4 (1851), p. 63 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: In Folge dieses Resultates hatte der Oberst Blein sofort Jerome einen Plan zum Angriff der Festung vorgelegt, dessen Gelingen den Gouverneur zur sofortigen Uebergabe zwingen sollte. Der Plan verlangte mehrere falsche Angriffe zur Ablenkung der Aufmerksamkeit der Garnison von dem wahren Angriffspunkt, der nicht revetirten Stelle in der Nähe des Ohlauer-Thores, wo vor Tages-Anbruch die beiden Gräben überschritten werden sollten. Jerome hatte den Plan genehmigt, und sofort waren alle Materialien zur Ausführung beigetrieben worden. Am 22. hatte der Oberst Blein, nach der Abreise Jerome's, dem General Hédouville gemeldet, daß Alles zur Ausführung bereit sei.

citations.locator: Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 4 (1851), p. 63 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: Die Aufgabe war, über zwei sehr breite und tiefe Wassergräben zu gehen und sich einer doppelten Umwallung zu bemächtigen. Der Oberst Blein hatte zu dem Ende Flöße von je 2 und 2 zusammengefügten Leitern bauen lassen, welche durch leere Fässer über dem Wasser gehalten und mit Brettern belegt werden sollten.

citations.locator: Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 4 (1851), p. 63 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: Da man der Besatzung die Vorbereitungen zu diesen Arbeiten nicht glaubte verbergen zu können, hatte man am 22. alle Uebergangsmittel bei Tage hinter Neudorf, dem Schweidnitzer-Thor gegenüber, zusammengebracht, um die Besatzung glauben zu machen, als beabsichtige man einen Angriff gegen diesen Punkt, und um noch mehr irre zu führen, waren auch alle Fahrzeuge, die sich auf der Ohlau befanden, nach der nämlichen Gegend transportirt worden.

citations.locator: Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 4 (1851), p. 64 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: Um 11 Uhr in der Nacht hatte sich der General Hédouville mit den Generalen Vandamme und Pernety und dem Obersten Blein ebenfalls nach der Ohlauer-Vorstadt begeben, um die noch erforderlichen Anordnungen an Ort und Stelle zu treffen.

citations.locator: Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 4 (1851), p. 64 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: Um 4 Uhr Morgens des 23. waren die beorderten Truppen in der Ohlauer-Vorstadt aufgestellt worden. Früher hatte man wegen des Mondlichts den Angriff nicht beginnen können. Man hatte besondere Arbeiter verlangt, um die Flöße zu tragen; sie waren aber nicht eingetroffen, und die angreifenden Truppen hatten nun auch zum Transport der Flöße benutzt werden müssen.

citations.locator: Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 4 (1851), p. 64 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: Erst um 5 Uhr hatte das erste Floß in den Vorgraben gebracht werden können; es war 30′ lang und man hatte noch 3 andere von 12—15′ einbringen müssen, um an das jenseitige Ufer zu gelangen. Die Sapeurs, unerfahren in dergleichen Arbeiten, hatten das Zusammenbinden der Flöße nur langsam zu Stande bringen können; ein betrunkener Offizier war auf die Flöße gekommen und hatte die Arbeiter ebenfalls sehr behindert, und endlich hatte ein unüberlegter Zuruf und der Sprung eines französischen Sapeur-Unteroffiziers ins Wasser, um die Flöße an den Pallisaden der angegriffenen Enveloppe zu befestigen, einen

citations.locator: Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 4 (1851), p. 65 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: Artilleristen auf dem Ohlauer-Ravelin aufmerksam gemacht; er hatte eine Lage Kartätschen nach dem Orte des Geräusches gefeuert, und alsbald waren in dies Feuer die Geschütze des Bernhard- und Taschenbastions, welche die Enveloppe kommandirten, und die Infanterie-Besatzung der anliegenden Wälle eingefallen. Zwei feindliche Soldaten, die ein Floß trugen, wurden gleich beim Beginn des Feuers erschossen, die übrigen Träger liefen davon und der Feind sah sich genöthigt, den Rückzug mit ansehnlichem Verlust anzutreten. Ein französischer Offizier, der sich auf den Flößen befand, mußte sich mit einigen Gemeinen gefangen geben.

citations.locator: Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 4 (1851), p. 79 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: Bei der Rückkehr des Generals Minucci glaubte der General Vandamme, der den Bau von 4 neuen Batterien befohlen hatte, um darin noch 8—24pfünder, 6—12pfünder und 2 Mörser, welche von Glogau anlangten, einzuführen, die Stadt ernsthaft in Brand setzen, und dem Gouverneur von der Niederlage der Entsatztruppen, so wie von den Mitteln Nachricht geben zu müssen, die er besaß, um die Stadt zu vernichten. Er erwartete, daß eine Bevölkerung von 60,000 Einwohnern nicht der Behauptung von Werken würde aufgeopfert werden, die ihre Erhaltung nur der gelinden Witterung verdankten. Das Alles geschah ohne Vorwissen des Generals Hédouville, obgleich dieser General, wie erwähnt, im Namen Jerome's den Befehl fortführen sollte.

citations.locator: Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 4 (1851), p. 79 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: Das Bombardement wurde daher am 25. nach 1 Uhr wie-

citations.locator: Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 4 (1851), p. 80 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: der eröffnet und dauerte bis 3 Uhr. Um diese Zeit erschien der Oberst Duveyrier, Generalstabs-Offizier des Generals Vandamme, mit der Aufforderung zur Uebergabe unter den prahlerischsten Angaben über die errungenen Vortheile gegen den Fürsten von Pleß, so wie in Polen und Preußen. Der Gouverneur ertheilte eine abschlägige Antwort.

citations.locator: Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 4 (1851), p. 80 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: Bald nachher, 10½ Uhr, erschien der Oberst Duveyrier abermals; der General Vandamme hatte den Waffenstillstand nicht genehmigt, dagegen dem Parlamentair Vollmacht gegeben, eine Kapitulation einzugehen. Der Gouverneur hielt sich an seine Forderung und sah die Unterhandlung als abgebrochen an.

citations.locator: Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 4 (1851), p. 80 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: Am 26. Dezember um 3 Uhr Morgens kehrte der Oberst Duveyrier abermals zurück, und brachte die Einwilligung des feindlichen Generals zum Waffenstillstand, der bis zum 27. Morgens 8 Uhr dauern sollte.

citations.locator: Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 4 (1851), p. 81 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: In Betracht dieser günstigen Stimmung der Bürger, und weil der Feind während des Waffenstillstandes die Arbeiten gegen die Festung fortsetzte, auch den Springstern allarmirte, kündigte der Gouverneur bereits um 10 Uhr des 26. den Waffenstillstand, so daß Nachmittags das Feuer von den Wällen aufs Neue begann.
