citations.locator: Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 4 (1851), p. 109 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: Am 2. Januar um 11 Uhr wurden der Oberst Duveyrier und der Hauptmann Hammerer eingelassen. Ihr Geschäft bestand in dem Gesuch um die Entlassung mehrerer Personen, meist weiblichen Geschlechts, und nächstdem in der bis zur Ermüdung wiederholten Aufzählung aller Gründe, welche die Ueber-

citations.locator: Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 4 (1851), p. 110 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: gabe der Festung nothwendig machen sollten. Beide Offiziere wurden mit Höflichkeitsbezeugungen entlassen, und um 3 Uhr fing das Feuer der Besatzung, um 5 Uhr ein 2stündiges Bombardement des Feindes wieder an.

citations.locator: Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 4 (1851), p. 110 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: Gegen 11 Uhr erschien der Hauptmann Hammerer abermals als Parlamentair, und nahm ein Schreiben des Gouverneurs mit dem Gesuch mit, den Obersten Duveyrier zum Anknüpfen von Unterhandlungen nach der Stadt zu senden. Dessenungeachtet wurde das Feuer von den Wällen unterhalten, und durch ein um 1¼ Uhr Nachmittags beginnendes Bombardement, das heftigste während der ganzen Belagerung, beantwortet.

citations.locator: Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 4 (1851), p. 111 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: Nachmittags 4 Uhr kam der Oberst Duveyrier, zu Unterhandlungen wegen der Uebergabe bevollmächtigt. Das Bombardement dauerte auch jetzt noch fort. Der Gouverneur konnte den verlangten Waffenstillstand auf 8 Tage, um dem Fürsten von Pleß Zeit zu einem neuen Entsatzversuch zu geben, so wenig erlangen, als die Absendung eines Offiziers nach Kalisch, durch den man sich überzeugen wollte, ob Russen im Anmarsch wären oder nicht. Lediglich zum Arrangement der Angelegenheiten der Stadt und der Garnison wurden 3 Tage bewilligt.

citations.locator: Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 4 (1851), p. 111 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: Am 5. Januar erschien der Oberst Duveyrier abermals, und die Kapitulationspunkte wurden von beiden Theilen nicht ohne Streitigkeiten, Vor- und Gegenvorstellungen, nach 6 Uhr unterzeichnet.

citations.locator: Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 4 (1851), p. 118 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: Was die Belagerungs-Arbeiten der Franzosen betrifft, so wurden dieselben sehr unregelmäßig geführt, und konnten wohl nur unter so eigenthümlichen Umständen zum Ziel führen.

citations.locator: Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 4 (1851), p. 118 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: Wie bereits erwähnt, und wie es auch der Ingenieur-Oberst Blein bestätigt, war der ganze Angriff ausschließlich auf die Stadt gerichtet. Man hielt eine Belagerung, welche gegen die Werke vorschreitet, für unnütz, weil alle Vortheile auf Seiten des Vertheidigers, wegen dessen überlegener Artillerie, gewesen seien, und man darauf rechnete, daß bei eintretendem Frost, welcher die Festung ihres einzigen Schutzmittels, der nassen Gräben, beraubte, die Kapitulation erfolgen müsse.

claims.value: Höpfner: when the arming of Breslau began on 19 October at General Lindener's instance, the government had the guns taken to the outworks and ordered their palisading, and divided the fortress into 4 main fronts, each under an infantry staff officer and an older artillery officer; it meant to hold all the outworks, but when Lindener arrived on 6 November he had the defence restricted to the main wall, keeping only the Nikolai crownwork, the Mühlberg redoubt, the Oder crownwork, the Ohlau ravelin and the ravelin R. occupied, the Dom and the Springstern being drawn in later. The suburbs were not cleared. On 7 December the government sent Lieutenant Fiebig with half the horse battery, some infantry and 30 horses to destroy the bridges over the old Oder and demolish the casemates at the Paßschleuse, which succeeded, and Captain Debruir was taken prisoner; the garrison set fire to the Nikolai suburb at 6 in the evening, by the order of the narrative on the 7th, to the nearest houses of the Oder suburb on the 8th and in the night to the 9th, to the Hinter-Dom suburb, and to the Ohlau suburb on the evening of the 11th; Fiebig was ordered with the horse artillery into the works on the Bürgerwerder, later held also by infantry, 8 heavy guns and some cavalry as an outpost. The governor decidedly rejected the summons of 10 December and did not stop firing during the parley, and rejected Lefebvre's summons of the 15th. On the 11th side A bombarded only from the left bank, the artillery Lieutenant Zimmermann on the Springstern, shot soon afterwards, having silenced its fire on the right, and on the left bank too the defender's fire at last gained the upper hand. On 16 December, on a report that side A had withdrawn its guns, the governor sent out a sortie of 2 officers, 60 marksmen and 80 horsemen with 300 workers from the Nikolai gate, without naming a leader; it was driven back. The garrison of the Bürgerwerder resisted its officers by force on the 16th; it was relieved and the two most involved were shot two days later. On the 17th the governor refused to exchange Captain Debruir; a deputation of burghers asking that the town be spared was sent away reassured, and another on the 21st without hope of relief. On 25 December the governor refused Duveyrier's summons; during the parley a petition of the magistracy and the merchants, followed by a deputation of 6 burghers, asked him to end the town's sufferings if possible, and he put the burghers' requests to the generals and staff officers, of whom only Major Lepel of the regiment Thile was unconditionally against regard for the town, and at 9 o'clock asked Vandamme for an armistice; offered a capitulation instead at 10½, he kept to his demand and regarded the negotiation as broken off. He accepted the armistice brought at 3 in the morning of the 26th, but after a second deputation at 8½ protested that the burghers would rather be killed than vote for surrender, he answered the petition that, being now convinced that by far the greatest part of the inhabitants dreaded any surrender, he could take no further account of it, and, because side A went on with its works and alarmed the Springstern, he ended the armistice at 10 o'clock. On 30 December, when firing and the burning of Dürgoy were reported from 6 in the morning, the governor answered that side A was manoeuvring to lure the garrison out; Lindener saw only some cavalry at Dürgoy, the commandant General Krafft rebuffed those who tried to persuade him that side A was not manoeuvring, and the garrison was assembled at 11 for a sortie only in case side A should be beaten, but the fire receded and the relief had been beaten; from then on the mood of the burghers and the troops turned very bad against the government, everyone ascribing the omission of a sortie to the most impure motives. When frost set in, measures were taken to break the ice of the Oder and the ditches. On 3 January, after a petition signed by a hundred and some sixty burghers and one of the magistracy, the governor asked for Duveyrier, consulted Krafft and Lindener, and resolved to capitulate; he could obtain neither an armistice of 8 days, to give the Prince of Pless time for a new relief, nor leave to send an officer to Kalisch, but only 3 days to arrange the affairs of the town and the garrison. Höpfner says the artillery had especially distinguished itself everywhere in the short siege and, with the Land reserves, alone kept the old Prussian discipline at the end, and cites Colonel Blein's report to Napoleon that the artillery of Breslau had shown it came from a good school, had adorned the French trenches and made many embrasure shots. Items 3-6 of a numbered list of the government's faults are the lack of attention to provisioning, the omission of the sortie on 30 December, the failure to open communication with the Prince of Pless by scouts, for which Lindener is said to have borne the particular blame, and the conclusion of a capitulation without the council of war prescribed by the regulations; Höpfner judges the abandonment of the outworks a fault to be ascribed solely to Lindener, against the engineer of the place. Not, he says, to charge the government with a particular omission but as a general point, and without a definite judgement, for which more adequate materials would be needed, he reckons that 4000 men, including 230 mounted cavalrymen, could still have left the fortress and joined the Prince of Pless.
claims.rationale: Side B's history, read from the page images of pp. 47-118. These were the decisions of the governor, the government and Lindener, so the claim is tagged commander-created; the artillery's conduct is kept with them. Höpfner names no source for the councils, the deputations or the negotiations; he prints the governor's reply of 26 December to the petition. The list of faults begins on p. 115, read in the OCR only and not used, so items 3-6 are given as the list's, not as Höpfner's own judgement; his own are the comment on the outworks and the break-out reckoning, which by his statement is a general point, not a charge. The disposition he proposes for a break-out, on p. 117, was read in the OCR only and not used. 'The Land reserves' renders 'Land-Reserven' (our reading). English renderings (ours): 'when on 19 October, at the instance of the engineer brigadier General Lindener, the arming works of Breslau began, the government had at once had the guns taken to the outworks and suitably placed, and had also ordered the palisading of these works, the repair of the drawbridges, etc.'; 'because of the extent of the works and their partly difficult connection with one another, the fortress was divided into 4 main fronts, and each was entrusted to a staff officer of the infantry as divisional commander and an older artillery officer, for the complete equipment of the works and their eventual defence'; 'it was thus the government's intention to hold and defend all the outworks, but when General Lindener arrived on 6 November he brought it about that this plan was abandoned and the defence restricted to the main wall, surrounded by wide water ditches; only the Nikolai crownwork, the Mühlberg redoubt, the Oder crownwork,' (the sentence continues on p. 48); 'the Ohlau ravelin and the ravelin R. before the Ziegel gate1) were to remain occupied, while the guns of the other outworks were to be brought back to the main wall' (the end of the sentence begun on p. 47; the note refers to Höpfner's plan XVIII of Breslau); 'only later, when the garrison had received some reinforcement, were the important and already palisaded outworks, the Dom and the Springstern, also drawn into the defence'; 'the clearing of the suburbs, which hindered a vigorous defence, was not done, partly in the hope of a relief by the Russian operations, partly because the government feared the mood of the numerous burghers if it destroyed these extensive buildings before the enemy forced it to, and partly, finally, because it was believed that when the enemy actually appeared it would still be possible to shoot them down and burn them'; 'in consequence of the news of the return of part of the Bavarian troops from South Prussia against Breslau, the government on 7 December sent Artillery Lieutenant Fiebig with half of the newly raised horse battery, some infantry and 30 horses to the right bank of the Oder, to destroy all the bridges over the old Oder and at the same time to demolish the casemates of the abandoned work at the Paßschleuse, where the old Oder leaves the new above Breslau'; 'both undertakings succeeded completely, and on the way the French Captain Debruir was taken prisoner, whom General Vandamme had sent from Lissa to Jerome to bring him the news of the capture of Glogau: from the dispatch, torn to pieces, it was learned that the enemy meant to throw a bridge over the Oder at Kosel, below Breslau, and the prisoner himself stated that Napoleon had most earnestly assured Jerome, and Marshal Berthier General Vandamme, that Breslau was an altogether untenable place that could not hold out 5 days'; 'since the enemy's tirailleurs lodged themselves in the houses of the Nikolai suburb and of the Schweidnitz Anger and harassed the foremost palisade tambours and even the communication between the Nikolai gate and the Scheeren bastion lying below it, the Nikolai suburb was set on fire in the evening at 6 o'clock.1)'; 'considering that the Bavarian advance guard enclosed the fortress on the right bank of the Oder too on the 8th, so that the use of the horse artillery on that bank was much restricted, while the Bürgerwerder was threatened by the enemy's works in the night to the 8th, the governor ordered Lieutenant Fiebig to move with the horse artillery into the works on the Bürgerwerder and take over their defence. La-' (the word and sentence continue on p. 54); 'ter these works were gradually also occupied by infantry, 8 heavy guns and some cavalry. The intention was to keep the Bürgerwerder occupied, as an outpost against the enemy's works, for as long as the enemy would allow it from the right side of the Oder, where the work covering the Werder had been left unoccupied' (the first word ends the one begun on p. 53); 'on 8 December and in the night to the 9th the defender also set fire to the nearest houses of the Oder suburb, to give the artillery of the Bürgerwerder and of the Oder crownwork a free view'; 'the garrison's artillery fired without pause on these works and set fire to the Hinter-Dom suburb, so as to be able to counter the enemy's batteries on the right bank and take from the enemy's tirailleurs the cover from which they could do harm to the troops on the low walls of the Dom'; 'on the 10th at 6 in the morning the enemy was able to begin the bombardment against the front at the Nikolai gate and the Dom; the enemy's shells did the burghers' hou-' (the word and sentence continue on p. 55); 'ses considerable damage without setting them on fire. Since in general the enemy's fire was directed more at the town than at the walls, the garrison was far safer on the walls than in its quarters' (the first word ends the one begun on p. 54); 'toward midday the fire fell silent, and after 1 o'clock Captain Desterno, a former Prussian dragoon lieutenant and at the time Jerome's adjutant, appeared as parlementaire and handed over a letter of summons in which the capture of Magdeburg, Stettin, Küstrin and Glogau and the entry of the French into Warsaw were communicated and the hopelessness of a relief was declared. The parlementaire added that the French had also crossed the Vistula at Thorn and had nowhere seen Russians, that the King had already gone back behind Memel, and that Napoleon had declared he would not make peace before he had humbled Russia and broken the alliance with Prussia'; 'the governor decidedly rejected the summons, and had not let the fire cease even during the negotiation'; 'on 11 December the enemy continued the bombardment, but only on the left bank of the Oder, since the artillery Lieutenant Zimmermann commanding on the Springstern, who was shot soon afterwards, had succeeded in silencing the enemy's fire. On the left side of the Oder too the defender's fire at last gained the upper hand'; 'in the evening the garrison had to set fire to the Ohlau suburb as well'; 'on 15 December at 6 in the morning the bombardment thus began anew and lasted until 1 in the afternoon. The town suffered considerably, especially the convent of the Elisabethines, but the fire was put out everywhere'; 'at 2 in the afternoon Jerome had the fortress summoned again by General Lefebvre. He was led with unbandaged eyes to the governor, to whom he had to say much that was flattering about the' (the sentence continues on p. 57); 'defence so far and declare that, if the garrison did not accept the honourable capitulation offered, the town would be turned into a heap of ashes, for which all the means were at hand. The general also added that Breslau was being besieged for the last time, since Napoleon had ordered the fortifications to be razed immediately after the capture. The proposal was rejected, whereupon at 3 o'clock the bombardment was renewed, though not with the violence of the morning, and toward evening it gradually fell silent' (the first words end the sentence begun on p. 56); 'on 16 December too the enemy kept quiet, and since the governor received the report that the besieger had withdrawn the guns from the batteries, he ordered that a detachment of 2 officers - Lieutenant Lehsten of the infantry regiment Thile and Lieutenant Seelstrang of the cuirassier regiment Henckel - 60 marksmen and 80 horsemen with 300 workers should advance from the Nikolai gate, clear the suburb of the enemy and destroy the enemy's works'; 'toward 1 o'clock at midday the sortie broke out, without a definite leader having been named, but it was met by a lively fire from the ruins of the burnt-down houses in the Nikolai suburb, into which it had incautiously gone, and was driven back with the loss of 1 officer - Lieutenant Lehsten - and 10 men dead and 7 missing. The cavalry brought back 10 prisoners'; 'the garrison of the Bürgerwerder resisted the officers commanding there by force on the 16th; a cavalry detachment had to be sent out to arrest the ringleaders. The garrison was relieved and the two most involved were shot two days later in the Zwinger bastion'; 'continued on 17 December at daybreak, until at 8½ o'clock an adjutant of Jerome's with a detachment brought the body of Lieutenant Lehsten and asked for the exchange of the captured Captain Debruir, which the governor, however, did not grant. With pauses the bombardment lasted into the night. The fire it caused was put out' (the first words end the sentence begun in the preceding paragraph); 'a deputation of the burghers made modest representations to the governor for sparing the town and was dismissed reassured'; 'on 21 December the bombardment was renewed from 2½ until' (the sentence continues on p. 62); '5 in the morning. A deputation of burghers again turned to the governor with the request to grant them, amid so many afflictions, the comfort and hope of an early relief. The governor had to dismiss them without such a hope' (the first words end the sentence begun on p. 61); 'the bombardment was therefore, on the 25th after 1 o'clock, o-' (the sentence continues on p. 80: 'opened again'); 'pened again and lasted until 3 o'clock. At that time Colonel Duveyrier, general staff officer of General Vandamme, appeared with the summons to surrender, with the most boastful statements about the advantages won against the Prince of Pless as well as in Poland and Prussia. The governor gave a refusal' (the first words end the sentence begun on p. 79); 'during the parlementaire's presence a petition had come in from the magistracy and the merchants, followed by a deputation of 6 burghers, which repeated orally the request to put an end, if possible, to the town's many sufferings'; 'the governor thereupon assembled the generals and staff officers of the garrison, put the burghers' requests before them and asked their opinion: whether an armistice should be sought from the enemy and negotiations opened to relieve the town, or not? Only Major Lepel of the regiment Thile was unconditionally against any regard for the town. Nevertheless the governor, to calm the petitioners, wrote to General Vandamme at 9 o'clock and sought an armistice, and then had the magistracy summoned to inform it of this'; 'soon afterwards, at 10½, Colonel Duveyrier appeared again; General Vandamme had not granted the armistice, but had given the parlementaire full power to conclude a capitulation. The governor kept to his demand and regarded the negotiation as broken off'; 'on 26 December at 3 in the morning Colonel Duveyrier came back again and brought the enemy general's consent to the armistice, which was to last until 8 in the morning of the 27th'; 'a second deputation of the burghers was therefore brought before the governor at 8½ on the 26th, protested against the request of the first deputation, and declared that the burghers would rather let themselves be killed than vote for the surrender.1)'; 'the governor therefore replied to the petition received the day before:'; '"To the magistracy and merchants, etc., I reply to their petition addressed to me yesterday and their request repeated orally that, since I have now convinced myself that by far the greatest part of the inhabitants is not of this mind, but rather trembles before any surrender, I can take no further account of the above-mentioned petition."'; 'in view of this favourable mood of the burghers, and because the enemy continued the works against the fortress during the armistice and also alarmed the Springstern, the governor ended the armistice as early as 10 o'clock on the 26th, so that in the afternoon the fire from the walls began anew'; 'on 30 December at 6 in the morning it was reported from the Schweidnitz and Ohlau gates that firing of heavy guns and small arms could be heard and that the village of Dürgoy was burning'; 'the governor gave for answer: "that the enemy was manoeuvring to lure the garrison out of the town"'; 'General Lindener would hear no firing on the Ohlau gate, but saw only some troops of cavalry at Dürgoy, at which he had 2 24-pounders aimed'; 'the commandant present, General Krafft, had been made aware of it, and an attempt had been made to dissuade him from the opinion that the enemy was manoeuvring; but he had spoken harshly to everyone and finally dismissed them with the words: "that was nobody's business, he himself possessed sufficient judgement, etc."'; 'at 11 o'clock the garrison was assembled to make a sortie in case the enemy should be beaten. The fog now grew thicker; one could observe no further, but only heard that the fire moved further and further away in the direction of the Zobtenberg until toward 3 o'clock, so that the relief had been beaten'; 'from this moment the mood of the burghers and the troops turned very bad against the government; for everyone was convinced of the necessity of a sortie and ascribed its omission to the most impure motives'; 'at 3 in the afternoon the sky cleared and it began to freeze. That was the most unfavourable thing that could befall the garrison; for only by open water was the fortress, given the unreliability and weakness of the garrison, secured against a coup de main. The necessary measures were taken for breaking the ice of the Oder and the fortress ditches'; 'on the morning of the 3rd it lay out for signature at the town hall, where the opposition of a numerous counter-party made itself known. Nevertheless this request, signed by a hundred and some sixty burghers of all the guilds and trades, was handed to the governor together with a petition of the magistracy on the same matter, and a special list was attached by which only about 20,000 pounds of meat, mostly salted, were said to be left in the town, and a shortage of wood threatened bakers and brewers' ('it' is the circular petition named in the preceding sentence); 'toward 11 o'clock Captain Hammerer appeared again as parlementaire and took with him a letter of the governor with the request to send Colonel Duveyrier into the town to open negotiations. Nevertheless the fire from the walls was kept up, and was answered by a bombardment beginning at 1¼ in the afternoon, the most violent of the whole siege'; 'the governor summoned the commandant, Major General Krafft, and General Lindener, laid before them the report of the chief commissariat office and the burghers' peti-' (the word and sentence continue on p. 111); 'tions, and asked their opinion. The result of the deliberation was that they resolved to enter into a capitulation' (the first word ends the one begun on p. 110); 'at 4 in the afternoon Colonel Duveyrier came, empowered to negotiate the surrender. The bombardment still went on even now. The governor could no more obtain the armistice of 8 days he asked for, to give the Prince of Pless time for a new attempt at relief, than the dispatch of an officer to Kalisch, by whom he wished to make sure whether Russians were approaching or not. Only for arranging the affairs of the town and the garrison were 3 days granted'; 'only the artillery and the Land reserves kept the old Prussian discipline, as indeed the artillery had especially distinguished itself everywhere in this sho-' (the word and sentence continue on p. 112); 'rt siege.1)' (the end of the word and sentence begun on p. 111); '1) Colonel Blein says in his report to Napoleon: "the artillery of Breslau has proved that it came from a good school; it has adorned our trenches and made many embrasure shots"'; 'the abandonment of the outworks must therefore be regarded as a fault that, as we have seen, is to be ascribed solely to General Lindener, in contradiction with the engineer of the place. The enemy, when he found the outworks abandoned, at once took on another air; he recognised from it the weakness of the garrison and the faint-heartedness of the government, which wished only to secure itself against a coup de main and to secure a good capitulation'; '3) lack of attention to the provisioning of the place, on the part of the garrison as well as of the burghers. For the supply of baking wood too it would only have been necessary to have the thousands of Klafter of firewood before the Ziegel gate carried into the town by the many Oder boats'; '4) the omission of the sortie on 30 December, of which we have already spoken in detail above'; '5) the omission to open communications with the Prince of Pless by scouts. General Lindener is said to have borne the particular blame for this'; '6) that a capitulation was concluded without first having called the council of war prescribed by the regulations'; 'not to accuse the government of a particular omission, but to point out in general that in single cases, where the commandant sees the impossibility of holding the fortress longer, the possibility still remains of cutting through with the garrison to the field army or to fortresses nearby, we mention such a possibility at Breslau too. For a definite judgement on this, more adequate materials would have to be available'; 'if one reckons that about 1000 men, excluding the sick, remained behind in the town to conclude a capitulation for the protection of the inhabitants the next morning, and that about 150 men remained behind at the lower Ohlau bridges to prevent the enemy from restoring them quickly, then still 4000 men, including 230 mounted cavalrymen, could have left the fortress and joined the Prince of Pless'.

citations.locator: Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 4 (1851), p. 47 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: Als auf Veranlassung des Ingenieur-Brigadiers General Lindener am 19. Oktober die Armirungs-Arbeiten von Breslau ihren Anfang nahmen, hatte das Gouvernement sofort die Geschütze nach den Außenwerken abführen und angemessen aufstellen lassen, auch die Pallisadirung dieser Werke, die Instandsetzung der Zugbrücken ꝛc. angeordnet.

citations.locator: Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 4 (1851), p. 47 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: Wegen der Weitläuftigkeit der Werke und deren zum Theil schwierigen Verbindung unter einander, wurde die Festung in 4 Hauptfronten eingetheilt, und jede einem Stabsoffizier der Infanterie als Divisionär und einem älteren Artillerie-Offizier zur vollkommenen Ausrüstung der Werke und deren dereinstigen Vertheidigung übertragen.

citations.locator: Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 4 (1851), p. 47 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: Es stand somit in der Absicht des Gouvernements, sämmtliche Außenwerke festzuhalten und zu vertheidigen, doch als am 6. November der General Lindener eintraf, brachte er es dahin, daß man von diesem Vorhaben abging und die Vertheidigung auf den mit breiten Wassergräben umgebenen Hauptwall beschränkte; nur das Nikolai-Kronwerk, die Mühlbergschanze, das Oder-Kronwerk,

citations.locator: Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 4 (1851), p. 48 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: das Ohlauer Ravelin und das Ravelin R. vor dem Ziegelthor¹) sollten besetzt bleiben, von den übrigen Außenwerken aber das Geschütz nach dem Hauptwall zurückgeführt werden.

citations.locator: Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 4 (1851), p. 48 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: Erst später, als die Besatzung einige Verstärkung erhalten hatte, wurden die wichtigen und bereits pallisadirten Außenwerke: der Dom und der Springstern, ebenfalls in die Vertheidigung hineingezogen.

citations.locator: Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 4 (1851), p. 50 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: Die Wegräumung der, einer kräftigen Vertheidigung hinderlichen, Vorstädte unterblieb, theils in der Hoffnung eines Entsatzes durch die russischen Operationen, theils weil man die Stimmung der zahlreichen Bürgerschaft scheute, wenn man, bevor der Feind dazu nöthigte, diese weitläuftigen Baulichkeiten zerstörte, theils endlich auch, weil man glaubte, daß beim wirklichen Erscheinen des Feindes ein Niederschießen und Niederbrennen derselben immer noch möglich bleiben würde.

citations.locator: Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 4 (1851), p. 52 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: In Folge der Nachricht von der Rückkehr eines Theiles der bayerschen Truppen aus Südpreußen gegen Breslau sandte das Gouvernement am 7. Dezember den Artillerie-Lieutn. Fiebig mit der Hälfte der neu errichteten reitenden Batterie, einiger Infanterie und 30 Pferden auf das rechte Oder-Ufer, um alle Brücken über die alte Oder zu zerstören, und zugleich die Kasematten des verlassenen Werkes an der Paßschleuse, beim Ausfluß der alten Oder aus der neuen oberhalb Breslau, zu demoliren.

citations.locator: Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 4 (1851), p. 52 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: Beide Unternehmen gelangen vollständig, und gelegentlich nahm man den französischen Hauptmann Debruir gefangen, der vom General Vandamme aus Lissa an Jerome geschickt worden war, um ihm die Nachricht von der Einnahme von Glogau zu bringen: Aus der in Stücken zerrissenen Depesche entnahm man, daß der Feind bei Kosel, unterhalb Breslau, eine Brücke über die Oder schlagen wolle, und der Gefangene selbst sagte aus, daß Napoleon dem Jerome, und der M. Berthier dem General Vandamme aufs Ernstlichste versichert hätten, Breslau sei ein durchaus unhaltbarer Platz, der sich nicht 5 Tage behaupten könne.

citations.locator: Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 4 (1851), p. 53 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: Da sich die feindlichen Tirailleurs in die Häuser der Nikolai-Vorstadt und des Schweidnitzer Angers einnisteten, die vordersten Pallisadentambours und sogar die Kommunikation zwischen dem Nikolai-Thor und dem unterhalb liegenden Scheeren-Bastion beunruhigten, so wurde Abends um 6 Uhr die Nikolai-Vorstadt in Brand gesetzt.¹)

citations.locator: Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 4 (1851), p. 53 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: In Betracht, daß die bayersche Avantgarde die Festung auch auf dem rechten Oder-Ufer am 8. einschloß, somit die Benutzung der reitenden Artillerie auf diesem Ufer sehr beschränkt, dagegen der Bürgerwerder durch die feindlichen Arbeiten in der Nacht zum 8. bedroht wurde, befahl der Gouverneur dem Lieutenant Fiebig, mit der reitenden Artillerie in die Werke auf dem Bürgerwerder zu rücken und die Vertheidigung derselben zu übernehmen. Spä-

citations.locator: Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 4 (1851), p. 54 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: ter wurden diese Werke allmälig auch durch Infanterie, 8 schwere Geschütze und einige Kavallerie besetzt. Man beabsichtigte den Bürgerwerder, als einen Vorposten gegen die feindlichen Arbeiten, so lange besetzt zu behalten, als dies der Feind von der rechten Oderseite her gestatten würde, wo man das den Werder deckende Werk unbesetzt gelassen hatte.

citations.locator: Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 4 (1851), p. 54 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: Am 8. Dezember und in der Nacht zum 9. zündete der Vertheidiger auch die nächsten Häuser der Oder-Vorstadt an, um der Artillerie des Bürgerwerders und des Oder-Kronwerks freie Aussicht zu verschaffen.

citations.locator: Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 4 (1851), p. 54 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: Die Artillerie der Garnison feuerte unausgesetzt auf diese Arbeiten und zündete die Vorstadt Hinter-Dom an, um den feindlichen Batterien auf dem rechten Ufer begegnen zu können und den feindlichen Tirailleurs die Deckungen zu nehmen, aus welchen sie den Truppen auf den niedrigen Domwällen Schaden zufügen konnten.

citations.locator: Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 4 (1851), p. 54 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: Am 10. Morgens 6 Uhr war der Feind im Stande, das Bombardement gegen die Front am Nikolai-Thor und den Dom zu beginnen; die feindlichen Wurfgeschosse fügten den Bürgerhäu-

citations.locator: Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 4 (1851), p. 55 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: sern erheblichen Schaden zu, ohne zu zünden. Da im Allgemeinen das feindliche Feuer sich mehr auf die Stadt als auf die Wälle richtete, so befand sich die Besatzung auf diesen weit sicherer als in ihren Quartieren.

citations.locator: Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 4 (1851), p. 55 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: Gegen Mittag schwieg das Feuer, und nach 1 Uhr erschien der Kapitain Desterno, ehemaliger preußischer Dragoner-Lieutenant und zur Zeit Adjutant Jerome's, als Parlamentair und überreichte ein Aufforderungsschreiben, in welchem die Einnahme von Magdeburg, Stettin, Küstrin und Glogau, der Einzug der Franzosen in Warschau mitgetheilt und die Hoffnungslosigkeit für einen Entsatz ausgesprochen wurde. Der Parlamentair fügte hinzu, daß die Franzosen auch bei Thorn die Weichsel überschritten und nirgends Russen gesehen hätten, daß der König bereits bis hinter Memel zurückgegangen sei und Napoleon erklärt habe, nicht früher Frieden zu machen, als bis er Rußland gedemüthigt und das Bündniß mit Preußen gesprengt habe.

citations.locator: Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 4 (1851), p. 55 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: Der Gouverneur wies die Aufforderung entschieden zurück, und hatte auch während des Unterhandelns das Feuer nicht einstellen lassen.

citations.locator: Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 4 (1851), p. 55 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: Am 11. Dezember setzte der Feind das Bombardement fort, doch nur auf dem linken Oder-Ufer, da es dem auf dem Springstern kommandirenden Artillerie-Lieutenant Zimmermann, der bald darauf erschossen wurde, gelungen war, das feindliche Feuer zum Schweigen zu bringen. Auch auf der linken Oderseite gewann endlich das Feuer des Vertheidigers die Oberhand.

citations.locator: Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 4 (1851), p. 55 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: Am Abend mußte auch die Ohlauer-Vorstadt von der Besatzung angezündet werden.

citations.locator: Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 4 (1851), p. 56 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: Am 15. Dezember Morgens 6 Uhr begann das Bombardement somit aufs Neue und dauerte bis 1 Uhr Nachmittags. Die Stadt litt bedeutend, besonders das Kloster der Elisabethinerin, doch wurde das Feuer überall gelöscht.

citations.locator: Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 4 (1851), p. 56 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: Um 2 Uhr Nachmittags ließ Jerome die Festung abermals durch den General Lefebvre auffordern. Derselbe wurde mit unverbundenen Augen zum Gouverneur geführt, dem er viel Schmeichelhaftes über die

citations.locator: Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 4 (1851), p. 57 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: bisherige Vertheidigung sagen und erklären mußte, daß, wenn die Besatzung die angebotene ehrenvolle Kapitulation nicht annähme, die Stadt in einen Aschenhaufen verwandelt werden würde, wozu alle Mittel vorhanden wären. Auch fügte der General hinzu, daß Breslau zum Letztenmale belagert würde, indem Napoleon befohlen habe, gleich nach der Einnahme die Festungswerke zu schleifen. Der Antrag wurde zurückgewiesen, worauf um 3 Uhr das Bombardement erneuert wurde, jedoch nicht mit der Heftigkeit als am Morgen, und gegen Abend verstummte es allmälig.

citations.locator: Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 4 (1851), p. 57 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: Auch am 16. Dezember verhielt sich der Feind ruhig, und da der Gouverneur die Meldung erhielt, daß der Belagerer die Geschütze aus den Batterien zurückgenommen habe, so befahl er, daß eine Abtheilung von 2 Offizieren — Lieutenant Lehsten vom Infanterie-Regiment Thile und Lieutenant Seelstrang vom Kürassier-Regiment Henckel — 60 Schützen und 80 Reitern mit 300 Arbeitern aus dem Nikolai-Thor vorgehen, die Vorstadt vom Feinde säubern und die feindlichen Arbeiten zerstören sollte.

citations.locator: Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 4 (1851), p. 57 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: Gegen 1 Uhr Mittags brach der Ausfall, ohne daß ein bestimmter Führer ernannt worden, vor, wurde aber aus den Trümmern der niedergebrannten Häuser in der Nikolai-Vorstadt, in welche man unvorsichtig einging, durch ein lebhaftes Feuer empfangen und mit dem Verluste von 1 Offizier — Lieutenant Lehsten — und 10 Mann Todten und 7 Vermißten zurückgetrieben. Die Kavallerie brachte 10 Gefangene zurück.

citations.locator: Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 4 (1851), p. 58 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: Die Besatzung des Bürgerwerders widersetzte sich am 16. thätlich den daselbst kommandirenden Offizieren; es mußte ein Kavallerie-Kommando hinausgesandt werden, um die Rädelsführer zu verhaften. Die Besatzung wurde abgelöst und die beiden am meisten Betheiligten zwei Tage darauf im Zwinger-Bastion erschossen.

citations.locator: Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 4 (1851), p. 58 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: am 17. Dezember mit Tagesanbruch fortgesetzt, bis um 8½ Uhr ein Adjutant Jerome's mit einem Kommando den Leichnam des Lieutenants Lehsten überbrachte und die Auswechselung des gefangenen Hauptmanns Debruir erbat, die indessen der Gouverneur nicht genehmigte. In Pausen dauerte das Bombardement bis in die Nacht. Das dadurch verursachte Feuer wurde gelöscht.

citations.locator: Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 4 (1851), p. 58 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: Eine Deputation der Bürgerschaft machte dem Gouverneur bescheidene Vorstellungen wegen Schonung der Stadt und wurde beruhigt entlassen.

citations.locator: Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 4 (1851), p. 61 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: Am 21. Dezember wurde das Bombardement von 2½ bis

citations.locator: Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 4 (1851), p. 62 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: 5 Uhr Morgens erneuert. Eine Deputation von Bürgern wandte sich abermals an den Gouverneur mit der Bitte, ihr bei so vielen Drangsalen den Trost- und die Hoffnung eines baldigen Entsatzes zu gewähren. Der Gouverneur mußte sie ohne eine solche Hoffnung entlassen.

citations.locator: Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 4 (1851), p. 79 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: Das Bombardement wurde daher am 25. nach 1 Uhr wie-

citations.locator: Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 4 (1851), p. 80 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: der eröffnet und dauerte bis 3 Uhr. Um diese Zeit erschien der Oberst Duveyrier, Generalstabs-Offizier des Generals Vandamme, mit der Aufforderung zur Uebergabe unter den prahlerischsten Angaben über die errungenen Vortheile gegen den Fürsten von Pleß, so wie in Polen und Preußen. Der Gouverneur ertheilte eine abschlägige Antwort.

citations.locator: Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 4 (1851), p. 80 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: Während der Anwesenheit des Parlamentairs war eine Bittschrift vom Magistrat und der Kaufmannschaft eingegangen, welcher eine Deputation von 6 Bürgern folgte, die das Ansuchen mündlich wiederholte, den vielen Leiden der Stadt wo möglich ein Ende zu machen.

citations.locator: Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 4 (1851), p. 80 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: Der Gouverneur versammelte hierauf die Generale und Stabsoffiziere der Garnison, trug ihnen die Bitten der Bürgerschaft vor und fragte sie um ihre Meinung: ob man beim Feinde einen Waffenstillstand nachsuchen und Unterhandlungen zur Erleichterung der Stadt anknüpfen solle oder nicht? Nur der Major Lepel vom Regiment Thile war unbedingt gegen eine Berücksichtigung der Stadt. Dessenungeachtet schrieb der Gouverneur zur Beruhigung der Bittsteller an den General Vandamme um 9 Uhr, suchte einen Waffenstillstand nach, und ließ hierauf den Magistrat vorfordern, um ihm davon Mittheilung zu machen.

citations.locator: Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 4 (1851), p. 80 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: Bald nachher, 10½ Uhr, erschien der Oberst Duveyrier abermals; der General Vandamme hatte den Waffenstillstand nicht genehmigt, dagegen dem Parlamentair Vollmacht gegeben, eine Kapitulation einzugehen. Der Gouverneur hielt sich an seine Forderung und sah die Unterhandlung als abgebrochen an.

citations.locator: Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 4 (1851), p. 80 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: Am 26. Dezember um 3 Uhr Morgens kehrte der Oberst Duveyrier abermals zurück, und brachte die Einwilligung des feindlichen Generals zum Waffenstillstand, der bis zum 27. Morgens 8 Uhr dauern sollte.

citations.locator: Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 4 (1851), p. 81 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: Eine zweite Deputation der Bürgerschaft wurde daher um 8½ Uhr des 26. dem Gouverneur vorgeführt, protestirte gegen den Antrag der ersten Deputation, und erklärte, die Bürger würden sich eher todtschlagen lassen, als für die Uebergabe stimmen.¹)

citations.locator: Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 4 (1851), p. 81 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: Der Gouverneur erwiederte daher auf die am vergangenen Tage eingegangene Bittschrift:

citations.locator: Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 4 (1851), p. 81 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: „Einem ꝛc. Magistrat und Kaufmannschaft erwiedere auf deren gestern an mich erlassene Bittschrift und mündlich wiederholtes Ersuchen, daß, da ich mich jetzt überzeugt habe, daß bei weitem der größte Theil der Einwohner nicht dieses Sinnes ist, vielmehr vor jeder Uebergabe zittert, ich auf oben angeführte Bittschrift weiter keine Rücksicht nehmen kann.“

citations.locator: Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 4 (1851), p. 81 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: In Betracht dieser günstigen Stimmung der Bürger, und weil der Feind während des Waffenstillstandes die Arbeiten gegen die Festung fortsetzte, auch den Springstern allarmirte, kündigte der Gouverneur bereits um 10 Uhr des 26. den Waffenstillstand, so daß Nachmittags das Feuer von den Wällen aufs Neue begann.

citations.locator: Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 4 (1851), p. 86 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: Am 30. Dezember Morgens 6 Uhr wurde vom Schweidnitzer- und Ohlauer-Thor gemeldet, daß man Feuern aus grobem Geschütz und kleinem Gewehr höre, und daß das Dorf Dürgoy brenne.

citations.locator: Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 4 (1851), p. 86 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: Der Gouverneur ertheilte zur Antwort: „daß der Feind manövrire, um die Besatzung aus der Stadt zu locken.“

citations.locator: Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 4 (1851), p. 86 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: Der General Lindener wollte auf dem Ohlauer-Thor kein Feuern hören, sondern lediglich bei Dürgoy einige Kavallerietrupps sehen, auf welche er 2—24pfünder richten ließ.

citations.locator: Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 4 (1851), p. 87 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: Man hatte den anwesenden Kommandanten, General Krafft, darauf aufmerksam gemacht und versucht, ihn von der Meinung, der Feind manövrire, abzubringen; er hatte indessen jedermann hart angelassen und endlich mit den Worten abgefertigt: „es ginge das Niemand was an, er besitze selbst genügendes Urtheils-Vermögen ꝛc.“

citations.locator: Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 4 (1851), p. 87 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: Um 11 Uhr wurde die Garnison versammelt, um für den Fall, daß der Feind geschlagen würde, einen Ausfall zu machen. Der Nebel wurde nun stärker; man konnte nicht weiter beobachten, sondern hörte nur, daß das Feuer sich in der Richtung des Zobtenberges bis gegen 3 Uhr mehr und mehr entfernte, der Entsatz mithin geschlagen sei.

citations.locator: Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 4 (1851), p. 87 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: Die Stimmung der Bürgerschaft und der Truppen wurde von diesem Augenblick an eine sehr üble gegen das Gouvernement; denn Jedermann war von der Nothwendigkeit eines Ausfalls durchdrungen, und schrieb das Unterlassen desselben den unlautersten Motiven zu.

citations.locator: Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 4 (1851), p. 109 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: Um 3 Uhr Nachmittags klärte sich der Himmel auf, und es fing an zu frieren. Das war das Ungünstigste, was der Besatzung begegnen konnte; denn nur durch offenes Wasser war die Festung bei der Unsicherheit und Schwäche der Besatzung gegen einen Handstreich gesichert. Man traf die erforderlichen Maßregeln zum Aufeisen der Oder und der Festungsgräben.

citations.locator: Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 4 (1851), p. 110 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: Am 3. Morgens lag sie auf dem Rathhause zur Unterschrift aus, wobei der Widerspruch einer zahlreichen Gegenpartei sich zu erkennen gab. Dessenungeachtet wurde dieses Gesuch, unterzeichnet von hundert und etlichen sechszig Bürgern aus allen Innungen und Gewerken, nebst einer Bittschrift des Magistrats in gleicher Angelegenheit, dem Gouverneur überreicht, und ein spezielles Verzeichniß beigefügt, nach welchem nur noch etwa 20,000 Pfund Fleisch, größtentheils gepökeltes, in der Stadt vorhanden sein, und Holzmangel bei Bäckern und Brauern drohen sollte.

citations.locator: Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 4 (1851), p. 110 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: Gegen 11 Uhr erschien der Hauptmann Hammerer abermals als Parlamentair, und nahm ein Schreiben des Gouverneurs mit dem Gesuch mit, den Obersten Duveyrier zum Anknüpfen von Unterhandlungen nach der Stadt zu senden. Dessenungeachtet wurde das Feuer von den Wällen unterhalten, und durch ein um 1¼ Uhr Nachmittags beginnendes Bombardement, das heftigste während der ganzen Belagerung, beantwortet.

citations.locator: Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 4 (1851), p. 110 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: Der Gouverneur ließ den Kommandanten, den General-Major Krafft, und den General Lindener zu sich bescheiden, legte ihnen die Meldung des Ober-Proviant-Amts und die Bittschrif-

citations.locator: Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 4 (1851), p. 111 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: ten der Bürgerschaft vor, und befragte sie um ihre Meinung. Das Resultat der Berathung war, daß man sich entschloß, eine Kapitulation einzugehen.

citations.locator: Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 4 (1851), p. 111 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: Nachmittags 4 Uhr kam der Oberst Duveyrier, zu Unterhandlungen wegen der Uebergabe bevollmächtigt. Das Bombardement dauerte auch jetzt noch fort. Der Gouverneur konnte den verlangten Waffenstillstand auf 8 Tage, um dem Fürsten von Pleß Zeit zu einem neuen Entsatzversuch zu geben, so wenig erlangen, als die Absendung eines Offiziers nach Kalisch, durch den man sich überzeugen wollte, ob Russen im Anmarsch wären oder nicht. Lediglich zum Arrangement der Angelegenheiten der Stadt und der Garnison wurden 3 Tage bewilligt.

citations.locator: Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 4 (1851), p. 111 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: Nur die Artillerie und die Land-Reserven beobachteten die alte preußische Zucht, wie denn überhaupt die Artillerie in dieser kur-

citations.locator: Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 4 (1851), p. 112 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: zen Belagerung sich überall besonders hervorgethan hatte.¹)

citations.locator: Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 4 (1851), p. 112 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: 1) Der Oberst Blein sagt in seinem Bericht an Napoleon: „die Artillerie von Breslau hat bewiesen, daß sie aus einer guten Schule war; sie hat unsere Laufgräben ausgeschmückt, und viele Schartenschüsse gemacht.“

citations.locator: Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 4 (1851), p. 116 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: Das Aufgeben der Außenwerke muß daher als ein Fehler betrachtet werden, der lediglich, wie wir gesehen haben, dem General Lindener, im Widerspruch mit dem Ingenieur vom Platz, zuzuschreiben ist. Der Feind nahm, als er die Außenwerke verlassen fand, alsbald eine andere Miene an; er erkannte daraus die Schwäche der Garnison, die Zaghaftigkeit des Gouvernements, das sich nur gegen einen Handstreich und eine gute Kapitulation sichern wollte.

citations.locator: Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 4 (1851), p. 116 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: 3) Mangel an Aufmerksamkeit auf die Verproviantirung des Orts, sowohl von Seiten der Besatzung als der Bürgerschaft. Auch zur Versorgung mit Backholz wäre es nur erforderlich gewesen, die Tausende von Klaftern Brennholz vor dem Ziegelthor durch die vielen Oderschiffe in die Stadt transportiren zu lassen.

citations.locator: Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 4 (1851), p. 116 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: 4) Das Unterlassen des Ausfalls am 30. Dezember, wovon wir bereits oben das Nähere gesprochen haben.

citations.locator: Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 4 (1851), p. 116 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: 5) Das Unterlassen des Anknüpfens von Verbindungen mit dem Fürsten von Pleß durch Kundschafter. Der General Lindener soll hiervon besonders die Schuld getragen haben.

citations.locator: Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 4 (1851), p. 116 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: 6) Daß eine Kapitulation abgeschlossen worden, ohne vorher den vom Reglement vorgeschriebenen Kriegsrath zusammenberufen zu haben.

citations.locator: Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 4 (1851), p. 116 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: Nicht um das Gouvernement einer bestimmten Verabsäumung zu zeihen, sondern um im Allgemeinen aufmerksam zu machen, daß in einzelnen Fällen, wo der Kommandant die Unmöglichkeit sieht, die Festung länger zu behaupten, noch die Möglichkeit vorhanden bleibt, sich mit der Besatzung zur Feld-Armee oder nach nahe gelegenen Festungen durchzuschlagen, erwähnen wir einer solchen Möglichkeit auch bei Breslau. Zu einem bestimmten Urtheil hierüber müßten genügendere Materialien vorliegen.

citations.locator: Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 4 (1851), p. 118 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: Rechnet man, daß etwa 1000 Mann, excl. Kranke, in der Stadt zurückblieben, um zum Schutz der Einwohner am folgenden Morgen eine Kapitulation einzugehen, daß etwa 150 Mann an den untern Ohlaubrücken zurückblieben, um den Feind an der schnellen Wiederherstellung zu verhindern, so würden immer noch 4000 Mann, incl. 230 Mann berittener Kavalleristen, die Festung verlassen und zum Fürsten Pleß haben stoßen können.

claims.value: Bodart records the siege and capture of Breslau from 6 December 1806 to 6 January 1807: the French, Bavarians and Württembergers under Prince Jérôme compelled the Prussian garrison under Lieutenant General v. Thiele to surrender the place; the garrison was allowed to march out with all military honours but had to lay down its arms and fell into captivity as prisoners of war, and the officers, 135, were set free on their word of honour not to serve again in this war against France or its allies. Höpfner: on the 3rd, after a petition of the burghers and the magistracy, the governor, Krafft and Lindener resolved to capitulate; at 4 in the afternoon Duveyrier came empowered to negotiate, and 3 days were granted only to arrange the affairs of the town and the garrison; on 5 January the points of capitulation were signed by both sides after 6 o'clock, not without disputes. That day insubordination broke out among the troops, with gross defiance of superiors and the destruction and sale of royal property and war stores, and on the 6th the excesses of soldiers and town rabble grew until the Nikolai and Oder gates had to be handed over to side A that evening. On 7 January the garrison marched out toward 10 in the morning and laid down its arms, the worse part smashing many muskets and drums; the besiegers, with Jérôme at their head, filed through Breslau and out by the Schweidnitz gate, and General Minucci remained in Breslau with 9 battalions, 1 squadron and some batteries. The officers were released on their word of honour, the foresters and Jäger called in for fortress service returned to their former service and the invalids and married non-commissioned officers and soldiers to their families, and the rest of the men were escorted into captivity by the Bavarian 13th Infantry Regiment. Foucart's narrative: Breslau capitulated only on 3 January; the governor at once resumed the negotiations he had broken off, the capitulation was signed on 3 January at 9 in the evening, and Jérôme, who had left Pultusk on 30 December, arrived at Lissa on the 6th to see the garrison, 5,500 men strong, file past him on the 8th. The Emperor wrote from Warsaw on 7 January, 'Breslau having surrendered', ordering the investment of Brieg, Kosel and Schweidnitz.
claims.rationale: The frozen frame outcome with Höpfner's, Foucart's and the Emperor's accounts, read from the page images (Bodart's from the frame transcription); no source read gives a different result. The capitulation's text was not seen; its terms are Höpfner's summary and Bodart's. The dates differ: Foucart has the capitulation signed on 3 January at 9 in the evening, Höpfner the decision and the opening of the negotiation on the 3rd and the signature on the 5th after 6; Bodart's end date, 6 January, is the evening Höpfner has the gates handed over; and Höpfner has the march-out on the 7th, Foucart the garrison filing past Jérôme on the 8th (our comparison). Bodart's honours of war are not in the passages read; Höpfner has the garrison lay down its arms on marching out (our comparison). The garrison's numbers at the end are in claim side-b-losses. English renderings (ours): Bodart, as in claim bodart-strength; 'on the morning of the 3rd it lay out for signature at the town hall, where the opposition of a numerous counter-party made itself known. Nevertheless this request, signed by a hundred and some sixty burghers of all the guilds and trades, was handed to the governor together with a petition of the magistracy on the same matter, and a special list was attached by which only about 20,000 pounds of meat, mostly salted, were said to be left in the town, and a shortage of wood threatened bakers and brewers' ('it' is the circular petition named in the preceding sentence); 'the governor summoned the commandant, Major General Krafft, and General Lindener, laid before them the report of the chief commissariat office and the burghers' peti-' (the word and sentence continue on p. 111); 'tions, and asked their opinion. The result of the deliberation was that they resolved to enter into a capitulation' (the first word ends the one begun on p. 110); 'at 4 in the afternoon Colonel Duveyrier came, empowered to negotiate the surrender. The bombardment still went on even now. The governor could no more obtain the armistice of 8 days he asked for, to give the Prince of Pless time for a new attempt at relief, than the dispatch of an officer to Kalisch, by whom he wished to make sure whether Russians were approaching or not. Only for arranging the affairs of the town and the garrison were 3 days granted'; 'on 5 January Colonel Duveyrier appeared again, and the points of capitulation were signed by both sides, not without disputes, representations and counter-representations, after 6 o'clock'; 'already on this day, when the certainty of the capitulation was received, the spirit of insubordination broke out among the troops and showed itself in gross defiance of superiors, destruction of royal property, and sale of the royal effects and war stores'; 'on the 6th these excesses were continued to an increased degree by the military together with the rabble of the town, on the walls as well as in the town, especially at royal buildings, magazines, etc., and neither by the town police nor by cavalry patrols could the debauchery, plundering, shooting in the streets, etc., be stopped, so that they finally saw themselves compelled to have the Nikolai and Oder gates occupied by the enemy as early as the evening of the 6th'; 'on 7 January the garrison marched out toward 10 in the morning and laid down its arms; the worse part of the garrison continued the disorders even here, and a great number of muskets and drums were smashed'; 'the besiegers, at their head Jerome, who had arrived again, filed through Breslau and marched out again by the Schweidnitz gate. General Minucci remained behind in Breslau with 9 battalions, 1 squadron and some batteries'; 'the foresters and Jäger called in for fortress service returned to their former service, and the invalids and the married non-commissioned officers and soldiers to their families; the officers were released on their word of honour; the rest of the men were escorted into captivity by the Bavarian 13th Infantry Regiment'; 'immediately after the capture of Glogau, the corps of allied troops had begun operations against Breslau, which capitulated only on 3 January1'; 'the governor of Breslau at once resumed the negotiations he had broken off. On 3 January at 9 in the evening the capitulation was signed'; 'Prince Jérôme, having left Pultusk on 30 December, arrived at Lissa on the 6th to see the garrison of Breslau, 5,500 men strong, file past him on the 8th'; 'the Emperor to the major general. Warsaw, 7 January 1807'; '... Breslau having surrendered, you will give Prince Jérôme the order to invest Brieg, Kosel and Schweidnitz at once, so that only Neisse and Glatz remain, and to keep a reserve corps of infantry, cavalry and artillery at Breslau, where he will stay in person, visiting the three blockades every fortnight, however...'.

citations.quote: 1806 6./12. bis 1807 6./1. BELAGERUNG und EINNAHME von Breslau

Die Franzosen, Bayern und Württemberger (zus. 27.000 M. mit 52 Feld- und Belagerungsgeschützen) unter Pz. Jerôme Bonaparte nötigen die preußische Besatzung (6.000 M. mit 272 Geschützen) unter Gen.-Lt. v. Thiele zur Übergabe des Platzes.
Die Garnison durfte mit allen militärischen Ehren ausmarschieren, mußte jedoch die Waffen niederlegen und geriet in Kriegsgefangenschaft.
Die Offiziere (135) wurden gegen ehrenwörtliche Verpflichtung, in diesem Kriege nicht mehr gegen Frankreich oder dessen Bundesgenossen zu dienen, auf freien Fuß gesetzt.

claims.value: Side A's losses in the passages read are partial. Höpfner: on 7 December side B's expedition took prisoner Captain Debruir, whom Vandamme had sent to Jérôme; by the 12th side A awaited replacements from Glogau for its dismounted guns; on 16 December the cavalry of side B's sortie brought back 10 prisoners; in the night to the 23rd the garrison's musket fire inflicted considerable losses on the Bavarians approaching the works; and in the storm of the 23rd two soldiers carrying a raft were shot at the start of the fire, the attackers retreated with considerable loss, a French officer on the rafts surrendered with some privates, and the two Bavarian companies and the volunteer detachments withdrew with loss. No passage read gives a total loss for side A.
claims.rationale: Höpfner, read from the page images; the figures were checked on full-resolution crops. They cover only parts of the siege and are not a total; Bodart's entry gives no loss for side A (claim bodart-strength). 'Considerable' is Höpfner's word, without a figure. No passage read gives side A's losses in the bombardments, in the covering detachments or from sickness, though Höpfner says the besieging troops were suffering exceedingly from the bad season (claim side-a-strength); Foucart's narrative, which leaves the operations against the place aside, gives none. English renderings (ours): 'in consequence of the news of the return of part of the Bavarian troops from South Prussia against Breslau, the government on 7 December sent Artillery Lieutenant Fiebig with half of the newly raised horse battery, some infantry and 30 horses to the right bank of the Oder, to destroy all the bridges over the old Oder and at the same time to demolish the casemates of the abandoned work at the Paßschleuse, where the old Oder leaves the new above Breslau'; 'both undertakings succeeded completely, and on the way the French Captain Debruir was taken prisoner, whom General Vandamme had sent from Lissa to Jerome to bring him the news of the capture of Glogau: from the dispatch, torn to pieces, it was learned that the enemy meant to throw a bridge over the Oder at Kosel, below Breslau, and the prisoner himself stated that Napoleon had most earnestly assured Jerome, and Marshal Berthier General Vandamme, that Breslau was an altogether untenable place that could not hold out 5 days'; 'on the 12th and in the night to the 13th the town was indeed fired on, but only slowly, since the enemy was still awaiting munition and, in place of the dismounted guns, replacements from Glogau'; 'on 16 December too the enemy kept quiet, and since the governor received the report that the besieger had withdrawn the guns from the batteries, he ordered that a detachment of 2 officers - Lieutenant Lehsten of the infantry regiment Thile and Lieutenant Seelstrang of the cuirassier regiment Henckel - 60 marksmen and 80 horsemen with 300 workers should advance from the Nikolai gate, clear the suburb of the enemy and destroy the enemy's works'; 'toward 1 o'clock at midday the sortie broke out, without a definite leader having been named, but it was met by a lively fire from the ruins of the burnt-down houses in the Nikolai suburb, into which it had incautiously gone, and was driven back with the loss of 1 officer - Lieutenant Lehsten - and 10 men dead and 7 missing. The cavalry brought back 10 prisoners'; 'on 22 December from 3 in the morning with pauses until the evening, and the fire raged most violently in the night to the 23rd, when fires broke out in several places' (the end of the sentence begun in the preceding paragraph); 'since Lieutenant Fiebig reported from the Bürgerwerder in the night that the enemy was approaching on the Oder with 12 vessels, to all appearance to land on the Werder, the general alarm was beaten. During the violent bombardment the enemy also approached the works at several other places, thus near the Nikolai gate, the Schweidnitz gate, along the Ohlau, etc., whereby the musket fire opened by the garrison inflicted considerable losses on the Bavarians'; 'on 23 December at 6 in the morning it became apparent that the enemy, under the protection of the fire and of those demonstrations, was trying to cross the wet outer ditch at the ravelin R. by two cask bridges, so as to storm the fortress from there'; 'only at 5 o'clock could the first raft be brought into the outer ditch; it was 30 feet long, and 3 others of 12-15 feet had to be brought in to reach the far bank. The sappers, inexperienced in such work, had been able to bind the rafts together only slowly; a drunken officer had come onto the rafts and also greatly hindered the workers; and finally a thoughtless shout, and the leap of a French sapper non-commissioned officer into the water to fasten the rafts to the palisades of the enveloppe under attack, had drawn the attention of an' (the sentence continues on p. 65); 'artilleryman on the Ohlau ravelin; he had fired a round of canister at the place of the noise, and at once the guns of the Bernhard and Taschen bastions, which commanded the enveloppe, and the infantry garrison of the adjacent walls had joined in this fire. Two enemy soldiers carrying a raft were shot at the very beginning of the fire, the other carriers ran away, and the enemy saw himself forced to retreat with considerable loss. A French officer who was on the rafts had to surrender with some privates' (the first words end the sentence begun on p. 64); 'the two Bavarian companies had meanwhile attacked the Ohlau tambour and already tried to cut down the palisades, but had to withdraw with loss, like the detachments of volunteers'.

claims.value: Side B (Prussian) lost the fortress and its garrison. Höpfner: the sortie of 16 December was driven back with the loss of 1 officer, Lieutenant Lehsten, and 10 men dead and 7 missing; the two men most involved in the Bürgerwerder mutiny were shot; desertion was increasing very considerably by mid-December and still in the days before 30 December, and was practised ever more boldly at the turn of the year, deserters especially of the regiment Thile betraying the state of the fortress, such as the time and place of the daily relief of the guard, on which side A fired so that several men were killed and wounded at the assembly place; by General Lindener's journal the garrison had 13 dead, 24 wounded and 568 sick. There marched out in all 116 officers and 5270 non-commissioned officers and privates, and 240 guns and 3640 Centner of powder were handed over; the officers were released on their word of honour, the foresters and Jäger returned to their former service and the invalids and married non-commissioned officers and soldiers to their families, and the rest were escorted into captivity. Foucart's narrative: the garrison that filed past Jérôme on the 8th was 5,500 men strong. Bodart: the garrison fell into captivity as prisoners of war, its officers, 135, set free on their word of honour. The town, separately, by Höpfner: 7 inhabitants were killed and 22 wounded in the bombardment of 21 December; in all, in the houses alone, 35 persons were killed and 88 wounded, 7 houses were burnt and over 1500 damaged, and in the suburbs over 350 properties, excluding Neudorf and Siebenhufen, were burnt down; the magistracy put the town's damage on 3 January at 1 million, a figure later reduced by judicial assessment to 249,145 Thaler.
claims.rationale: Separate accounts, read from the page images (Bodart's from the frame transcription), not combined. The journal's 13 dead are not reconciled with the sortie's 1 officer and 10 men dead, the two men shot and Lieutenant Zimmermann's death (claim side-b-command); no passage read counts the deserters. The 116 officers and 5270 men who marched out are 19 officers and 571 men fewer than the return of 1 January (claim side-b-strength), and Höpfner does not say whether the sick or the men sent home are in his count (our arithmetic and reading). Foucart's 5,500 compare with Höpfner's 116 officers and 5270 men, and Bodart's 135 officers with Höpfner's return of 1 January rather than his 116 officers who marched out (our comparison). The 240 guns handed over are compared with the guns on the walls in claim bodart-strength. The town's losses are the inhabitants' and are kept apart from the garrison's. English renderings (ours): Bodart, as in claim bodart-strength; 'on 16 December too the enemy kept quiet, and since the governor received the report that the besieger had withdrawn the guns from the batteries, he ordered that a detachment of 2 officers - Lieutenant Lehsten of the infantry regiment Thile and Lieutenant Seelstrang of the cuirassier regiment Henckel - 60 marksmen and 80 horsemen with 300 workers should advance from the Nikolai gate, clear the suburb of the enemy and destroy the enemy's works'; 'toward 1 o'clock at midday the sortie broke out, without a definite leader having been named, but it was met by a lively fire from the ruins of the burnt-down houses in the Nikolai suburb, into which it had incautiously gone, and was driven back with the loss of 1 officer - Lieutenant Lehsten - and 10 men dead and 7 missing. The cavalry brought back 10 prisoners'; 'the garrison of the Bürgerwerder resisted the officers commanding there by force on the 16th; a cavalry detachment had to be sent out to arrest the ringleaders. The garrison was relieved and the two most involved were shot two days later in the Zwinger bastion'; 'desertion was already increasing very considerably in the garrison, although the men were cared for as well as possible; they' (the sentence continues on p. 58); 'had for the most part been provided with greatcoats from the cloth procured for the army by contributions, and each relief of the garrison of the walls received warm beer and brandy, for whose purchase the burghers had made a collection' (the end of the sentence begun on p. 57); 'on 30 December at 6 in the morning it was reported from the Schweidnitz and Ohlau gates that firing of heavy guns and small arms could be heard and that the village of Dürgoy was burning'; 'desertion was still increasing'; 'complaint came in to the government that desertion was being practised ever more boldly. The locks on the gates of a palisade tambour were found knocked off, and even heaps of earth thrown up against the palisades to climb over them more easily. It was also evident that much about the state of the fortress was betrayed to the enemy by deserters, especially of the infantry regiment Thile; for example, the time and place of the daily relief. At that time the enemy then fired so briskly that several men were killed and wounded at the assembly place, and it was found necessary to change the time of the relief more often'; 'the garrison had, by General Lindener's journal, 13 dead, 24 wounded and 568 sick'; 'there marched out in all still: 116 officers, 5270 non-commissioned officers and privates; 240 guns and 3640 Centner of powder were handed over to the enemy'; 'the foresters and Jäger called in for fortress service returned to their former service, and the invalids and the married non-commissioned officers and soldiers to their families; the officers were released on their word of honour; the rest of the men were escorted into captivity by the Bavarian 13th Infantry Regiment'; 'Prince Jérôme, having left Pultusk on 30 December, arrived at Lissa on the 6th to see the garrison of Breslau, 5,500 men strong, file past him on the 8th'; 'on 21 December the bombardment was renewed from 2½ until' (the sentence continues on p. 62); '5 in the morning. A deputation of burghers again turned to the governor with the request to grant them, amid so many afflictions, the comfort and hope of an early relief. The governor had to dismiss them without such a hope' (the first words end the sentence begun on p. 61); 'from the fortress the burning of the market town of Hundsfeld was observed and taken as a sign that the Russians were approaching and the enemy withdrawing and burning the villages of the neighbourhood. But already at 10 o'clock the bombardment began anew, was continued until 1 at midday and did particular damage, since a mass of inhabitants had left their shelters on the strength of that news. 7 inhabitants were killed, 22 wounded'; 'of the burghers, in the houses alone, 35 persons had been killed and 88 wounded; 7 houses had been laid in ashes and over 1500 damaged, and in the suburbs over 350 properties - excluding Neudorf and Siebenhufen - had been burnt down'; 'the damage to the town given by the magistracy on 3 January was said to amount to 1 million; a statement that was later reduced by judicial assessment to 249,145 Thaler'.
