claims.value: Bodart calls Breslau the capital of Prussian Silesia. Höpfner: the works were extensive and partly hard to connect, and the fortress was divided into 4 main fronts; the main wall was surrounded by wide water ditches, with outworks including the Nikolai crownwork, the Mühlberg redoubt, the Oder crownwork, the Ohlau ravelin, the ravelin R. before the Ziegel gate, the Dom and the Springstern, and an enveloppe around the fortress; the Bürgerwerder, whose works were held as an outpost, was separated from side A's approaches by an arm of the Oder; the Oder bank where side A's left parallel rested lay 10-12 feet above the water, with a sandbank reachable unseen from the Bürgerwerder; and the extensive suburbs, which hindered the defence and were not cleared, gave side A's skirmishers cover until the garrison burnt the Nikolai, Hinter-Dom and Ohlau suburbs and the nearest houses of the Oder suburb. Blein found the main wall unrevetted at the Schweidnitz and Ohlau gates, the wet main ditch over 120 feet wide, an earthen enveloppe with lunettes at its salients, and the outer ditch around it 60-70 feet wide and 6-7 feet deep. In Vandamme's expectation, as Höpfner gives it, a population of 60,000 would not be sacrificed to works that owed their preservation only to the mild weather. Foucart places Höflchen, Montbrun's first position, a league from the town, and Gnichwitz 20 km from Breslau on the road to Schweidnitz. Höpfner has frost set in at 3 in the afternoon of a day before 2 January, open water being the fortress's only protection against a coup de main given the unreliability and weakness of the garrison, and, after the night to the 3rd, the weather turn milder again and the water stay open.
claims.rationale: Location, works and weather as described, read from the page images (Bodart's from the frame transcription). Höpfner's Plan XVIII of Breslau was not inspected, and where each work stood is taken only from the descriptions; the works' state and occupation are in claim fortification. Blein's findings are Höpfner's report of his reconnaissance. The ground is tagged inherited; the weather is kept with it. The day the frost set in is dated on p. 108, which was read in the OCR only and not registered. Foucart prints 'Schweibnitz' on p. 95 and 'Schweidnitz' on p. 97; the renderings keep his spelling. English renderings (ours): Bodart, '(capital of Prussian Silesia)'; 'because of the extent of the works and their partly difficult connection with one another, the fortress was divided into 4 main fronts, and each was entrusted to a staff officer of the infantry as divisional commander and an older artillery officer, for the complete equipment of the works and their eventual defence'; 'it was thus the government's intention to hold and defend all the outworks, but when General Lindener arrived on 6 November he brought it about that this plan was abandoned and the defence restricted to the main wall, surrounded by wide water ditches; only the Nikolai crownwork, the Mühlberg redoubt, the Oder crownwork,' (the sentence continues on p. 48); 'the Ohlau ravelin and the ravelin R. before the Ziegel gate1) were to remain occupied, while the guns of the other outworks were to be brought back to the main wall' (the end of the sentence begun on p. 47; the note refers to Höpfner's plan XVIII of Breslau); 'only later, when the garrison had received some reinforcement, were the important and already palisaded outworks, the Dom and the Springstern, also drawn into the defence'; 'the enveloppe that surrounded the fortress was to be occupied only by day, by single marksmen and Jäger'; 'considering that the Bavarian advance guard enclosed the fortress on the right bank of the Oder too on the 8th, so that the use of the horse artillery on that bank was much restricted, while the Bürgerwerder was threatened by the enemy's works in the night to the 8th, the governor ordered Lieutenant Fiebig to move with the horse artillery into the works on the Bürgerwerder and take over their defence. La-' (the word and sentence continue on p. 54); 'ter these works were gradually also occupied by infantry, 8 heavy guns and some cavalry. The intention was to keep the Bürgerwerder occupied, as an outpost against the enemy's works, for as long as the enemy would allow it from the right side of the Oder, where the work covering the Werder had been left unoccupied' (the first word ends the one begun on p. 53); 'from the left second parallel an approach trench with a small place of arms was to be pushed forward, so that from it the Württemberg Jäger could harass the Prussian gunners on the Bürgerwerder; but in the night to the 14th they struck quite unexpectedly on the arm of the Oder that separated the enemy from the works of the Bürgerwerder'; 'since the bank of the Oder where the first-named parallel rested lay 10-12 feet above the water level, and from the parallel one could reach a sandbank lying there unseen from the Bürgerwerder, this junction gave the besieger great advantages'; 'the clearing of the suburbs, which hindered a vigorous defence, was not done, partly in the hope of a relief by the Russian operations, partly because the government feared the mood of the numerous burghers if it destroyed these extensive buildings before the enemy forced it to, and partly, finally, because it was believed that when the enemy actually appeared it would still be possible to shoot them down and burn them'; 'since the enemy's tirailleurs lodged themselves in the houses of the Nikolai suburb and of the Schweidnitz Anger and harassed the foremost palisade tambours and even the communication between the Nikolai gate and the Scheeren bastion lying below it, the Nikolai suburb was set on fire in the evening at 6 o'clock.1)'; 'on 8 December and in the night to the 9th the defender also set fire to the nearest houses of the Oder suburb, to give the artillery of the Bürgerwerder and of the Oder crownwork a free view'; 'the garrison's artillery fired without pause on these works and set fire to the Hinter-Dom suburb, so as to be able to counter the enemy's batteries on the right bank and take from the enemy's tirailleurs the cover from which they could do harm to the troops on the low walls of the Dom'; 'in the evening the garrison had to set fire to the Ohlau suburb as well'; 'for want of a good plan of Breslau, already on 17, 18 and 19 December the engineer Colonel' (the sentence continues on p. 63); 'Blein had reconnoitred the works on the left bank of the Oder as thoroughly as possible and in doing so established that the main wall was not revetted at two extended places, namely at the Schweidnitz and Ohlau gates; that before the wet main ditch, over 120 feet wide, there was an enveloppe of earth, covered at its salient angles by lunettes with retired flanks; that these works were indeed provided with storm-poles and palisades, but were occupied only before the revetted front of the Nikolai gate, against which the siege works had so far been directed; and finally that the outer ditch surrounding the enveloppe had a width of 60-70 feet and a depth of 6-7 feet' (the end of the sentence begun on p. 62); 'on General Minucci's return, General Vandamme, who had ordered the building of 4 new batteries in order to bring into them a further 8 24-pounders, 6 12-pounders and 2 mortars that were arriving from Glogau, believed he must set the town seriously on fire and inform the governor of the defeat of the relief troops and of the means he possessed to destroy the town. He expected that a population of 60,000 inhabitants would not be sacrificed to the holding of works that owed their preservation only to the mild weather. All this was done without the knowledge of General Hédouville, although this general, as mentioned, was to continue the command in Jerome's name'; 'General Montbrun, preceding the Württemberg division, moved before Breslau by the left bank of the Oder. On the morning of the 6th he was a league from the town, at Höflchen, where he took position; he at once sent a party over to the right bank of the Oder to gather information on the arrival of the Bavarian troops, sent a detachment of 25 men and an officer to take post at Gnichwitz, 20 km from Breslau on the road to Schweibnitz, and dispatched to Schweibnitz a trusted man he had with him, with the task of reporting to him within two days the composition of the garrison of that place'; 'at 3 in the afternoon the sky cleared and it began to freeze. That was the most unfavourable thing that could befall the garrison; for only by open water was the fortress, given the unreliability and weakness of the garrison, secured against a coup de main. The necessary measures were taken for breaking the ice of the Oder and the fortress ditches'; 'on 2 January at 11 o'clock Colonel Duveyrier and Captain Hammerer were let in. Their business consisted in the request for the release of several persons, mostly of the female sex, and besides in the enumeration, repeated to weariness, of all the reasons that were to make the sur-' (the word and sentence continue on p. 110); 'render of the fortress necessary. Both officers were dismissed with expressions of courtesy, and at 3 o'clock the garrison's fire began again, at 5 o'clock a 2-hour bombardment by the enemy' (the first word ends the one begun on p. 109); 'in the night to the 3rd the enemy bombarded from 11 until 4 o'clock'; 'the weather turned milder again; the water stayed open'.

claims.value: Side B (Prussian), in Höpfner: 208 pieces of various calibres stood on the walls and 46 guns were partly in reserve and partly unusable in the arsenal; there were very considerable stores of finished munition, loose powder and iron munition, mostly in a single magazine under the cavalier of the Taschen bastion, whose weak vaults a bomb could have blown up with much of the town. Food had been laid in for only 5-6 weeks, except some articles: the provincial authority had at first called for provisioning for 4 weeks, the government took no energetic measures after the first investment in mid-November, and the burghers' provisioning for 6 months was ordered only on 17 November. Time was too short to restore the works fully, the fortress had only two engineer officers, and the garrison was too weak to help much with the works. Most of the men had greatcoats from cloth bought by contributions, and each relief on the walls got warm beer and brandy paid for by a collection among the burghers. The chief commissariat office reported that wood for baking bread was beginning to run short, and the list attached to the petition of the 3rd gave only about 20,000 pounds of meat, mostly salted, left in the town, with bakers and brewers threatened by a shortage of wood; Höpfner reckons from the commissariat's figures, 40 Klafter used in 10 weeks and 12 handed over, a 3-week supply of baking wood left, and says that thousands of Klafter of firewood before the Ziegel gate could have been brought in by the Oder boats. At the capitulation 240 guns and 3640 Centner of powder were handed over; the fortress is said to have fired about 50,000 rounds. Side A: the capture of Glogau put a considerable mass of heavy guns and great stores of munition into Vandamme's hands; the Emperor wrote on 3 December that the mortars would follow, and the major general that Jérôme was to have a bridge thrown over the Oder to communicate with Vandamme. Höpfner: the vessels of the boat bridge below Glogau were brought up the Oder, a large raft at Kosel serving until they came; in the night to the 10th 2 mortars and 3 howitzers, 3 howitzers, and 3 mortars, 1 siege howitzer and 3 field howitzers were brought into the batteries on the left bank and the 10 pieces named into those on the right bank, where 4 12-pounders and 6 field howitzers had stayed with Lefebvre's brigade; on the 12th side A awaited munition and replacements for its dismounted guns from Glogau; in the night to the 15th the first parallel's batteries received 2 heavy mortars and 3 light howitzers and 2 light mortars and 3 heavy howitzers, and the second parallel's 2 light howitzers and 4 6-pounders and 4 light howitzers and 4 6-pounders, and 8 field howitzers were in action on the right bank, while two 24-pounders and a heavy mortar had not yet come from Glogau; Deroy had a furnace for heated shot built so as to fire on the town from the right bank with 6 howitzers and 2 12-pounders; the 24-pounders held back and 2 heavy mortars arrived by water were brought in during the night to the 20th; and Vandamme ordered 4 new batteries for 8 24-pounders, 6 12-pounders and 2 mortars arriving from Glogau. The guns in the French batteries, mostly cannon and howitzers, were mostly Prussian. By the statement of side A's artillery officers over 13,000 shells, bombs and heated shot were fired into the town. Foucart: Lefebvre's brigade covered the road to Glogau by Neumarkt and Parchwitz, the allied corps' line of operations; in Höpfner's dispositions after Deroy's arrival Lefebvre's brigade, reinforced, stood before Lissa toward Neumarkt to cover headquarters and secure the transports from the lower part of Silesia.
claims.rationale: Höpfner, the French letters and Foucart's narrative, read from the page images; the figures were checked on full-resolution crops. Side B's guns and stores were set before the investment, side A's guns and supplies came from the commanders' dispositions; one claim carries one phase, so it is unresolved. The armaments Höpfner names make 25 pieces for the night to the 10th and 32 for the 15th, and Vandamme's new batteries 16 (our arithmetic); he does not say whether the earlier batteries kept their guns, how many 24-pounders were brought in on the 20th, or how many of Vandamme's pieces were in place, so no total of side A's guns is given here; Bodart's 52 guns are in claim bodart-strength. Höpfner's '10 pieces named' are read as the 4 12-pounders and 6 field howitzers left on the right bank on the 9th (our reading). The 13,000 projectiles are side A's artillery officers' figure as Höpfner reports it, and the 50,000 rounds a figure he gives as hearsay; no passage read counts the stores found at the capitulation beyond the powder. Whether the mortars the Emperor announced arrived, and which they were, is not shown beyond Höpfner's mortars from Glogau (our reading). English renderings (ours): 'of ordnance, 208 pieces of various calibres were distributed on the walls, and 46 guns were partly in reserve, partly unusable in the arsenal'; 'of finished munition, and of loose powder and iron munition, there were very considerable stores, which for the' (the sentence continues on p. 49); 'greater part were housed in a single magazine under the cavalier of the Taschen bastion. Light fell into this magazine through an open tower, and the vaults were weak, so that a bomb, if it fell unluckily, could blow the magazine and with it a great part of the town into the air' (the end of the sentence begun on p. 48); 'with food it had provided itself, except for some articles, only for 5-6 weeks. The highest provincial authority had at first called for provisioning for only 4 weeks, and the government had failed, when after the first investment, in the middle of November, the enemy had left the neighbourhood of Breslau again, to take energetic measures to complete the provisions speedily. The burghers had provided themselves with food just as deficiently; for only on 17 November had the government issued the order for provisioning for 6 months, and by then bringing in the food had already met with difficulties'; 'for a complete restoration of the works, for raising the parapets as required, making bonnets and cover, and building the banquette, the time was too short with so extensive an enceinte. The fortress had only two engineer officers, and the garrison was too weak to contribute materially to the works'; 'desertion was already increasing very considerably in the garrison, although the men were cared for as well as possible; they' (the sentence continues on p. 58); 'had for the most part been provided with greatcoats from the cloth procured for the army by contributions, and each relief of the garrison of the walls received warm beer and brandy, for whose purchase the burghers had made a collection' (the end of the sentence begun on p. 57); 'the governor received a report from the chief commissariat office that wood for baking bread was beginning to run short'; 'on the morning of the 3rd it lay out for signature at the town hall, where the opposition of a numerous counter-party made itself known. Nevertheless this request, signed by a hundred and some sixty burghers of all the guilds and trades, was handed to the governor together with a petition of the magistracy on the same matter, and a special list was attached by which only about 20,000 pounds of meat, mostly salted, were said to be left in the town, and a shortage of wood threatened bakers and brewers' ('it' is the circular petition named in the preceding sentence); 'since the commissariat office showed that it had used 40 Klafter of wood for baking in 10 weeks, and 12 Klafter more were handed over to the enemy, there would by this reckoning still have been a 3-week supply of wood'; '3) lack of attention to the provisioning of the place, on the part of the garrison as well as of the burghers. For the supply of baking wood too it would only have been necessary to have the thousands of Klafter of firewood before the Ziegel gate carried into the town by the many Oder boats'; 'there marched out in all still: 116 officers, 5270 non-commissioned officers and privates; 240 guns and 3640 Centner of powder were handed over to the enemy'; 'by the statement of the enemy's artillery officers over 13,000 shells, bombs and heated shot were sent into the town, while from the fortress about 50,000 rounds are said to have been fired'; 'the capture of Glogau put so considerable a mass of heavy guns and such great stores of munition into General Vandamme's hands that he could at once advance against Breslau'; 'the Emperor to Prince Jérôme. Posen, 3 December 1806'; 'I wish you to have the honour of taking it in person. You will receive through the staff the order to go there with Wrede's division. General Vandamme, with the Württembergers, is going there for his part. The mortars will follow. The major general is sending you instructions on the conduct of the siege. I do not doubt that in four days it will fall into your hands. Deroy's division stays where it is, with half the cavalry'; 'the major general to Prince Jérôme. Posen, 3 December 1806'; '(the major general informs the prince of the Emperor's instructions)' (Foucart's summary); '.... you will have a bridge thrown over the Oder to establish your communications with General Vandamme; you will take command of the siege...'; 'all the vessels of the boat bridge below Glogau were brought up the Oder to be used below Breslau for' (the sentence continues on p. 53); 'the same purpose, and until their arrival the connection between the two banks was kept up by means of a large raft at Kosel' (the end of the sentence begun on p. 52); 'in the night to the 10th the enemy brought, on the left bank, 2 mortars and 3 howitzers into the battery right of the Nikolai suburb, 3 howitzers into the battery in the prolongation of the Nikolai suburb, 3 mortars, 1 siege howitzer and 3 field howitzers into the battery at the left parallel, and finally the 10 pieces named into the batteries on the right bank of the Oder'; 'on 9 December the Bavarian infantry that had arrived crossed to the left bank of the Oder at Kosel; only the two light battalions and the cavalry brigade Lefebvre, with 4 12-pounders and 6 field howitzers, remained behind on the right bank. Jerome moved his headquarters to Lissa'; 'on the 12th and in the night to the 13th the town was indeed fired on, but only slowly, since the enemy was still awaiting munition and, in place of the dismounted guns, replacements from Glogau'; 'in the nights to the 14th and the 15th the besieger worked at the zigzags connecting the two parallels right of the suburb of St. Nikolai, and in the latter night the batteries built one after another were armed: the 2 batteries of the first parallel right of that suburb, counted from the left wing, with 2 heavy mortars and 3 light howitzers, and with 2 light mortars and 3 heavy howitzers; the batteries of the second parallel with 2 light howitzers and 4 6-pounders and with 4 light howitzers and 4 6-pounders respectively, these last batteries for firing on the batteries of the place. On the right bank of the Oder 8 field howitzers could be brought into action. Two 24-pounders and a heavy mortar had not yet arrived from Glogau'; 'General Deroy, on his arrival, had at once had the works begun by General Lefebvre resumed, the batteries completed and a furnace built for heated shot, so as to be able to bombard the town seriously from the right side of the Oder too with 6 howitzers and 2 12-pounders'; 'in the night to the 20th the 24-pounders held back until then and 2 heavy mortars that had arrived by water were also brought into the batteries, and from 4 until 9 in the morning of 20 December the town was most violently shelled. The main loss fell on the burghers, since the besiegers directed their fire exclusively at the town'; 'on General Minucci's return, General Vandamme, who had ordered the building of 4 new batteries in order to bring into them a further 8 24-pounders, 6 12-pounders and 2 mortars that were arriving from Glogau, believed he must set the town seriously on fire and inform the governor of the defeat of the relief troops and of the means he possessed to destroy the town. He expected that a population of 60,000 inhabitants would not be sacrificed to the holding of works that owed their preservation only to the mild weather. All this was done without the knowledge of General Hédouville, although this general, as mentioned, was to continue the command in Jerome's name'; 'the French batteries were built very irregularly; the guns in them, for the majority cannon and howitzers and mostly Prussian, stood behind embrasures raised toward the front; the elevating wedges had been taken out and the barrels laid on the transoms of the carriages, so that the guns were elevated between 15 and 20 degrees and their projectiles went at random into the town'; 'General Lefebvre's brigade covered the road to Glogau by Neumarkt and Parchwitz, the allied corps' line of operations'; 'the division had arrived, and the siege corps now took the following positions: General Vandamme on the left bank of the Oder, with the Württembergers on the right wing, the division Wrede in the centre and part of the division Deroy on the left wing at Pöpelwitz on the Oder, from where these last troops occupied the parallels on the Oder; further General Deroy on the right bank with the rest of his infantry, of which 3 companies of the light battalion Taxis were detached to Steinersdorf - south-east of Breslau - toward Brieg, and the cavalry brigade Mezzanelli, which was to reconnoitre the neighbourhood and especially watch Brieg, where the Prince of Anhalt-Pless was believed to be assembling the relief corps; further the cavalry brigade Lefebvre, reinforced by the light battalion Zoller, in front of Lissa toward Neumarkt, to cover headquarters and secure the transports from the lower part of Silesia; finally the cavalry brigade Montbrun in front of Krietern, which in connection with the brigade Lefebvre was to watch all the roads to Breslau on the left bank of the Oder by pickets and patrols pushed forward, so as to be able to report the approach of the relief troops early. The dragoon regiment Taxis had been detached to Liegnitz'.

citations.quote: Bei der Rückkehr des Generals Minucci glaubte der General Vandamme, der den Bau von 4 neuen Batterien befohlen hatte, um darin noch 8—24pfünder, 6—12pfünder und 2 Mörser, welche von Glogau anlangten, einzuführen, die Stadt ernsthaft in Brand setzen, und dem Gouverneur von der Niederlage der Entsatztruppen, so wie von den Mitteln Nachricht geben zu müssen, die er besaß, um die Stadt zu vernichten. Er erwartete, daß eine Bevölkerung von 60,000 Einwohnern nicht der Behauptung von Werken würde aufgeopfert werden, die ihre Erhaltung nur der gelinden Witterung verdankten. citations.locator: Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 4 (1851), p. 118 (transcribed from the page image)

citations.locator: Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 4 (1851), p. 60 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: Die Division war eingetroffen, und das Belagerungskorps erhielt nunmehr folgende Aufstellung: der General Vandamme auf dem linken Oder-Ufer, mit den Württembergern auf dem rechten Flügel, der Division Wrede in der Mitte und einem Theil der Division Deroy auf dem linken Flügel bei Pöpelwitz an der Oder, von wo letztere Truppen die Parallelen an der Oder besetzten; ferner der General Deroy auf dem rechten Ufer mit dem Rest seiner Infänterie, von der 3 Kompagnien des leichten Bataillons Taxis nach Steinersdorf — s. ö. von Breslau — gegen Brieg detaschirt wurden, und der Kavallerie-Brigade Mezzanelli, welche die Umgegend aufklären und besonders Brieg beobachten sollte, wo man den Fürsten von Anhalt Pleß in der Versammlung des Entsatzkorps begriffen glaubte; weiter die Kavallerie-Brigade Lefebvre, verstärkt durch das leichte Bataillon Zoller, vorwärts von Lissa gegen Neumarkt zur Deckung des Hauptquartiers und zur Sicherung der Transporte aus dem unteren Theile von Schlesien; endlich die Kavallerie-Brigade Montbrun vorwärts von Krietern, welche, in Verbindung mit der Brigade Lefebvre, alle Straßen nach Breslau auf dem linken Oder-Ufer durch vorgeschobene Pikets und Patrouillen beobachten sollte, um frühzeitig von der Annäherung der Entsatztruppen unterrichten zu können. Das Dragoner-Regiment Taxis war nach Liegnitz detaschirt worden.

claims.value: Side A: the Emperor wrote on 3 December that intercepted letters showed Breslau had only a fifth of the garrison necessary for its defence and that its general declared he would have to surrender if blockaded for several days by infantry, that a hundred or so bombs would force the town to surrender, and that he did not doubt it would fall into Jérôme's hands in four days; the captured Captain Debruir stated that Napoleon had most earnestly assured Jérôme, and Berthier Vandamme, that Breslau was an altogether untenable place that could not hold out 5 days. Foucart: on the 6th Montbrun sent a party to the right bank for news of the Bavarian troops, which learned nothing at Auras, and sent a trusted man to Schweidnitz to report within two days on the composition of its garrison. Höpfner: on 7 December Vandamme, Pernety and Blein reconnoitred the place to determine the point of attack, Blein hoping to find an earthen batardeau before the Nikolai suburb; the approach trench pushed from the left second parallel struck unexpectedly on an arm of the Oder in the night to the 14th; for want of a good plan of Breslau Blein reconnoitred the works on the left bank on 17, 18 and 19 December and found the main wall unrevetted at two places and the enveloppe occupied only before the Nikolai front; Jérôme received from all sides news that the Prince of Anhalt-Pless was assembling 15-16,000 men in Upper Silesia to relieve Breslau and that the garrison of Schweidnitz was said to count 6000 infantry and 400 horse; Vandamme expected that a population of 60,000 would not be sacrificed to the works; and deserters, especially of the regiment Thile, betrayed much about the state of the fortress, such as the time and place of the daily relief, on which side A then fired. Foucart: Vandamme received the news that the Prince of Pless was gathering troops behind the Neisse and sent Montbrun toward Ohlau on the 28th. Höpfner judges that side A, finding the outworks abandoned, recognised the weakness of the garrison and the faint-heartedness of the government.
claims.rationale: Side A's letters and Foucart's narrative, read from the page images, with Höpfner. The intercepted letters and Jérôme's and Blein's reports were not seen; Debruir's statement is the prisoner's, as Höpfner gives it. The passages read do not show what side A knew of the garrison's true strength; the Emperor's 'fifth of the garrison necessary' and the expectation of four or five days stand against a siege of about a month (our comparison). Blein's findings and Vandamme's expectation are Höpfner's account. English renderings (ours): 'the Emperor to Prince Jérôme. Posen, 3 December 1806'; 'it appears from intercepted letters that Breslau has only a fifth of the garrison necessary for the defence of the place, and that the general commanding there declares that he will be obliged to surrender if he is blockaded for several days in succession by infantry. A hundred or so bombs thrown into this large and beautiful town will force it to surrender'; 'I wish you to have the honour of taking it in person. You will receive through the staff the order to go there with Wrede's division. General Vandamme, with the Württembergers, is going there for his part. The mortars will follow. The major general is sending you instructions on the conduct of the siege. I do not doubt that in four days it will fall into your hands. Deroy's division stays where it is, with half the cavalry'; 'both undertakings succeeded completely, and on the way the French Captain Debruir was taken prisoner, whom General Vandamme had sent from Lissa to Jerome to bring him the news of the capture of Glogau: from the dispatch, torn to pieces, it was learned that the enemy meant to throw a bridge over the Oder at Kosel, below Breslau, and the prisoner himself stated that Napoleon had most earnestly assured Jerome, and Marshal Berthier General Vandamme, that Breslau was an altogether untenable place that could not hold out 5 days'; 'General Montbrun, preceding the Württemberg division, moved before Breslau by the left bank of the Oder. On the morning of the 6th he was a league from the town, at Höflchen, where he took position; he at once sent a party over to the right bank of the Oder to gather information on the arrival of the Bavarian troops, sent a detachment of 25 men and an officer to take post at Gnichwitz, 20 km from Breslau on the road to Schweibnitz, and dispatched to Schweibnitz a trusted man he had with him, with the task of reporting to him within two days the composition of the garrison of that place'; 'the party sent to the right bank had spent the night of the 6th to the 7th at Auras without having learned any news of the arrival of Prince Jérôme's troops, which is not at all surprising, since the Bavarians were coming from Kalisch'; 'likewise on the 7th General Vandamme, accompanied by the artillery General Pernety and the engineer Colonel Blein, reconnoitred the place to determine the point of attack'; 'the troops disposable for the siege were too weak to deploy on the upper Oder, where they seemed too exposed to harassment by the Prussian parties from the other fortresses; they therefore restricted themselves for the time being to the ground on the lower Oder and meant to extend on the right up to the Ohlau suburb. The building of two parallels and two mortar batteries, right and left of the Nikolai suburb, was decided, and this suburb was chosen as the point of attack all the more because Colonel Blein hoped to find there an earthen batardeau that could ease the crossing of the ditch'; 'from the left second parallel an approach trench with a small place of arms was to be pushed forward, so that from it the Württemberg Jäger could harass the Prussian gunners on the Bürgerwerder; but in the night to the 14th they struck quite unexpectedly on the arm of the Oder that separated the enemy from the works of the Bürgerwerder'; 'for want of a good plan of Breslau, already on 17, 18 and 19 December the engineer Colonel' (the sentence continues on p. 63); 'Blein had reconnoitred the works on the left bank of the Oder as thoroughly as possible and in doing so established that the main wall was not revetted at two extended places, namely at the Schweidnitz and Ohlau gates; that before the wet main ditch, over 120 feet wide, there was an enveloppe of earth, covered at its salient angles by lunettes with retired flanks; that these works were indeed provided with storm-poles and palisades, but were occupied only before the revetted front of the Nikolai gate, against which the siege works had so far been directed; and finally that the outer ditch surrounding the enveloppe had a width of 60-70 feet and a depth of 6-7 feet' (the end of the sentence begun on p. 62); 'when Jerome now received from all sides the news that the Prince of Anhalt-Pless was assembling in Upper Silesia a force of 15-16,000 men to relieve Breslau as soon as possible, that line troops were being drawn for it from all the fortified places to form the core of a force that was to be reinforced by recruits and volunteers called to the colours by a proclamation of the aide-de-camp Count Götzen, and when he further learned that the garrison of Schweidnitz was said to have been reinforced by 3000 recruits, so that it now counted 6000 men of infantry and 400 horse, he had, in view of the obstinacy of the governor of Breslau, the troops available at Polnisch Wartenberg ordered up on the 16th, so as to be equal to every possible event. The besieging troops were already suffering exceedingly from the bad season and their comparatively small strength'; 'on General Minucci's return, General Vandamme, who had ordered the building of 4 new batteries in order to bring into them a further 8 24-pounders, 6 12-pounders and 2 mortars that were arriving from Glogau, believed he must set the town seriously on fire and inform the governor of the defeat of the relief troops and of the means he possessed to destroy the town. He expected that a population of 60,000 inhabitants would not be sacrificed to the holding of works that owed their preservation only to the mild weather. All this was done without the knowledge of General Hédouville, although this general, as mentioned, was to continue the command in Jerome's name'; 'complaint came in to the government that desertion was being practised ever more boldly. The locks on the gates of a palisade tambour were found knocked off, and even heaps of earth thrown up against the palisades to climb over them more easily. It was also evident that much about the state of the fortress was betrayed to the enemy by deserters, especially of the infantry regiment Thile; for example, the time and place of the daily relief. At that time the enemy then fired so briskly that several men were killed and wounded at the assembly place, and it was found necessary to change the time of the relief more often'; 'on the 25th the governor of Breslau, on the news of the unfortunate combat of Strehlen, entered into talks for the surrender of the place. But having learned the next day that the Prince of Pless was gathering behind the Neisse the remains of his first column and other troops, he broke off the negotiations'; 'the same information had reached General Vandamme, who on the 28th directed General Montbrun with his cavalry and two Bavarian battalions on Ohlau and had him supported by General Minucci'; 'the abandonment of the outworks must therefore be regarded as a fault that, as we have seen, is to be ascribed solely to General Lindener, in contradiction with the engineer of the place. The enemy, when he found the outworks abandoned, at once took on another air; he recognised from it the weakness of the garrison and the faint-heartedness of the government, which wished only to secure itself against a coup de main and to secure a good capitulation'.

citations.quote: Je désire que vous ayez l'honneur de la prendre en personne. Vous recevrez par l'état-major l'ordre de vous y rendre avec la division de Wrede. Le général Vandamme, avec les Wurtembergeois, s'y rend de son côté. Les mortiers suivront. Le major général vous envoie des instructions sur la conduite du siége. Je ne doute pas qu'en quatre jours elle ne tombe entre vos mains. La division Deroy reste où elle est, avec la moitié de la cavalerie.

citations.locator: Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 4 (1851), p. 52 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: Beide Unternehmen gelangen vollständig, und gelegentlich nahm man den französischen Hauptmann Debruir gefangen, der vom General Vandamme aus Lissa an Jerome geschickt worden war, um ihm die Nachricht von der Einnahme von Glogau zu bringen: Aus der in Stücken zerrissenen Depesche entnahm man, daß der Feind bei Kosel, unterhalb Breslau, eine Brücke über die Oder schlagen wolle, und der Gefangene selbst sagte aus, daß Napoleon dem Jerome, und der M. Berthier dem General Vandamme aufs Ernstlichste versichert hätten, Breslau sei ein durchaus unhaltbarer Platz, der sich nicht 5 Tage behaupten könne.

citations.locator: Foucart, Campagne de Pologne (1806-1807): Pultusk et Golymin, t. II (1882), p. 95 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: Le général Montbrun, précédant la division wurtembergeoise, se portait devant Breslau par la rive gauche de l'Oder. Le 6 au matin, il était à une lieue de la ville, à Höflchen, où il prenait position; il faisait aussitôt passer un parti sur la rive droite de l'Oder pour prendre des informations sur l'arrivée des troupes bavaroises, envoyait un détachement de 25 hommes et un officier prendre poste à Gnichwitz, à 20 kil. de Breslau sur la route de Schweibnitz, et expédiait à Schweibnitz un homme de confiance qu'il avait près de lui avec mission de lui rapporter dans deux jours la composition de la garnison de cette place.

citations.locator: Foucart, Campagne de Pologne (1806-1807): Pultusk et Golymin, t. II (1882), p. 95 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: Le parti envoyé sur la rive droite avait passé la nuit du 6 au 7 à Auras sans avoir appris de nouvelles de l'arrivée des troupes du prince Jérôme, ce qui n'est point étonnant puisque les Bavarois venaient de Kalisch.

citations.locator: Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 4 (1851), p. 52 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: Ebenfalls am 7. rekognoszirte der General Vandamme, begleitet vom Artillerie-General Pernety und vom Ingenieur-Obersten Blein, den Platz, um den Angriffspunkt zu ermitteln.

citations.locator: Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 4 (1851), p. 52 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: Die zur Belagerung disponiblen Truppen waren zu schwach, um sich an der obern Oder aufzustellen, wo man den Beunruhigungen der preußischen Parteien aus den übrigen Festungen zu sehr ausgesetzt schien; man beschränkte sich daher vorläufig auf das Terrain an der untern Oder und wollte sich rechts bis gegen die Ohlauer Vorstadt ausdehnen. Der Bau zweier Parallelen und zweier Wurfbatterien, rechts und links der Nikolai-Vorstadt, wurde beschlossen, und zwar um so mehr diese Vorstadt zum Angriffspunkt bestimmt, als der Oberst Blein die Hoffnung hegte, daß er daselbst auf ein Batardeau in Erde treffen würde, das den Uebergang über den Graben erleichtern könne.

citations.locator: Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 4 (1851), p. 56 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: Aus der zweiten Parallele links sollte ein Laufgraben mit einem kleinen Waffenplatz vorgeschoben werden, um aus demselben durch die württembergischen Jäger die preußischen Kanoniere auf dem Bürgerwerder zu beunruhigen; man stieß indessen in der Nacht zum 14. sehr unerwartet auf den Oderarm, der den Feind von den Werken des Bürgerwerders trennte.

citations.locator: Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 4 (1851), p. 62 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: In Ermangelung eines guten Planes von Breslau hatte bereits am 17., 18. und 19. Dezember der Ingenieur-Oberst

citations.locator: Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 4 (1851), p. 63 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: Blein die Werke auf dem linken Oder-Ufer so gründlich als möglich rekognoszirt und hierbei ermittelt, daß der Hauptwall an zwei ausgedehnten Stellen, nämlich am Schweidnitzer- und Ohlauer-Thor, nicht bekleidet sei; daß sich vor dem nassen, über 120′ breiten Hauptgraben aber eine Enveloppe von Erde befände, die auf ihren vorspringenden Winkeln durch Lünetten mit zurückgezogenen Flanken gedeckt würde; daß diese Werke zwar mit Sturmpfählen und Pallisaden versehen, aber nur vor der revetirten Front des Nikolai-Thores, gegen welche bisher die Angriffs-Arbeiten geführt worden waren, besetzt seien; daß endlich der Vorgraben, der die Enveloppe umgab, eine Breite von 60—70′ und eine Tiefe von 6—7′ habe.

citations.locator: Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 4 (1851), p. 59 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: Als nun Jerome von allen Seiten die Nachricht erhielt, daß der Fürst von Anhalt Pleß in Oberschlesien eine Macht von 15—16,000 Mann versammele, um so bald als möglich Breslau zu entsetzen, daß hierzu aus allen festen Plätzen Linientruppen herangezogen würden, um den Kern einer Macht zu bilden, die mittelst Rekruten und Freiwilliger, durch eine Proklamation des Flügel-Adjutanten Grafen Götzen zu den Fahnen gerufen, verstärkt werden sollte, als er ferner erfuhr, daß die Garnison von Schweidnitz durch 3000 Rekruten verstärkt sein solle, so daß sie nunmehr 6000 Mann Infanterie und 400 Reiter zähle, ließ er, in Betracht der Hartnäckigkeit des Gouverneurs von Breslau, am 16. die bei Poln. Wartenberg zur Disposition stehenden Truppen herbeibeordern, um allen möglichen Ereignissen gewachsen zu sein. Die Belagerungstruppen litten bei der üblen Jahreszeit und der verhältnißmäßig geringen Stärke bereits ungemein.

citations.locator: Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 4 (1851), p. 79 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: Bei der Rückkehr des Generals Minucci glaubte der General Vandamme, der den Bau von 4 neuen Batterien befohlen hatte, um darin noch 8—24pfünder, 6—12pfünder und 2 Mörser, welche von Glogau anlangten, einzuführen, die Stadt ernsthaft in Brand setzen, und dem Gouverneur von der Niederlage der Entsatztruppen, so wie von den Mitteln Nachricht geben zu müssen, die er besaß, um die Stadt zu vernichten. Er erwartete, daß eine Bevölkerung von 60,000 Einwohnern nicht der Behauptung von Werken würde aufgeopfert werden, die ihre Erhaltung nur der gelinden Witterung verdankten. Das Alles geschah ohne Vorwissen des Generals Hédouville, obgleich dieser General, wie erwähnt, im Namen Jerome's den Befehl fortführen sollte.

citations.locator: Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 4 (1851), p. 109 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: Beim Gouvernement ging die Klage ein, daß die Desertion immer frecher betrieben werde. Die Schlösser an den Thoren eines Pallisadentambours fand man abgeschlagen, selbst Erdhaufen an die Pallisaden aufgeschüttet, um leichter übersteigen zu können. Auch war es offenbar, daß durch Deserteurs, besonders vom Infanterie-Regiment Thile, dem Feinde Vieles über den Zustand der Festung verrathen wurde. So z. B. über Zeit und Ort der täglichen Ablösung. Zu dieser Zeit feuerte der Feind dann so lebhaft, daß mehrere Leute auf dem Sammelplatz getödtet und verwundet wurden, und man sich genöthigt sah, mit der Zeit der Ablösung öfter zu wechseln.

citations.locator: Foucart, Campagne de Pologne (1806-1807): Pultusk et Golymin, t. II (1882), p. 108 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: Le 25, le gouverneur de Breslau, à la nouvelle du combat malheureux de Strehlen, entra en pourparlers pour la reddition de la place. Mais ayant appris le lendemain que le prince de Pless réunissait derrière la Neisse les débris de sa première colonne ainsi que d'autres troupes, il rompit les négociations.

citations.locator: Foucart, Campagne de Pologne (1806-1807): Pultusk et Golymin, t. II (1882), p. 108 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: Les mêmes renseignements étaient parvenus au général Vandamme, qui dirigeait le 28 sur Ohlau le général Montbrun avec sa cavalerie et deux bataillons bavarois et le faisait appuyer par le général Minucci.

citations.locator: Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 4 (1851), p. 116 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: Das Aufgeben der Außenwerke muß daher als ein Fehler betrachtet werden, der lediglich, wie wir gesehen haben, dem General Lindener, im Widerspruch mit dem Ingenieur vom Platz, zuzuschreiben ist. Der Feind nahm, als er die Außenwerke verlassen fand, alsbald eine andere Miene an; er erkannte daraus die Schwäche der Garnison, die Zaghaftigkeit des Gouvernements, das sich nur gegen einen Handstreich und eine gute Kapitulation sichern wollte.

claims.value: Side B (Prussian), in Höpfner: on news of the return of part of the Bavarian troops from South Prussia against Breslau the government sent Fiebig's expedition on 7 December, which captured Captain Debruir; from his torn dispatch it learned that side A meant to bridge the Oder at Kosel, and Debruir stated that Napoleon and Berthier had assured Jérôme and Vandamme that Breslau could not hold out 5 days. Desterno's summons of 10 December announced the capture of Magdeburg, Stettin, Küstrin and Glogau and the French entry into Warsaw and declared relief hopeless, and he added that the French had crossed the Vistula at Thorn and seen no Russians, that the King had gone back behind Memel, and that Napoleon would not make peace before humbling Russia; Lefebvre's summons of the 15th added that Napoleon had ordered the works razed after the capture. On 16 December the governor sent out the sortie on a report that side A had withdrawn its guns from the batteries. On 18 December Jérôme's adjutant Ducaudras assured the governor that Deroy's division, 10,000 strong, would arrive that day and bring the siege corps to 22,000, and considerable movements were indeed soon seen. The burning of Hundsfeld on the 21st was taken for a sign that the Russians were approaching and side A withdrawing. In the night to the 23rd Fiebig reported side A approaching on the Oder with 12 vessels, and side A approached the works at several other places. On 25 December Duveyrier summoned the town with the most boastful statements about side A's successes against the Prince of Pless and in Poland and Prussia. On 30 December the governor took the firing and the burning of Dürgoy, reported from 6 in the morning, for a manoeuvre to lure the garrison out: the engineer of the place made the same report at 7, but the governor first asked for Lindener's opinion, and Lindener, who went to the Ohlau gate only at 8, heard no firing there and saw only some cavalry at Dürgoy; Lieutenant Schorlemmer reported toward 9 that side A was hurrying with its light guns and many troops out of the trenches toward the Schweidnitz road and that the fire was coming nearer, and again between 9 and 10 that side A was not manoeuvring and the relief troops could clearly be made out; the governor kept to his preconceived opinion, which Lindener seems not to have taken from him, and Krafft would not be persuaded otherwise, though from the cavalier of the Taschen bastion shells exchanged by the opposing troops were seen bursting and others saw side A's infantry leave the trenches for the fight; only after the parole did the governor and Lindener, from the loft of the Hatzfeld palace, make out troops and gunfire between Oltaschin and Dürjentsch, and the fog then hid the fight. Afterwards Bachiarelli, carrying side commissions of the enemy general, tried to open the governor's eyes about the 30th and convince him that relief had become impossible, and on 2 January Duveyrier and Hammerer repeated all the reasons that should make surrender necessary. On the 3rd the governor could not obtain leave to send an officer to Kalisch to learn whether Russians were approaching.
claims.rationale: Side B's history, read from the page images. These were the reports and messages on which the governor and the government acted, so the phase is left unresolved. The summonses' claims are side A's, kept as Höpfner gives them; the summonses were not seen. Höpfner's account of 30 December rests on reports from the gates and bastions; whether the governor knew the relief's plan is not shown in the pages read, and Höpfner blames the lack of scouts toward the Prince of Pless chiefly on Lindener (claim side-b-command); his judgement of the governor's conduct on the 30th, on p. 108, was read in the OCR only and not used. The date of Bachiarelli's visit is on p. 108, read in the OCR only and not registered. English renderings (ours): 'in consequence of the news of the return of part of the Bavarian troops from South Prussia against Breslau, the government on 7 December sent Artillery Lieutenant Fiebig with half of the newly raised horse battery, some infantry and 30 horses to the right bank of the Oder, to destroy all the bridges over the old Oder and at the same time to demolish the casemates of the abandoned work at the Paßschleuse, where the old Oder leaves the new above Breslau'; 'both undertakings succeeded completely, and on the way the French Captain Debruir was taken prisoner, whom General Vandamme had sent from Lissa to Jerome to bring him the news of the capture of Glogau: from the dispatch, torn to pieces, it was learned that the enemy meant to throw a bridge over the Oder at Kosel, below Breslau, and the prisoner himself stated that Napoleon had most earnestly assured Jerome, and Marshal Berthier General Vandamme, that Breslau was an altogether untenable place that could not hold out 5 days'; 'on the 10th at 6 in the morning the enemy was able to begin the bombardment against the front at the Nikolai gate and the Dom; the enemy's shells did the burghers' hou-' (the word and sentence continue on p. 55); 'ses considerable damage without setting them on fire. Since in general the enemy's fire was directed more at the town than at the walls, the garrison was far safer on the walls than in its quarters' (the first word ends the one begun on p. 54); 'toward midday the fire fell silent, and after 1 o'clock Captain Desterno, a former Prussian dragoon lieutenant and at the time Jerome's adjutant, appeared as parlementaire and handed over a letter of summons in which the capture of Magdeburg, Stettin, Küstrin and Glogau and the entry of the French into Warsaw were communicated and the hopelessness of a relief was declared. The parlementaire added that the French had also crossed the Vistula at Thorn and had nowhere seen Russians, that the King had already gone back behind Memel, and that Napoleon had declared he would not make peace before he had humbled Russia and broken the alliance with Prussia'; 'on 15 December at 6 in the morning the bombardment thus began anew and lasted until 1 in the afternoon. The town suffered considerably, especially the convent of the Elisabethines, but the fire was put out everywhere'; 'at 2 in the afternoon Jerome had the fortress summoned again by General Lefebvre. He was led with unbandaged eyes to the governor, to whom he had to say much that was flattering about the' (the sentence continues on p. 57); 'defence so far and declare that, if the garrison did not accept the honourable capitulation offered, the town would be turned into a heap of ashes, for which all the means were at hand. The general also added that Breslau was being besieged for the last time, since Napoleon had ordered the fortifications to be razed immediately after the capture. The proposal was rejected, whereupon at 3 o'clock the bombardment was renewed, though not with the violence of the morning, and toward evening it gradually fell silent' (the first words end the sentence begun on p. 56); 'on 16 December too the enemy kept quiet, and since the governor received the report that the besieger had withdrawn the guns from the batteries, he ordered that a detachment of 2 officers - Lieutenant Lehsten of the infantry regiment Thile and Lieutenant Seelstrang of the cuirassier regiment Henckel - 60 marksmen and 80 horsemen with 300 workers should advance from the Nikolai gate, clear the suburb of the enemy and destroy the enemy's works'; 'on 18 December Captain Ducaudras, Jerome's adjutant, presented himself and demanded the release of all the Prussian officers who were prisoners of war released on their word of honour and were staying in Breslau without' (the sentence continues on p. 60); 'taking part in the defence. By the adjutant's assurance the Bavarian division Deroy, 10,000 men strong, was to arrive on that day and reinforce the siege corps to 22,000 men. Indeed considerable movements in the enemy's positions were observed soon afterwards' (the first words end the sentence begun on p. 59); 'on 21 December the bombardment was renewed from 2½ until' (the sentence continues on p. 62); '5 in the morning. A deputation of burghers again turned to the governor with the request to grant them, amid so many afflictions, the comfort and hope of an early relief. The governor had to dismiss them without such a hope' (the first words end the sentence begun on p. 61); 'from the fortress the burning of the market town of Hundsfeld was observed and taken as a sign that the Russians were approaching and the enemy withdrawing and burning the villages of the neighbourhood. But already at 10 o'clock the bombardment began anew, was continued until 1 at midday and did particular damage, since a mass of inhabitants had left their shelters on the strength of that news. 7 inhabitants were killed, 22 wounded'; 'on 22 December from 3 in the morning with pauses until the evening, and the fire raged most violently in the night to the 23rd, when fires broke out in several places' (the end of the sentence begun in the preceding paragraph); 'since Lieutenant Fiebig reported from the Bürgerwerder in the night that the enemy was approaching on the Oder with 12 vessels, to all appearance to land on the Werder, the general alarm was beaten. During the violent bombardment the enemy also approached the works at several other places, thus near the Nikolai gate, the Schweidnitz gate, along the Ohlau, etc., whereby the musket fire opened by the garrison inflicted considerable losses on the Bavarians'; 'the bombardment was therefore, on the 25th after 1 o'clock, o-' (the sentence continues on p. 80: 'opened again'); 'pened again and lasted until 3 o'clock. At that time Colonel Duveyrier, general staff officer of General Vandamme, appeared with the summons to surrender, with the most boastful statements about the advantages won against the Prince of Pless as well as in Poland and Prussia. The governor gave a refusal' (the first words end the sentence begun on p. 79); 'on 30 December at 6 in the morning it was reported from the Schweidnitz and Ohlau gates that firing of heavy guns and small arms could be heard and that the village of Dürgoy was burning'; 'at 7 o'clock the engineer of the place made the same report to the governor. The governor, however, first asked for the opinion of General Lindener, who only at 8 o'clock went with the engineer of the place to the Ohlau gate to see for himself what was happening'; 'toward 9 o'clock a new report came to the governor from Lieutenant Schorlemmer that the enemy was hurrying with his light guns and many troops out of the trenches toward the Schweidnitz road, and that the fire was coming nearer and nearer to the fortress'; 'the governor gave for answer: "that the enemy was manoeuvring to lure the garrison out of the town"'; 'General Lindener would hear no firing on the Ohlau gate, but saw only some troops of cavalry at Dürgoy, at which he had 2 24-pounders aimed'; 'only between 9 and 10 o'clock did he go to the governor, where Lieutenant Schorlemmer again had it reported: "the enemy is not manoeuvring, one can clearly make out the relief troops"'; 'the governor kept to his preconceived opinion, which General Lindener' (the sentence continues on p. 87); 'seems not to have taken from him' (the end of the sentence begun on p. 86); 'from the cavalier of the Taschen bastion it had been clearly seen how the shells that the opposing troops exchanged burst in the air'; 'the commandant present, General Krafft, had been made aware of it, and an attempt had been made to dissuade him from the opinion that the enemy was manoeuvring; but he had spoken harshly to everyone and finally dismissed them with the words: "that was nobody's business, he himself possessed sufficient judgement, etc."'; 'others had seen the enemy's infantrymen running singly out of the trenches in the direction of the fight, so that they had become convinced that the trenches had been abandoned by the enemy at least for the greatest part, and that a sortie was therefore not only justified but required'; 'only after the parole did the governor go with General Lindener to the loft of the Hatzfeld palace to see for himself. Now indeed troops, rising smoke and the flash of powder from heavy guns were made out between Oltaschin and Dürjentsch, though everything was wrapped in fog; the fire also seemed to be coming nearer the town'; 'at 11 o'clock the garrison was assembled to make a sortie in case the enemy should be beaten. The fog now grew thicker; one could observe no further, but only heard that the fire moved further and further away in the direction of the Zobtenberg until toward 3 o'clock, so that the relief had been beaten'; 'it turned out, however, that it was not a negotiator sent by General Vandamme but a former Polish privy councillor Bachiarelli, who was trying to rescue his wife, a Pole, from the town and contrived on this occasion to deliver some side commissions of the enemy general. He tried to bring the besieger and the governor together in a friendly way, to open the latter's eyes about what had happened on the 30th, and to convince him that a relief had become impossible'; 'on 2 January at 11 o'clock Colonel Duveyrier and Captain Hammerer were let in. Their business consisted in the request for the release of several persons, mostly of the female sex, and besides in the enumeration, repeated to weariness, of all the reasons that were to make the sur-' (the word and sentence continue on p. 110); 'render of the fortress necessary. Both officers were dismissed with expressions of courtesy, and at 3 o'clock the garrison's fire began again, at 5 o'clock a 2-hour bombardment by the enemy' (the first word ends the one begun on p. 109); 'at 4 in the afternoon Colonel Duveyrier came, empowered to negotiate the surrender. The bombardment still went on even now. The governor could no more obtain the armistice of 8 days he asked for, to give the Prince of Pless time for a new attempt at relief, than the dispatch of an officer to Kalisch, by whom he wished to make sure whether Russians were approaching or not. Only for arranging the affairs of the town and the garrison were 3 days granted'.

Berthier dem General Vandamme aufs Ernstlichste versichert hätten, Breslau sei ein durchaus unhaltbarer Platz, der sich nicht 5 Tage behaupten könne.

citations.quote: Am 10. Morgens 6 Uhr war der Feind im Stande, das Bombardement gegen die Front am Nikolai-Thor und den Dom zu beginnen; die feindlichen Wurfgeschosse fügten den Bürgerhäu-

citations.locator: Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 4 (1851), p. 55 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: sern erheblichen Schaden zu, ohne zu zünden. Da im Allgemeinen das feindliche Feuer sich mehr auf die Stadt als auf die Wälle richtete, so befand sich die Besatzung auf diesen weit sicherer als in ihren Quartieren.

citations.locator: Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 4 (1851), p. 55 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: Gegen Mittag schwieg das Feuer, und nach 1 Uhr erschien der Kapitain Desterno, ehemaliger preußischer Dragoner-Lieutenant und zur Zeit Adjutant Jerome's, als Parlamentair und überreichte ein Aufforderungsschreiben, in welchem die Einnahme von Magdeburg, Stettin, Küstrin und Glogau, der Einzug der Franzosen in Warschau mitgetheilt und die Hoffnungslosigkeit für einen Entsatz ausgesprochen wurde. Der Parlamentair fügte hinzu, daß die Franzosen auch bei Thorn die Weichsel überschritten und nirgends Russen gesehen hätten, daß der König bereits bis hinter Memel zurückgegangen sei und Napoleon erklärt habe, nicht früher Frieden zu machen, als bis er Rußland gedemüthigt und das Bündniß mit Preußen gesprengt habe.

citations.locator: Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 4 (1851), p. 56 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: Am 15. Dezember Morgens 6 Uhr begann das Bombardement somit aufs Neue und dauerte bis 1 Uhr Nachmittags. Die Stadt litt bedeutend, besonders das Kloster der Elisabethinerin, doch wurde das Feuer überall gelöscht.

citations.locator: Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 4 (1851), p. 56 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: Um 2 Uhr Nachmittags ließ Jerome die Festung abermals durch den General Lefebvre auffordern. Derselbe wurde mit unverbundenen Augen zum Gouverneur geführt, dem er viel Schmeichelhaftes über die

citations.locator: Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 4 (1851), p. 57 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: bisherige Vertheidigung sagen und erklären mußte, daß, wenn die Besatzung die angebotene ehrenvolle Kapitulation nicht annähme, die Stadt in einen Aschenhaufen verwandelt werden würde, wozu alle Mittel vorhanden wären. Auch fügte der General hinzu, daß Breslau zum Letztenmale belagert würde, indem Napoleon befohlen habe, gleich nach der Einnahme die Festungswerke zu schleifen. Der Antrag wurde zurückgewiesen, worauf um 3 Uhr das Bombardement erneuert wurde, jedoch nicht mit der Heftigkeit als am Morgen, und gegen Abend verstummte es allmälig.

citations.locator: Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 4 (1851), p. 57 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: Auch am 16. Dezember verhielt sich der Feind ruhig, und da der Gouverneur die Meldung erhielt, daß der Belagerer die Geschütze aus den Batterien zurückgenommen habe, so befahl er, daß eine Abtheilung von 2 Offizieren — Lieutenant Lehsten vom Infanterie-Regiment Thile und Lieutenant Seelstrang vom Kürassier-Regiment Henckel — 60 Schützen und 80 Reitern mit 300 Arbeitern aus dem Nikolai-Thor vorgehen, die Vorstadt vom Feinde säubern und die feindlichen Arbeiten zerstören sollte.

claims.value: Side A: the Emperor wrote to Jérôme from Posen on 3 December that he wished him to have the honour of taking Breslau in person, going there with Wrede's division while Vandamme went with the Württembergers and the mortars followed, and that he did not doubt it would fall in four days; Deroy's division was to stay where it was with half the cavalry, so that if Breslau was taken and the Emperor had an action in front of Warsaw, Jérôme could be there with it; and once Breslau was taken, Vandamme was to invest Brieg at once, without the Württembergers entering Breslau. The major general's letter of the same day, as Foucart summarises it, gave the Emperor's instructions: Jérôme was to have a bridge thrown over the Oder to communicate with Vandamme and take command of the siege, and Vandamme was to leave 1,000 men at Glogau. Höpfner: the point of attack was chosen at the Nikolai suburb; Napoleon had expected the quick surrender of Breslau, but on Jérôme's report of serious resistance he had Deroy's division, already directed from Kalisch on Petrikau, turned back to Polnisch Wartenberg to be ready to reinforce the troops before Breslau, and Jérôme, hearing of the relief force gathering under the Prince of Pless and in view of the governor's obstinacy, called Deroy's troops up on the 16th. Foucart's narrative: the inexperience of the allied troops did not allow the siege to be pressed as vigorously as the French generals wished, and the delays gave the Prince of Pless time to gather part of the garrisons of the other fortresses, so that it became indispensable to cover the siege troops very seriously; from 15 December two squadrons watched the roads from Brieg level with Ohlau. On 17 December the Emperor told the major general to send Jérôme the order to leave the command of the siege to Vandamme and reach Warsaw on the 21st or 22nd, Jérôme to order Deroy's division from Wartenberg on Lowicz. Höpfner: Lefebvre's summons of the 15th said Napoleon had ordered the works razed immediately after the capture; Blein's plan of attack was meant to force the governor to immediate surrender, and Jérôme approved it; Vandamme meant to set the town seriously on fire and tell the governor of the relief's defeat and of his means to destroy the town; and the whole attack was directed at the town, side A counting on the capitulation once frost robbed the fortress of its wet ditches. The Emperor wrote on 7 January that, Breslau having surrendered, Jérôme was to have Brieg, Kosel and Schweidnitz invested at once, leaving only Neisse and Glatz, and keep a reserve at Breslau.
claims.rationale: The Emperor's and the major general's letters and Foucart's narrative, read from the page images, with Höpfner. The aims moved from a quick capture by Jérôme in person (3 December), through a siege covered against relief, to Jérôme's departure with the command of the siege left to Vandamme (17 December), a storm (23 December) and the bombardment of the town to force surrender; they came from the Emperor and from the commanders, so the phase is left unresolved. Höpfner's statements on Napoleon's expectation and on the order to Deroy cite no document. The passages read do not show what became of the order of 17 December sending Deroy's division on Lowicz; Höpfner and Foucart both have the division arrive before Breslau (our comparison). Foucart's narrative leaves the operations against the place aside by its own footnote and gives those that protected the investment. Lefebvre's statement on razing the works is part of a summons, as Höpfner reports it. English renderings (ours): 'the Emperor to Prince Jérôme. Posen, 3 December 1806'; 'I wish you to have the honour of taking it in person. You will receive through the staff the order to go there with Wrede's division. General Vandamme, with the Württembergers, is going there for his part. The mortars will follow. The major general is sending you instructions on the conduct of the siege. I do not doubt that in four days it will fall into your hands. Deroy's division stays where it is, with half the cavalry'; 'in this way, if Breslau is taken and I have an action in front' (the sentence continues on p. 94); 'of Warsaw, you will be able to be there with Deroy's division. Meanwhile this division will rest' (the end of the sentence begun on p. 93); 'once Breslau is taken, General Vandamme must be sent to invest Brieg at once, without the Württembergers entering Breslau. It will be quite sufficient for you to enter with the Bavarian corps'; 'the major general to Prince Jérôme. Posen, 3 December 1806'; '(the major general informs the prince of the Emperor's instructions)' (Foucart's summary); '.... you will have a bridge thrown over the Oder to establish your communications with General Vandamme; you will take command of the siege...'; '.... General Vandamme is to leave 1,000 men at Glogau'; 'the troops disposable for the siege were too weak to deploy on the upper Oder, where they seemed too exposed to harassment by the Prussian parties from the other fortresses; they therefore restricted themselves for the time being to the ground on the lower Oder and meant to extend on the right up to the Ohlau suburb. The building of two parallels and two mortar batteries, right and left of the Nikolai suburb, was decided, and this suburb was chosen as the point of attack all the more because Colonel Blein hoped to find there an earthen batardeau that could ease the crossing of the ditch'; 'Napoleon had expected the quick surrender of Breslau, but when he had received from his brother the report that he had met serious resistance, he had at once had the order given to the Bavarian division Deroy, which had already been directed from Kalisch on Petrikau, to return as far as Polnisch Wartenberg, so as to be ready to reinforce the troops before Breslau'; 'when Jerome now received from all sides the news that the Prince of Anhalt-Pless was assembling in Upper Silesia a force of 15-16,000 men to relieve Breslau as soon as possible, that line troops were being drawn for it from all the fortified places to form the core of a force that was to be reinforced by recruits and volunteers called to the colours by a proclamation of the aide-de-camp Count Götzen, and when he further learned that the garrison of Schweidnitz was said to have been reinforced by 3000 recruits, so that it now counted 6000 men of infantry and 400 horse, he had, in view of the obstinacy of the governor of Breslau, the troops available at Polnisch Wartenberg ordered up on the 16th, so as to be equal to every possible event. The besieging troops were already suffering exceedingly from the bad season and their comparatively small strength'; 'the inexperience of the allied troops did not allow the siege of Breslau to be pressed as vigorously as the French general officers would have wished. These delays were all the more unfortunate as they left the Prince of Pless, commanding in Silesia, time to gather part of the garrisons of Schweibnitz, Brieg, Neiss and Kosel to come to the place's help'; 'it therefore became indispensable to cover the siege troops very seriously1'; '1. The operations directed against the place do not come within the frame of this work; I shall leave them aside; but it is not the same with those whose aim was to protect the investment'; 'on 15 December two squadrons went up the Oder, one by the right bank, the other by the left, and stayed in observation level with Ohlau on the two roads leading from Brieg to Breslau'; 'the Emperor to the major general. Kutno, 17 December 1806'; 'send a Pole to the camp before Breslau with the order to Prince Jérôme to leave the command of the siege to General Vandamme and to set out in person with all speed, so as to reach Warsaw on the 21st or 22nd. He will order General Deroy to march with his division from Wartenberg, where it must be, on Lowicz'; 'at 2 in the afternoon Jerome had the fortress summoned again by General Lefebvre. He was led with unbandaged eyes to the governor, to whom he had to say much that was flattering about the' (the sentence continues on p. 57); 'defence so far and declare that, if the garrison did not accept the honourable capitulation offered, the town would be turned into a heap of ashes, for which all the means were at hand. The general also added that Breslau was being besieged for the last time, since Napoleon had ordered the fortifications to be razed immediately after the capture. The proposal was rejected, whereupon at 3 o'clock the bombardment was renewed, though not with the violence of the morning, and toward evening it gradually fell silent' (the first words end the sentence begun on p. 56); 'in consequence of this result Colonel Blein had at once laid before Jerome a plan for the attack on the fortress, whose success was to force the governor to immediate surrender. The plan required several false attacks to divert the garrison's attention from the true point of attack, the unrevetted place near the Ohlau gate, where both ditches were to be crossed before daybreak. Jerome had approved the plan, and all materials for its execution had at once been collected. On the 22nd, after Jerome's departure, Colonel Blein had reported to General Hédouville that all was ready for execution'; 'on General Minucci's return, General Vandamme, who had ordered the building of 4 new batteries in order to bring into them a further 8 24-pounders, 6 12-pounders and 2 mortars that were arriving from Glogau, believed he must set the town seriously on fire and inform the governor of the defeat of the relief troops and of the means he possessed to destroy the town. He expected that a population of 60,000 inhabitants would not be sacrificed to the holding of works that owed their preservation only to the mild weather. All this was done without the knowledge of General Hédouville, although this general, as mentioned, was to continue the command in Jerome's name'; 'as already mentioned, and as the engineer Colonel Blein also confirms, the whole attack was directed exclusively at the town. A siege advancing against the works was held to be useless, because all the advantages were on the defender's side owing to his superior artillery, and it was counted on that when frost set in, robbing the fortress of its only means of protection, the wet ditches, the capitulation must follow'; 'the Emperor to the major general. Warsaw, 7 January 1807'; '... Breslau having surrendered, you will give Prince Jérôme the order to invest Brieg, Kosel and Schweidnitz at once, so that only Neisse and Glatz remain, and to keep a reserve corps of infantry, cavalry and artillery at Breslau, where he will stay in person, visiting the three blockades every fortnight, however...'.

citations.locator: Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 4 (1851), p. 52 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: Die zur Belagerung disponiblen Truppen waren zu schwach, um sich an der obern Oder aufzustellen, wo man den Beunruhigungen der preußischen Parteien aus den übrigen Festungen zu sehr ausgesetzt schien; man beschränkte sich daher vorläufig auf das Terrain an der untern Oder und wollte sich rechts bis gegen die Ohlauer Vorstadt ausdehnen. Der Bau zweier Parallelen und zweier Wurfbatterien, rechts und links der Nikolai-Vorstadt, wurde beschlossen, und zwar um so mehr diese Vorstadt zum Angriffspunkt bestimmt, als der Oberst Blein die Hoffnung hegte, daß er daselbst auf ein Batardeau in Erde treffen würde, das den Uebergang über den Graben erleichtern könne.

citations.locator: Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 4 (1851), p. 58 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: Napoleon hatte die schnelle Uebergabe von Breslau erwartet, doch als er von seinem Bruder die Meldung erhalten hatte, daß derselbe auf ernsten Widerstand gestoßen sei, alsbald der bayerschen Division Deroy, die bereits von Kalisch auf Petrikau dirigirt worden war, den Befehl ertheilen lassen, bis Polnisch Wartenberg zurückzukehren, um bereit zu sein, die Truppen vor Breslau zu verstärken.

citations.locator: Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 4 (1851), p. 59 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: Als nun Jerome von allen Seiten die Nachricht erhielt, daß der Fürst von Anhalt Pleß in Oberschlesien eine Macht von 15—16,000 Mann versammele, um so bald als möglich Breslau zu entsetzen, daß hierzu aus allen festen Plätzen Linientruppen herangezogen würden, um den Kern einer Macht zu bilden, die mittelst Rekruten und Freiwilliger, durch eine Proklamation des Flügel-Adjutanten Grafen Götzen zu den Fahnen gerufen, verstärkt werden sollte, als er ferner erfuhr, daß die Garnison von Schweidnitz durch 3000 Rekruten verstärkt sein solle, so daß sie nunmehr 6000 Mann Infanterie und 400 Reiter zähle, ließ er, in Betracht der Hartnäckigkeit des Gouverneurs von Breslau, am 16. die bei Poln. Wartenberg zur Disposition stehenden Truppen herbeibeordern, um allen möglichen Ereignissen gewachsen zu sein. Die Belagerungstruppen litten bei der üblen Jahreszeit und der verhältnißmäßig geringen Stärke bereits ungemein.

citations.locator: Foucart, Campagne de Pologne (1806-1807): Pultusk et Golymin, t. II (1882), p. 96 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: L'inexpérience des troupes alliées ne permettait pas de mener le siége de Breslau aussi vigoureusement que les officiers généraux français l'eussent désiré.
