claims.value: Side B (Prussian): under 22 November the King communicated to the commandants' offices the appointments of the Prince of Anhalt-Pless and of Count Götzen and charged them again, in case of an enemy attack, to defend the fortress entrusted to them most obstinately on their honour and duty until relieved with the help of the Russian operations, and on pain of their heads so to use all their means that they need not surrender it or, after a misfortune, could submit to the strictest court-martial when peace was restored. Höpfner: the government at first meant to hold and defend all the outworks; the suburbs were not cleared, partly in hope of relief by the Russian operations and partly from fear of the burghers' mood. The arrival of the Prince of Anhalt-Pless was delayed until 18 December; a formal relief being no longer possible, it still seemed possible by a surprise attack to communicate with Breslau long enough to throw in 1 or 2 battalions of good troops and supplies and bring out the cash, the horse artillery and the muskets handed in by the burghers. On the 3rd the governor asked in vain for an armistice of 8 days to give the Prince of Pless time for a new relief. The governor gave as reasons for the capitulation the weakness of the garrison and its bad quality, shown in insubordination and heavy desertion; the lack of meat and baking wood; the burning of the town to be expected, since the mortar batteries behind the ruins of the suburbs could not be destroyed; the nearness of the large suburbs; and the frost, since the complete freezing of the Oder and the ditches made a general storm to be feared and the weak garrison could not keep the ice broken. Höpfner answers that insubordination on a larger scale showed itself only 2 days before the surrender, that by the commissariat's figures a 3-week supply of baking wood remained, so that only the lack of meat would remain as a reason, the governor fearing to impose privations on a garrison inclined to desert that no longer counted on relief and fearing that at the moment of a storm it would think more of excesses than of resistance, with the plundering of the town to follow, and that, as he said at Glogau, the burning of the town may be no reason for capitulation, the commandant having to look exclusively to the defence of the works.
claims.rationale: The King's order as Höpfner prints it, and Höpfner's account, read from the page images. The aims moved from defence to the utmost under the King's order, in expectation of relief, to a capitulation once relief failed; they came from the King's order and from the governor and government, so the phase is left unresolved. The governor's reasons are given as Höpfner quotes them; reasons 3-5 are on p. 113, and the end of reason 9 with Höpfner's answer to it on p. 115, read in the OCR only and not used. Höpfner's answers are his judgement. The passage read addresses the order of 22 November to the commandants' offices and does not name Breslau (our reading). English renderings (ours): 'under 22 November the King communicated to the commandants' offices the appointments of the Prince of Anhalt-Pless and of Count Götzen, and added:'; '"I charge you repeatedly, in case of an enemy attack, to defend the fortress entrusted to you most obstinately on your honour and duty, until it is relieved with the help of the Russian operations, and on pain of losing your head you must so use and apply all the means at your command for this purpose that you need not surrender the fortress, or, in case of a misfortune, can submit yourselves on that account to the strictest court-martial after peace has been restored, etc."'; 'it was thus the government's intention to hold and defend all the outworks, but when General Lindener arrived on 6 November he brought it about that this plan was abandoned and the defence restricted to the main wall, surrounded by wide water ditches; only the Nikolai crownwork, the Mühlberg redoubt, the Oder crownwork,' (the sentence continues on p. 48); 'the Ohlau ravelin and the ravelin R. before the Ziegel gate1) were to remain occupied, while the guns of the other outworks were to be brought back to the main wall' (the end of the sentence begun on p. 47; the note refers to Höpfner's plan XVIII of Breslau); 'the clearing of the suburbs, which hindered a vigorous defence, was not done, partly in the hope of a relief by the Russian operations, partly because the government feared the mood of the numerous burghers if it destroyed these extensive buildings before the enemy forced it to, and partly, finally, because it was believed that when the enemy actually appeared it would still be possible to shoot them down and burn them'; 'the arrival of the Prince of Anhalt-Pless was unfortunately delayed until 18 December; the enemy had by now already reinforced himself, but seemed not yet to have all his forces together; if a formal relief was therefore no longer to be thought of, it still seemed possible by a surprise attack to enter into communication with Breslau for long enough to throw in 1 or 2 battalions of good troops and the necessities the town perhaps already lacked, and to bring out the considerable cash holdings, the horse artillery and the muskets handed in by the burghers'; 'at 4 in the afternoon Colonel Duveyrier came, empowered to negotiate the surrender. The bombardment still went on even now. The governor could no more obtain the armistice of 8 days he asked for, to give the Prince of Pless time for a new attempt at relief, than the dispatch of an officer to Kalisch, by whom he wished to make sure whether Russians were approaching or not. Only for arranging the affairs of the town and the garrison were 3 days granted'; 'the governor gave as reasons for the capitulation:'; '"1) the weakness and' (the sentence continues in the next paragraph); '"2) the bad quality of the garrison, which showed itself in insubordination and heavy desertion"' (the end of the sentence begun in the preceding paragraph); '- insubordination on a larger scale, however, showed itself only 2 days before the surrender of the town, when the garrison regarded itself as sold and nothing was done on the government's side to meet such suspicion'; '"6) the lack of meat and of wood for baking"'; 'since the commissariat office showed that it had used 40 Klafter of wood for baking in 10 weeks, and 12 Klafter more were handed over to the enemy, there would by this reckoning still have been a 3-week supply of wood'; 'so only the lack of meat would remain as a reason for the capitulation. The governor was anxious about imposing considerable privations on the weak, fatigued garrison, inclined to desert, and feared that the garrison, which no longer counted on any relief since the news of the Prince of Pless's defeat had spread in the town, would at the decisive moment of the enemy's storm think more of excesses than of resistance, and that a plundering of the town would be the inevitable consequence'; '"7) the burning down of the town that was to be expected, since it had not been possible to destroy the enemy's mortar batteries placed behind the ruins of houses in the suburbs"'; 'we have already stated at Glogau that the burning down of the town may be no reason for capitulation, but that the commandant has to direct his attention exclusively to the defence of the works'; '"8) the nearness of the large suburbs, which made all operations easier for the enemy and made the defence very difficult"'; '"9) the frost that had set in, since the complete freezing of the Oder and the ditches made a general storm to be feared. The breaking of the ice could not be managed by the weak garrison, and the inhabitants requisitioned from the town appeared extremely irregularly, because of the danger to be feared, so that' (the sentence continues on p. 115, which was not registered).

claims.value: Side A attacked: Bodart has the French, Bavarians and Württembergers compel the garrison to surrender the place. Höpfner and Foucart: side A's cavalry appeared before Breslau on 6 December, the left bank was invested on the 7th and the right bank on the 8th; side A opened siege works in the night to the 8th, bombarded the town from 10 December on many days, summoned the fortress on 10, 15 and 25 December, attempted a storm on 23 December that was repulsed, and negotiated the capitulation, signed on 5 January by Höpfner and on 3 January by Foucart. Side B defended the fortress: it destroyed the bridges over the old Oder on 7 December, burnt the suburbs that covered side A, made a sortie on 16 December, which was driven back, repulsed the storm, and did not sortie on 30 December while the relief was fought nearby.
claims.rationale: Coded A_attacked: side A invested, bombarded, summoned and tried to storm the fortress, and side B, apart from the expedition of 7 December and the sortie of 16 December in the passages read, defended it until it capitulated. The phase is left unresolved: the investment followed the Emperor's and Jérôme's orders, while the summonses, the bombardments, the storm and the terms were the commanders' own (claims side-a-command, side-a-objectives). English renderings (ours): Bodart, as in claim bodart-strength; 'on 6 December in the afternoon the enemy thus appeared with his cavalry for the second time on the left bank of the Oder at the suburbs of Breslau, and drove the Prussian cavalry patrols back through the Nikolai suburb up to the works. On the right bank of the Oder the outposts were pushed back to the Weyda, and kept the bridge at Protsch and Hundsfeld occupied. The works fired on the skirmishers who showed themselves at the nearest houses of the suburbs'; 'General Montbrun, preceding the Württemberg division, moved before Breslau by the left bank of the Oder. On the morning of the 6th he was a league from the town, at Höflchen, where he took position; he at once sent a party over to the right bank of the Oder to gather information on the arrival of the Bavarian troops, sent a detachment of 25 men and an officer to take post at Gnichwitz, 20 km from Breslau on the road to Schweibnitz, and dispatched to Schweibnitz a trusted man he had with him, with the task of reporting to him within two days the composition of the garrison of that place'; 'the next day, the 7th, the general formed the investment of Breslau on the left bank; he placed the 2nd regiment of chevau-légers at Gross-Möchbern, the chasseurs à pied at Neukirch and Höflchen (headquarters), the 1st of chevau-légers, 2 squadrons at Klein-Möchbern and the two others at Kleinburg, with a reconnaissance of 25 horse toward Schweibnitz and a post of the same strength at Roth-Kretschen'; 'considering that the Bavarian advance guard enclosed the fortress on the right bank of the Oder too on the 8th, so that the use of the horse artillery on that bank was much restricted, while the Bürgerwerder was threatened by the enemy's works in the night to the 8th, the governor ordered Lieutenant Fiebig to move with the horse artillery into the works on the Bürgerwerder and take over their defence. La-' (the word and sentence continue on p. 54); 'ter these works were gradually also occupied by infantry, 8 heavy guns and some cavalry. The intention was to keep the Bürgerwerder occupied, as an outpost against the enemy's works, for as long as the enemy would allow it from the right side of the Oder, where the work covering the Werder had been left unoccupied' (the first word ends the one begun on p. 53); 'the siege works began as early as the night to the 8th, with so small a number of workers that they had to be limited to building two short parallels toward the projected batteries; one parallel was to rest on the left on the Oder, the other on the left on the Nikolai suburb'; 'on the 10th at 6 in the morning the enemy was able to begin the bombardment against the front at the Nikolai gate and the Dom; the enemy's shells did the burghers' hou-' (the word and sentence continue on p. 55); 'ses considerable damage without setting them on fire. Since in general the enemy's fire was directed more at the town than at the walls, the garrison was far safer on the walls than in its quarters' (the first word ends the one begun on p. 54); 'toward midday the fire fell silent, and after 1 o'clock Captain Desterno, a former Prussian dragoon lieutenant and at the time Jerome's adjutant, appeared as parlementaire and handed over a letter of summons in which the capture of Magdeburg, Stettin, Küstrin and Glogau and the entry of the French into Warsaw were communicated and the hopelessness of a relief was declared. The parlementaire added that the French had also crossed the Vistula at Thorn and had nowhere seen Russians, that the King had already gone back behind Memel, and that Napoleon had declared he would not make peace before he had humbled Russia and broken the alliance with Prussia'; 'on 15 December at 6 in the morning the bombardment thus began anew and lasted until 1 in the afternoon. The town suffered considerably, especially the convent of the Elisabethines, but the fire was put out everywhere'; 'at 2 in the afternoon Jerome had the fortress summoned again by General Lefebvre. He was led with unbandaged eyes to the governor, to whom he had to say much that was flattering about the' (the sentence continues on p. 57); 'defence so far and declare that, if the garrison did not accept the honourable capitulation offered, the town would be turned into a heap of ashes, for which all the means were at hand. The general also added that Breslau was being besieged for the last time, since Napoleon had ordered the fortifications to be razed immediately after the capture. The proposal was rejected, whereupon at 3 o'clock the bombardment was renewed, though not with the violence of the morning, and toward evening it gradually fell silent' (the first words end the sentence begun on p. 56); 'the bombardment was therefore, on the 25th after 1 o'clock, o-' (the sentence continues on p. 80: 'opened again'); 'pened again and lasted until 3 o'clock. At that time Colonel Duveyrier, general staff officer of General Vandamme, appeared with the summons to surrender, with the most boastful statements about the advantages won against the Prince of Pless as well as in Poland and Prussia. The governor gave a refusal' (the first words end the sentence begun on p. 79); 'on 23 December at 6 in the morning it became apparent that the enemy, under the protection of the fire and of those demonstrations, was trying to cross the wet outer ditch at the ravelin R. by two cask bridges, so as to storm the fortress from there'; 'only at 5 o'clock could the first raft be brought into the outer ditch; it was 30 feet long, and 3 others of 12-15 feet had to be brought in to reach the far bank. The sappers, inexperienced in such work, had been able to bind the rafts together only slowly; a drunken officer had come onto the rafts and also greatly hindered the workers; and finally a thoughtless shout, and the leap of a French sapper non-commissioned officer into the water to fasten the rafts to the palisades of the enveloppe under attack, had drawn the attention of an' (the sentence continues on p. 65); 'artilleryman on the Ohlau ravelin; he had fired a round of canister at the place of the noise, and at once the guns of the Bernhard and Taschen bastions, which commanded the enveloppe, and the infantry garrison of the adjacent walls had joined in this fire. Two enemy soldiers carrying a raft were shot at the very beginning of the fire, the other carriers ran away, and the enemy saw himself forced to retreat with considerable loss. A French officer who was on the rafts had to surrender with some privates' (the first words end the sentence begun on p. 64); 'on 5 January Colonel Duveyrier appeared again, and the points of capitulation were signed by both sides, not without disputes, representations and counter-representations, after 6 o'clock'; 'the governor of Breslau at once resumed the negotiations he had broken off. On 3 January at 9 in the evening the capitulation was signed'; 'in consequence of the news of the return of part of the Bavarian troops from South Prussia against Breslau, the government on 7 December sent Artillery Lieutenant Fiebig with half of the newly raised horse battery, some infantry and 30 horses to the right bank of the Oder, to destroy all the bridges over the old Oder and at the same time to demolish the casemates of the abandoned work at the Paßschleuse, where the old Oder leaves the new above Breslau'; 'since the enemy's tirailleurs lodged themselves in the houses of the Nikolai suburb and of the Schweidnitz Anger and harassed the foremost palisade tambours and even the communication between the Nikolai gate and the Scheeren bastion lying below it, the Nikolai suburb was set on fire in the evening at 6 o'clock.1)'; 'on 16 December too the enemy kept quiet, and since the governor received the report that the besieger had withdrawn the guns from the batteries, he ordered that a detachment of 2 officers - Lieutenant Lehsten of the infantry regiment Thile and Lieutenant Seelstrang of the cuirassier regiment Henckel - 60 marksmen and 80 horsemen with 300 workers should advance from the Nikolai gate, clear the suburb of the enemy and destroy the enemy's works'; 'toward 1 o'clock at midday the sortie broke out, without a definite leader having been named, but it was met by a lively fire from the ruins of the burnt-down houses in the Nikolai suburb, into which it had incautiously gone, and was driven back with the loss of 1 officer - Lieutenant Lehsten - and 10 men dead and 7 missing. The cavalry brought back 10 prisoners'; 'on 30 December at 6 in the morning it was reported from the Schweidnitz and Ohlau gates that firing of heavy guns and small arms could be heard and that the village of Dürgoy was burning'; 'at 11 o'clock the garrison was assembled to make a sortie in case the enemy should be beaten. The fog now grew thicker; one could observe no further, but only heard that the fire moved further and further away in the direction of the Zobtenberg until toward 3 o'clock, so that the relief had been beaten'.

citations.quote: Die Franzosen, Bayern und Württemberger (zus. 27.000 M. mit 52 Feld- und Belagerungsgeschützen) unter Pz. Jerôme Bonaparte nötigen die preußische Besatzung (6.000 M. mit 272 Geschützen) unter Gen.-Lt. v. Thiele zur Übergabe des Platzes.

citations.locator: Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 4 (1851), p. 51 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: Am 6. Dezember Nachmittags erschien somit der Feind mit seiner Kavallerie zum zweitenmal auf dem linken Oder-Ufer an den Vorstädten von Breslau, und trieb die preußischen Kavallerie-Patrouillen durch die Nikolai-Vorstadt bis gegen die Werke zurück. Auf dem rechten Oder-Ufer wurden die Vorposten bis an die Weyda zurückgedrückt, und behielten die Brücke bei Protsch und Hundsfeld besetzt. Die Werke feuerten auf die Plänkerer, die sich an den zunächst gelegenen Häusern der Vorstädte zeigten.

citations.locator: Foucart, Campagne de Pologne (1806-1807): Pultusk et Golymin, t. II (1882), p. 95 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: Le général Montbrun, précédant la division wurtembergeoise, se portait devant Breslau par la rive gauche de l'Oder. Le 6 au matin, il était à une lieue de la ville, à Höflchen, où il prenait position; il faisait aussitôt passer un parti sur la rive droite de l'Oder pour prendre des informations sur l'arrivée des troupes bavaroises, envoyait un détachement de 25 hommes et un officier prendre poste à Gnichwitz, à 20 kil. de Breslau sur la route de Schweibnitz, et expédiait à Schweibnitz un homme de confiance qu'il avait près de lui avec mission de lui rapporter dans deux jours la composition de la garnison de cette place.

citations.locator: Foucart, Campagne de Pologne (1806-1807): Pultusk et Golymin, t. II (1882), p. 95 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: Le lendemain 7, le général formait l'investissement de Breslau sur la rive gauche; il plaçait le 2e régiment de chevau-légers à Gross-Möchbern, les chasseurs à pied à Neukirch et Höflchen (quartier général), le 1er de chevau-légers, 2 escadrons à Klein-Möchbern, les deux autres à Kleinburg avec une reconnaissance de 25 chevaux sur Schweibnitz et un poste de même force à Roth-Kretschen.

citations.locator: Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 4 (1851), p. 53 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: In Betracht, daß die bayersche Avantgarde die Festung auch auf dem rechten Oder-Ufer am 8. einschloß, somit die Benutzung der reitenden Artillerie auf diesem Ufer sehr beschränkt, dagegen der Bürgerwerder durch die feindlichen Arbeiten in der Nacht zum 8. bedroht wurde, befahl der Gouverneur dem Lieutenant Fiebig, mit der reitenden Artillerie in die Werke auf dem Bürgerwerder zu rücken und die Vertheidigung derselben zu übernehmen. Spä-

citations.locator: Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 4 (1851), p. 54 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: ter wurden diese Werke allmälig auch durch Infanterie, 8 schwere Geschütze und einige Kavallerie besetzt. Man beabsichtigte den Bürgerwerder, als einen Vorposten gegen die feindlichen Arbeiten, so lange besetzt zu behalten, als dies der Feind von der rechten Oderseite her gestatten würde, wo man das den Werder deckende Werk unbesetzt gelassen hatte.

citations.locator: Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 4 (1851), p. 53 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: Die Angriffs-Arbeiten begannen bereits in der Nacht zum 8. mit einer so geringen Zahl von Arbeitern, daß man sich darauf beschränken mußte, zwei kurze Parallelen nach den projektirten Batterien zu erbauen; die eine Parallele sollte sich links an die Oder, die andere links an die Nikolai-Vorstadt lehnen.

citations.locator: Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 4 (1851), p. 54 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: Am 10. Morgens 6 Uhr war der Feind im Stande, das Bombardement gegen die Front am Nikolai-Thor und den Dom zu beginnen; die feindlichen Wurfgeschosse fügten den Bürgerhäu-

citations.locator: Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 4 (1851), p. 55 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: sern erheblichen Schaden zu, ohne zu zünden. Da im Allgemeinen das feindliche Feuer sich mehr auf die Stadt als auf die Wälle richtete, so befand sich die Besatzung auf diesen weit sicherer als in ihren Quartieren.

citations.locator: Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 4 (1851), p. 55 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: Gegen Mittag schwieg das Feuer, und nach 1 Uhr erschien der Kapitain Desterno, ehemaliger preußischer Dragoner-Lieutenant und zur Zeit Adjutant Jerome's, als Parlamentair und überreichte ein Aufforderungsschreiben, in welchem die Einnahme von Magdeburg, Stettin, Küstrin und Glogau, der Einzug der Franzosen in Warschau mitgetheilt und die Hoffnungslosigkeit für einen Entsatz ausgesprochen wurde. Der Parlamentair fügte hinzu, daß die Franzosen auch bei Thorn die Weichsel überschritten und nirgends Russen gesehen hätten, daß der König bereits bis hinter Memel zurückgegangen sei und Napoleon erklärt habe, nicht früher Frieden zu machen, als bis er Rußland gedemüthigt und das Bündniß mit Preußen gesprengt habe.

citations.locator: Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 4 (1851), p. 56 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: Am 15. Dezember Morgens 6 Uhr begann das Bombardement somit aufs Neue und dauerte bis 1 Uhr Nachmittags. Die Stadt litt bedeutend, besonders das Kloster der Elisabethinerin, doch wurde das Feuer überall gelöscht.

citations.locator: Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 4 (1851), p. 56 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: Um 2 Uhr Nachmittags ließ Jerome die Festung abermals durch den General Lefebvre auffordern. Derselbe wurde mit unverbundenen Augen zum Gouverneur geführt, dem er viel Schmeichelhaftes über die

citations.locator: Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 4 (1851), p. 57 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: bisherige Vertheidigung sagen und erklären mußte, daß, wenn die Besatzung die angebotene ehrenvolle Kapitulation nicht annähme, die Stadt in einen Aschenhaufen verwandelt werden würde, wozu alle Mittel vorhanden wären. Auch fügte der General hinzu, daß Breslau zum Letztenmale belagert würde, indem Napoleon befohlen habe, gleich nach der Einnahme die Festungswerke zu schleifen. Der Antrag wurde zurückgewiesen, worauf um 3 Uhr das Bombardement erneuert wurde, jedoch nicht mit der Heftigkeit als am Morgen, und gegen Abend verstummte es allmälig.

citations.locator: Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 4 (1851), p. 79 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: Das Bombardement wurde daher am 25. nach 1 Uhr wie-

citations.locator: Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 4 (1851), p. 80 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: der eröffnet und dauerte bis 3 Uhr. Um diese Zeit erschien der Oberst Duveyrier, Generalstabs-Offizier des Generals Vandamme, mit der Aufforderung zur Uebergabe unter den prahlerischsten Angaben über die errungenen Vortheile gegen den Fürsten von Pleß, so wie in Polen und Preußen. Der Gouverneur ertheilte eine abschlägige Antwort.

citations.locator: Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 4 (1851), p. 62 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: am 23. Dezember um 6 Uhr Morgens zeigte es sich, daß der Feind unter dem Schutz des Feuers und jener Demonstrationen den nassen Vorgraben bei dem Ravelin R. durch zwei Tonnenbrücken zu überschreiten suchte, um von dort die Festung zu stürmen.

citations.locator: Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 4 (1851), p. 64 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: Erst um 5 Uhr hatte das erste Floß in den Vorgraben gebracht werden können; es war 30′ lang und man hatte noch 3 andere von 12—15′ einbringen müssen, um an das jenseitige Ufer zu gelangen. Die Sapeurs, unerfahren in dergleichen Arbeiten, hatten das Zusammenbinden der Flöße nur langsam zu Stande bringen können; ein betrunkener Offizier war auf die Flöße gekommen und hatte die Arbeiter ebenfalls sehr behindert, und endlich hatte ein unüberlegter Zuruf und der Sprung eines französischen Sapeur-Unteroffiziers ins Wasser, um die Flöße an den Pallisaden der angegriffenen Enveloppe zu befestigen, einen

citations.locator: Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 4 (1851), p. 65 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: Artilleristen auf dem Ohlauer-Ravelin aufmerksam gemacht; er hatte eine Lage Kartätschen nach dem Orte des Geräusches gefeuert, und alsbald waren in dies Feuer die Geschütze des Bernhard- und Taschenbastions, welche die Enveloppe kommandirten, und die Infanterie-Besatzung der anliegenden Wälle eingefallen. Zwei feindliche Soldaten, die ein Floß trugen, wurden gleich beim Beginn des Feuers erschossen, die übrigen Träger liefen davon und der Feind sah sich genöthigt, den Rückzug mit ansehnlichem Verlust anzutreten. Ein französischer Offizier, der sich auf den Flößen befand, mußte sich mit einigen Gemeinen gefangen geben.

citations.locator: Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 4 (1851), p. 111 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: Am 5. Januar erschien der Oberst Duveyrier abermals, und die Kapitulationspunkte wurden von beiden Theilen nicht ohne Streitigkeiten, Vor- und Gegenvorstellungen, nach 6 Uhr unterzeichnet.

citations.locator: Foucart, Campagne de Pologne (1806-1807): Pultusk et Golymin, t. II (1882), p. 112 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: Le gouverneur de Breslau reprenait aussitôt les négociations qu'il avait rompues. Le 3 janvier à 9 heures du soir, la capitulation était signée.

citations.locator: Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 4 (1851), p. 52 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: In Folge der Nachricht von der Rückkehr eines Theiles der bayerschen Truppen aus Südpreußen gegen Breslau sandte das Gouvernement am 7. Dezember den Artillerie-Lieutn. Fiebig mit der Hälfte der neu errichteten reitenden Batterie, einiger Infanterie und 30 Pferden auf das rechte Oder-Ufer, um alle Brücken über die alte Oder zu zerstören, und zugleich die Kasematten des verlassenen Werkes an der Paßschleuse, beim Ausfluß der alten Oder aus der neuen oberhalb Breslau, zu demoliren.

citations.locator: Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 4 (1851), p. 53 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: Da sich die feindlichen Tirailleurs in die Häuser der Nikolai-Vorstadt und des Schweidnitzer Angers einnisteten, die vordersten Pallisadentambours und sogar die Kommunikation zwischen dem Nikolai-Thor und dem unterhalb liegenden Scheeren-Bastion beunruhigten, so wurde Abends um 6 Uhr die Nikolai-Vorstadt in Brand gesetzt.¹)

citations.locator: Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 4 (1851), p. 57 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: Auch am 16. Dezember verhielt sich der Feind ruhig, und da der Gouverneur die Meldung erhielt, daß der Belagerer die Geschütze aus den Batterien zurückgenommen habe, so befahl er, daß eine Abtheilung von 2 Offizieren — Lieutenant Lehsten vom Infanterie-Regiment Thile und Lieutenant Seelstrang vom Kürassier-Regiment Henckel — 60 Schützen und 80 Reitern mit 300 Arbeitern aus dem Nikolai-Thor vorgehen, die Vorstadt vom Feinde säubern und die feindlichen Arbeiten zerstören sollte.

citations.locator: Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 4 (1851), p. 57 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: Gegen 1 Uhr Mittags brach der Ausfall, ohne daß ein bestimmter Führer ernannt worden, vor, wurde aber aus den Trümmern der niedergebrannten Häuser in der Nikolai-Vorstadt, in welche man unvorsichtig einging, durch ein lebhaftes Feuer empfangen und mit dem Verluste von 1 Offizier — Lieutenant Lehsten — und 10 Mann Todten und 7 Vermißten zurückgetrieben. Die Kavallerie brachte 10 Gefangene zurück.

citations.locator: Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 4 (1851), p. 86 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: Am 30. Dezember Morgens 6 Uhr wurde vom Schweidnitzer- und Ohlauer-Thor gemeldet, daß man Feuern aus grobem Geschütz und kleinem Gewehr höre, und daß das Dorf Dürgoy brenne.

citations.locator: Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 4 (1851), p. 87 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: Um 11 Uhr wurde die Garnison versammelt, um für den Fall, daß der Feind geschlagen würde, einen Ausfall zu machen. Der Nebel wurde nun stärker; man konnte nicht weiter beobachten, sondern hörte nur, daß das Feuer sich in der Richtung des Zobtenberges bis gegen 3 Uhr mehr und mehr entfernte, der Entsatz mithin geschlagen sei.

claims.value: Side B held a permanent fortress. Höpfner: the arming began on 19 October; time was too short to restore the works fully, raise the parapets and make bonnets, cover and banquette, and the fortress had only two engineer officers; the defence was restricted on 6 November to the main wall with its wide water ditches and a few outworks, the Dom and the Springstern being drawn in later and the enveloppe held only by day by marksmen and Jäger; the Bürgerwerder works were held as an outpost; the main wall was unrevetted at the Schweidnitz and Ohlau gates, and the enveloppe, the bridge and the batardeau near the Ohlau gate were secured by palisade retrenchments under the canister fire of the adjacent works; the munition lay mostly in a single magazine with weak vaults. Side A: from the night to the 8th it dug two short parallels, one resting on the Oder bank 10-12 feet above the water; it built batteries from the night to the 9th and gun positions on the right bank; from the night to the 12th it extended the parallels and began second parallels and a parallel with a battery on the right bank 400 paces from the Oder crownwork; it laid out the left second parallel in saw-tooth form, dug cuts into the Nikolai suburb and zigzags joining the parallels, and worked at new batteries on the 19th, and Vandamme ordered 4 new batteries. Höpfner judges the siege works very irregular: the batteries were very irregularly built, the guns stood behind embrasures raised toward the front, and the mortars were mostly behind ruins of the suburbs and woodpiles.
claims.rationale: Coded both_fortified: side B defended permanent works, and side A dug parallels, approaches and batteries under the fortress's fire. The fortress is permanent (inherited); side A's works were made for the siege on its commanders' dispositions (commander-created); one claim carries one phase, so it is unresolved. A coding that counted only the defended fortress would give B_fortified. Höpfner's Plan XVIII was not inspected. English renderings (ours): 'when on 19 October, at the instance of the engineer brigadier General Lindener, the arming works of Breslau began, the government had at once had the guns taken to the outworks and suitably placed, and had also ordered the palisading of these works, the repair of the drawbridges, etc.'; 'for a complete restoration of the works, for raising the parapets as required, making bonnets and cover, and building the banquette, the time was too short with so extensive an enceinte. The fortress had only two engineer officers, and the garrison was too weak to contribute materially to the works'; 'it was thus the government's intention to hold and defend all the outworks, but when General Lindener arrived on 6 November he brought it about that this plan was abandoned and the defence restricted to the main wall, surrounded by wide water ditches; only the Nikolai crownwork, the Mühlberg redoubt, the Oder crownwork,' (the sentence continues on p. 48); 'the Ohlau ravelin and the ravelin R. before the Ziegel gate1) were to remain occupied, while the guns of the other outworks were to be brought back to the main wall' (the end of the sentence begun on p. 47; the note refers to Höpfner's plan XVIII of Breslau); 'only later, when the garrison had received some reinforcement, were the important and already palisaded outworks, the Dom and the Springstern, also drawn into the defence'; 'the enveloppe that surrounded the fortress was to be occupied only by day, by single marksmen and Jäger'; 'considering that the Bavarian advance guard enclosed the fortress on the right bank of the Oder too on the 8th, so that the use of the horse artillery on that bank was much restricted, while the Bürgerwerder was threatened by the enemy's works in the night to the 8th, the governor ordered Lieutenant Fiebig to move with the horse artillery into the works on the Bürgerwerder and take over their defence. La-' (the word and sentence continue on p. 54); 'ter these works were gradually also occupied by infantry, 8 heavy guns and some cavalry. The intention was to keep the Bürgerwerder occupied, as an outpost against the enemy's works, for as long as the enemy would allow it from the right side of the Oder, where the work covering the Werder had been left unoccupied' (the first word ends the one begun on p. 53); 'for want of a good plan of Breslau, already on 17, 18 and 19 December the engineer Colonel' (the sentence continues on p. 63); 'Blein had reconnoitred the works on the left bank of the Oder as thoroughly as possible and in doing so established that the main wall was not revetted at two extended places, namely at the Schweidnitz and Ohlau gates; that before the wet main ditch, over 120 feet wide, there was an enveloppe of earth, covered at its salient angles by lunettes with retired flanks; that these works were indeed provided with storm-poles and palisades, but were occupied only before the revetted front of the Nikolai gate, against which the siege works had so far been directed; and finally that the outer ditch surrounding the enveloppe had a width of 60-70 feet and a depth of 6-7 feet' (the end of the sentence begun on p. 62); 'the storm could hardly succeed unless the garrison was very inattentive or treachery was counted on. The enveloppe near the Ohlau gate, the Ohlau bridge and the batardeau over the main ditch near the Ohlau gate were secured by palisade retrenchments and lay under the strongest canister fire of the adjacent works'; 'of finished munition, and of loose powder and iron munition, there were very considerable stores, which for the' (the sentence continues on p. 49); 'greater part were housed in a single magazine under the cavalier of the Taschen bastion. Light fell into this magazine through an open tower, and the vaults were weak, so that a bomb, if it fell unluckily, could blow the magazine and with it a great part of the town into the air' (the end of the sentence begun on p. 48); 'the siege works began as early as the night to the 8th, with so small a number of workers that they had to be limited to building two short parallels toward the projected batteries; one parallel was to rest on the left on the Oder, the other on the left on the Nikolai suburb'; 'since the bank of the Oder where the first-named parallel rested lay 10-12 feet above the water level, and from the parallel one could reach a sandbank lying there unseen from the Bürgerwerder, this junction gave the besieger great advantages'; 'in the night to the 9th the besieger began building the projected batteries, and a third battery was worked at in the prolongation of the street of the Nikolai suburb; on the right bank of the Oder too, at the Elbing and behind the Mönchswiese, gun positions were completed'; 'in the night to the 12th the enemy extended the left parallel nearer to the Oder and the right parallel to the capital of the Hunde bastion, and began a second parallel on the left at the Oder and on the right of the suburb. A parallel with a battery was also laid out on the right side of the Oder, 400 paces from the Oder crownwork'; 'in the night to the 13th the besieger extended the two second parallels begun the night before and laid out the one on the left in saw-tooth form, to place in it light guns that were to take the artillery on the Bürgerwerder in the rear'; 'on 13 December 2 companies of French sappers and miners, of 66 men each, arrived, and were used at once to dig cuts into the Nikolai suburb and to the right of the churchyard there, and to build batteries in the second parallels'; 'in the nights to the 14th and the 15th the besieger worked at the zigzags connecting the two parallels right of the suburb of St. Nikolai, and in the latter night the batteries built one after another were armed: the 2 batteries of the first parallel right of that suburb, counted from the left wing, with 2 heavy mortars and 3 light howitzers, and with 2 light mortars and 3 heavy howitzers; the batteries of the second parallel with 2 light howitzers and 4 6-pounders and with 4 light howitzers and 4 6-pounders respectively, these last batteries for firing on the batteries of the place. On the right bank of the Oder 8 field howitzers could be brought into action. Two 24-pounders and a heavy mortar had not yet arrived from Glogau'; '19 December passed quietly; the enemy worked only at extending the second parallel to the right and at new batteries'; 'on General Minucci's return, General Vandamme, who had ordered the building of 4 new batteries in order to bring into them a further 8 24-pounders, 6 12-pounders and 2 mortars that were arriving from Glogau, believed he must set the town seriously on fire and inform the governor of the defeat of the relief troops and of the means he possessed to destroy the town. He expected that a population of 60,000 inhabitants would not be sacrificed to the holding of works that owed their preservation only to the mild weather. All this was done without the knowledge of General Hédouville, although this general, as mentioned, was to continue the command in Jerome's name'; 'as for the siege works of the French, they were conducted very irregularly and could probably lead to the goal only under such peculiar circumstances'; 'the French batteries were built very irregularly; the guns in them, for the majority cannon and howitzers and mostly Prussian, stood behind embrasures raised toward the front; the elevating wedges had been taken out and the barrels laid on the transoms of the carriages, so that the guns were elevated between 15 and 20 degrees and their projectiles went at random into the town'; 'the mortars were mostly placed behind ruins of the suburbs and woodpiles, especially in the area of the burnt-down church of St. Nikolai'.

citations.locator: Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 4 (1851), p. 47 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: Als auf Veranlassung des Ingenieur-Brigadiers General Lindener am 19. Oktober die Armirungs-Arbeiten von Breslau ihren Anfang nahmen, hatte das Gouvernement sofort die Geschütze nach den Außenwerken abführen und angemessen aufstellen lassen, auch die Pallisadirung dieser Werke, die Instandsetzung der Zugbrücken ꝛc. angeordnet.

Die Festung hatte nur zwei Ingenieur-Offiziere, und die Besatzung war zu schwach, um zu den Arbeiten wesentlich beizutragen.

citations.locator: Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 4 (1851), p. 48 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: Die Enveloppe, welche die Festung umgab, sollte nur bei Tage durch einzelne Schützen und Jäger besetzt werden.

citations.locator: Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 4 (1851), p. 53 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: In Betracht, daß die bayersche Avantgarde die Festung auch auf dem rechten Oder-Ufer am 8. einschloß, somit die Benutzung der reitenden Artillerie auf diesem Ufer sehr beschränkt, dagegen der Bürgerwerder durch die feindlichen Arbeiten in der Nacht zum 8. bedroht wurde, befahl der Gouverneur dem Lieutenant Fiebig, mit der reitenden Artillerie in die Werke auf dem Bürgerwerder zu rücken und die Vertheidigung derselben zu übernehmen. Spä-

citations.locator: Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 4 (1851), p. 54 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: ter wurden diese Werke allmälig auch durch Infanterie, 8 schwere Geschütze und einige Kavallerie besetzt. Man beabsichtigte den Bürgerwerder, als einen Vorposten gegen die feindlichen Arbeiten, so lange besetzt zu behalten, als dies der Feind von der rechten Oderseite her gestatten würde, wo man das den Werder deckende Werk unbesetzt gelassen hatte.

citations.locator: Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 4 (1851), p. 62 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: In Ermangelung eines guten Planes von Breslau hatte bereits am 17., 18. und 19. Dezember der Ingenieur-Oberst

citations.locator: Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 4 (1851), p. 63 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: Blein die Werke auf dem linken Oder-Ufer so gründlich als möglich rekognoszirt und hierbei ermittelt, daß der Hauptwall an zwei ausgedehnten Stellen, nämlich am Schweidnitzer- und Ohlauer-Thor, nicht bekleidet sei; daß sich vor dem nassen, über 120′ breiten Hauptgraben aber eine Enveloppe von Erde befände, die auf ihren vorspringenden Winkeln durch Lünetten mit zurückgezogenen Flanken gedeckt würde; daß diese Werke zwar mit Sturmpfählen und Pallisaden versehen, aber nur vor der revetirten Front des Nikolai-Thores, gegen welche bisher die Angriffs-Arbeiten geführt worden waren, besetzt seien; daß endlich der Vorgraben, der die Enveloppe umgab, eine Breite von 60—70′ und eine Tiefe von 6—7′ habe.

citations.locator: Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 4 (1851), p. 65 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: Der Sturm konnte nicht füglich gelingen, wenn die Besatzung nicht sehr unaufmerksam war oder auf Verrätherei gerechnet wurde. Die Enveloppe in der Nähe des Ohlauer-Thores, die Ohlauer-Brücke und der Batardeau über den Hauptgraben nahe dem Ohlauer-Thor waren durch Pallisaden-Abschnitte gesichert und lagen unter dem stärksten Kartätschfeuer der anliegenden Werke.

citations.locator: Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 4 (1851), p. 48 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: An fertiger Munition, so wie an losem Pulver und Eisen-Munition, waren sehr bedeutende Vorräthe vorhanden, die gro-

citations.locator: Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 4 (1851), p. 49 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: ßentheils in einem einzigen Magazin unter dem Kavalier des Taschen-Bastions untergebracht waren. In dieses Magazin fiel das Licht durch einen offenen Thurm, auch waren die Gewölbe schwach, so daß eine Bombe, wenn sie unglücklich fiel, das Magazin und mit ihm einen großen Theil der Stadt in die Luft sprengen konnte.

citations.locator: Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 4 (1851), p. 53 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: Die Angriffs-Arbeiten begannen bereits in der Nacht zum 8. mit einer so geringen Zahl von Arbeitern, daß man sich darauf beschränken mußte, zwei kurze Parallelen nach den projektirten Batterien zu erbauen; die eine Parallele sollte sich links an die Oder, die andere links an die Nikolai-Vorstadt lehnen.

citations.locator: Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 4 (1851), p. 53 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: Da das Oder-Ufer da, wo sich die erstgenannte Parallele anlehnte, 10—12′ über dem Wasserspiegel belegen, und man von der Parallele, ungesehen vom Bürgerwerder, auf eine daselbst liegende Sandbank gelangen konnte, so gewährte dieser Anschluß dem Belagerer große Vortheile.

citations.locator: Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 4 (1851), p. 54 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: In der Nacht zum 9. wurde von Seiten des Belagerers der Bau der projektirten Batterien begonnen, und eine dritte Batterie in der Verlängerung der Straße der Nikolai-Vorstadt gearbeitet; auch auf dem rechten Oder-Ufer beim Elbing und hinter der Mönchswiese wurden Geschütz-Aufstellungen zu Stande gebracht.

citations.locator: Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 4 (1851), p. 55 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: In der Nacht zum 12. verlängerte der Feind die Parallele links näher gegen die Oder, und die Parallele rechts bis zur Kapitale des Hundebastions, und begann eine zweite Parallele links an der Oder und rechts von der Vorstadt. Auch wurde eine Parallele mit einer Batterie auf der rechten Oder-Seite, 400 Schritt vom Oder-Kronwerk, angelegt.

citations.locator: Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 4 (1851), p. 56 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: In der Nacht zum 13. verlängerte der Belagerer die in der vergangenen Nacht begonnenen beiden zweiten Parallelen und führte die links gelegene sägeförmig, um in ihr leichte Geschütze aufzustellen, welche die Artillerie auf dem Bürgerwerder in den Rücken nehmen sollten.

citations.locator: Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 4 (1851), p. 56 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: Am 13. Dezember langten 2 Kompagnien französischer Sapeurs und Mineurs, je zu 66 Mann, an, und bediente man sich ihrer sogleich, um Einschnitte in die Nikolai-Vorstadt und rechts vom Kirchhof daselbst zu arbeiten, auch Batterien in den zweiten Parallelen zu bauen.

citations.locator: Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 4 (1851), p. 56 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: In den Nächten zum 14. und zum 15. arbeitete der Belagerer an den Zickzacks zur Verbindung der beiden Parallelen rechts der Vorstadt St. Nikolai, und in der letzteren Nacht wurden die nach und nach gebauten Batterien armirt, und zwar die 2 Batterien der ersten Parallele rechts der genannten Vorstadt, vom linken Flügel an gerechnet, durch 2 schwere Mörser und 3 leichte Haubitzen, und 2 leichte Mörser und 3 schwere Haubitzen, die Batterien der zweiten Parallele durch resp. 2 leichte Haubitzen und 4—6pfünder, 4 leichte Haubitzen und 4—6pfünder; diese letzteren Batterien zur Beschießung der Batterien des Platzes. Auf dem rechten Oder-Ufer konnten 8 Feldhaubitzen in Thätigkeit gesetzt werden. Zwei 24pfünder und ein schwerer Mörser waren noch nicht von Glogau eingetroffen.

citations.locator: Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 4 (1851), p. 61 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: Der 19. Dezember verfloß ruhig; der Feind arbeitete lediglich an der Verlängerung der zweiten Parallele nach rechts und an neuen Batterien.

citations.locator: Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 4 (1851), p. 79 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: Bei der Rückkehr des Generals Minucci glaubte der General Vandamme, der den Bau von 4 neuen Batterien befohlen hatte, um darin noch 8—24pfünder, 6—12pfünder und 2 Mörser, welche von Glogau anlangten, einzuführen, die Stadt ernsthaft in Brand setzen, und dem Gouverneur von der Niederlage der Entsatztruppen, so wie von den Mitteln Nachricht geben zu müssen, die er besaß, um die Stadt zu vernichten. Er erwartete, daß eine Bevölkerung von 60,000 Einwohnern nicht der Behauptung von Werken würde aufgeopfert werden, die ihre Erhaltung nur der gelinden Witterung verdankten. Das Alles geschah ohne Vorwissen des Generals Hédouville, obgleich dieser General, wie erwähnt, im Namen Jerome's den Befehl fortführen sollte.

citations.locator: Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 4 (1851), p. 118 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: Was die Belagerungs-Arbeiten der Franzosen betrifft, so wurden dieselben sehr unregelmäßig geführt, und konnten wohl nur unter so eigenthümlichen Umständen zum Ziel führen.

citations.locator: Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 4 (1851), p. 118 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: Die französischen Batterien waren sehr unregelmäßig erbaut; die Geschütze in denselben, der Mehrzahl nach Kanonen und Haubitzen und meistens preußische, standen hinter nach vorne erhöhten Schießscharten; die Richtkeile waren herausgenommen, die Röhre auf die Riegel der Laffeten gelegt, und dadurch die Geschütze zwischen 15—20° erhöht, so daß ihre Geschosse ins Blaue hinein nach der Stadt gingen.

citations.locator: Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 4 (1851), p. 118 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: Die Mörser waren meist hinter Vorstadtruinen und Holzstößen, namentlich in der Gegend der abgebrannten St. Nikolaikirche, aufgestellt.

open_questions: Deferred: Höpfner's Plan XVIII of Breslau, not inspected; the end of his chapter 15 and the start of chapter 16 (p. 32, the first move against Breslau in November, and pp. 33-35, 37-46, the governor-general of Silesia, Count Götzen's mission and the other Silesian fortresses), and his account of the relief attempts and of the siege between 23 and 30 December and after 30 December (pp. 66-78, 82-85, 88-108), not read beyond the OCR used to find where the siege narrative runs; pp. 108, 113, 115, 117, read in the OCR only (the day the frost set in and Bachiarelli came; the governor's reasons 3-5; the end of reason 9, Höpfner's answer to it and the heading and first items of the list of faults; and the disposition he proposes for a break-out), not cited; the capitulation's text, the summonses, the intercepted letters of the Emperor's letter of 3 December, Lindener's journal, Blein's report, Du Casse's Opérations du neuvième corps and the 'Geschichte der Belagerung von Breslau', which Höpfner cites, not seen; and Foucart, Campagne de Pologne, t. I, pp. 146, 242 (the end of the major general's letter of 22 November and an Emperor's letter expecting Breslau's early surrender), read in the OCR and not used. The contemporary account of the siege in the Lower Silesian Digital Library and Völderndorff's Bavarian history, noted for this entry earlier, were not read: the brief allows two families besides Bodart. No figure seen only in the OCR is restated.

Most consequential gap: side A's strength and guns before Breslau. Bodart's 27,000 men with 52 field and siege guns match no figure in the passages read: the adjutant's assurance of 18 December gave 22,000 after Deroy's arrival, Jérôme's letter of 8 December gave the 2nd division 4,700, the Emperor reckoned the corps on 7 January at more than 30,000 with two units arriving, and Höpfner names the armament of single batteries without a total. A return of the Silesian corps for late December or early January, or the French artillery's account of the siege, could close it; none was found in the pages read.

Disputes kept as separate claims or within them: the garrison (6,000 men with 272 guns, Bodart; 135 officers and 5841 men on 1 January and 6000 at the second investment, of whom 5000 real defenders, with 208 guns on the walls and 46 in reserve or unusable, Höpfner; a fifth of the garrison necessary, the Emperor from intercepted letters); the garrison at the end (116 officers and 5270 men marching out and 240 guns handed over, Höpfner; 5,500 men filing past, Foucart; 135 officers set free on parole, Bodart); side A (27,000 with 52 guns, Bodart; 22,000 with Deroy's 10,000, the adjutant's assurance; the 2nd division 4,700, Jérôme; more than 30,000 with two units arriving, the Emperor); the command after 20 December (the command of the siege left to Vandamme, the Emperor's order of 17 December; Jérôme still commanding through Hédouville while Vandamme acted on his own, Höpfner; Jérôme, Bodart); the investment (the 6th, Höpfner and Bodart; the left bank formed by Montbrun on the 7th and Vandamme arriving on the 8th, Foucart; Vandamme reconnoitring the place on the 7th and the right bank invested on the 8th, Höpfner); Deroy's arrival (about the 18th, Höpfner; on the 20th, Foucart); the storm of 23 December (two accounts in Höpfner: side A seen at 6 trying to cross by two cask bridges at the ravelin R., on the garrison's side; the first raft brought into the outer ditch at 5 near the Ohlau gate, in his account of the attack); the talks of 25-26 December (an armistice refused and then granted and ended by the governor because of the burghers' mood and side A's works, Höpfner; talks for surrender broken off on news of the Prince of Pless's reassembly, Foucart); the capitulation (signed on 3 January at 9 in the evening, Foucart; resolved on the 3rd and signed on 5 January after 6, Höpfner; Bodart's end date 6 January, the evening the gates were handed over in Höpfner); the march-out (7 January, Höpfner; the garrison filing past Jérôme on the 8th, Foucart); and the garrison's dead (13 by Lindener's journal, Höpfner, beside the sortie's 1 officer and 10 men).

Families and dependence: Bodart (a compilation; his sources for this entry were not checked; his 6,000 men are Höpfner's reckoning at the second investment and his 135 officers Höpfner's return of 1 January, while his 272 guns, 27,000 men and 52 guns match no figure in the passages read); Foucart, Campagne de Pologne, t. II, one family with t. I and with Campagne de Prusse (the same author's edition of the French side's documents, from the page images: the Emperor's letters to Jérôme of 3 December and to the major general of 17 December and 7 January, the major general's letter to Jérôme of 3 December, Jérôme's letter to Vandamme of 8 December, and Foucart's narrative, which by its own note leaves the operations against the place aside); Höpfner, Bd. 4 (the Prussian side's history, the same work and family as his first and second volumes; his formation table, read for the Glogau entry, is reused; he cites Lindener's journal, Blein's report, a statement of the French artillery officers, Du Casse and the 'Geschichte der Belagerung von Breslau', and otherwise names no source for the garrison's returns, the councils or the negotiations).
